🟡 **WAN Camera Control / Multi-Axis** — rung 2 source: physics-based camera paths; a claim of stacking up to 3 moves ⚠️ conflicts with the proven one-move rule — stack only with test budget.

records.title: Renderability: Green/Red Lists, Formats, Model Profiles
records.text:
# Renderability: Green/Red Lists, Formats, Model Profiles

What current video models render reliably vs. what fails. Tags and confidence labels: legend in sources.md.

records.title: 1. Green list (reliable)
records.text:
## 1. Green list (reliable)
Single-subject action with one camera move · dialogue in shot/reverse-shot coverage · weather, fog, dust, embers · fire/water/smoke as atmosphere (not as hero physics) · slow reveals · stylized 3D (most forgiving discipline) · high-action anime · UGC/handheld realism · reflections and light rhythm across cuts (Seedance 2.5) · macro/product turns · creatures from image references.

records.title: 2. Red/yellow list (avoid or mitigate)
records.text:
## 2. Red/yellow list (avoid or mitigate)
| Element | Failure | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| **In-frame text — unified rule** | Text, logos, subtitles, formulas render as scribble or drift between frames | Default: ALL exact on-screen text goes to post-compositing (officially confirmed [BD-off]). Three documented exceptions: (a) **static short text locked via master plate** — content frozen in the reference image + prompt lock "exactly this one line, frozen and identical in every frame" (production-proven, platforms-models ch. 13b); (b) 🟡 MiniMax H3 has an official quoted-text channel (visible text in double quotes, verbatim, untranslated [MM-off]) and renders UI/text comparatively stably — syntax documented, quality practitioner-rated: test before relying. Dynamic/changing text stays red everywhere. 🟡 Exception (c) — DESIGNED typography as the product: Higgsfield Marketing Studio's motion-design presets (launch video, hypermotion product ad, 2D and editorial explainer, 3D real-estate flythrough with pricing overlays) render text overlays, numbers and animated charts as the generation's subject, and the vendor shows them "locked, not melting" including minutes of editorial text [H-off, P68 — vendor demo, not frame-checked here]; a different generation class from a video model rendering incidental text. Every word and number is still checked against the script before delivery, and the rule for generative FILM shots is unchanged. 🟡 Exception (a) confirmed on 2.5 by [P54]: a one-word character-intro title generated INTO the Seedream 5.0 Pro still and carried by Seedance 2.5 over 20 s with a spelling lock in the prompt ("the name is Dan — exactly D-A-N, not Dann, not Dane") — single short static word, plate-locked; still the exception. |
| Crowds | Clone extras, melting faces in distance | Multi-variant sheet (production-pipeline ch. 3) with extras as silhouette-distinct CLASSES ("heavy brute" / "light scout") — classes, not outfit variants, kill the clone read; crowds to mid/background; small faces stay unreliable even at high res; fog capped as a visible relation ("everything past the third rank dissolves into fog" — never a distance in metres, SKILL rule 7) hides background glitches at army scale (less needed at 4K, still works) [H-off, P25]; formations (66 dancers in rings around a singer) hold across cuts when positions and facing come from blockout boxes and only the movement is prompted [H-off, P66]; a cast of ten distinct extras saved as one element stops per-shot face regeneration [H-off, P69] |
| Hands + fine object manipulation | Finger errors, object morphing | Close-ups only as short single-action beats, cut away before the fine work; the handling invariant is written once as a lock sentence — inside the beat on the Caption Spine (ch. 12h), as a POSITIVE LOCKS line in the block structure ("ALWAYS by the handle") — there is no separate CRITICAL block |
| Vehicles/wheels/mechanics | Wrong rotation, illogical mechanics | See rescue paths below |
| Long continuous camera moves | Collapse after several moves (proven in 2.5 too) | One move per shot; cuts instead of tours |
| Instrument fingering, precise sports technique | Approximate only | Frame around it; cutaways |
| Physics as hero (glass shattering exactly, complex fluid pours) | Plausible-but-wrong | Describe end state; hide peak behind cut |
| Tiny hero object carrying the beat (a key, a pill, a seed in a hand) | Object morphs, vanishes or changes size between frames; detail vs. size contradiction (ch. 24b) | Cut to an insert as its own short shot at close scale; carry the beat by the character's reaction; object as a prop sheet (production-pipeline ch. 4) |
| Dark, figure-less macro (no scale anchor, no figure, low light) | No scale read, no material read — the model fills with generic texture or invents a subject | Add a scale anchor or a figure (SKILL rule 9 on stylized projects), lift a motivated practical, or replace by a still + ellipsis |
| Continuous approach over distance (a walk/drive/flight that must close the gap on camera) | Scale collapses on the way (same class as wide-shot scale, above); the approach stalls or teleports | Two shots: departure state, arrival state — the distance is an ellipsis (manual cut); never one continuous take |
| Cut back onto the same emissive object (lamp, screen, fire) whose state must match frame-exactly | Brightness, colour temperature and shape differ between takes; the object appears "re-lit" | One state per state sheet (production-pipeline ch. 4); the second view inside the same take, or the object kept in one setup (W10 anchor composition); otherwise accept a grade-side match (post-audio-legal ch. 17) |
| **Wide shots** (stylized 3D; photoreal crowd scale too) | Scale and distance break at wide range; a flat camera path at constant height/speed leaves characters as dots (vendor-confirmed on Higgsfield's own short and its Hell Grind rebuild) | Open the take on a close/medium of the character and transition into the wide inside the same generation; positions locked by the previs/clay render, not by the wide (pixar-look §10) |
| Faces that must stay blank (silent passengers, listeners with no beat) | Model animates them anyway — micro-expressions, drift | Hide by design with a motivated occlusion: reflective glass, backlight silhouette, hat brim, distance — copy-ready GLASS block in video-prompting 12e |
| **Mirror/reflection beats** where a reflected face or pose must match the subject frame-exactly | Reflected face/pose diverges from the subject; reflection doubled, missing, or lagging a beat behind | 🟡 (derivation, not yet [PP]-tested) Reflections as texture/light — glass, water, wet street, chrome — stay GREEN on Seedance 2.5 (§1). For a story mirror beat: Seedance 2.5 only, static camera, ONE readable face in frame — either the reflection alone (subject from behind / over the shoulder) or the subject alone with the mirror as shape (film-craft §2 frame-in-frame); never subject and reflection both readable; otherwise split subject and reflection across a cut. 🟢 Blockout rescue [H-off, P66]: a camera passing THROUGH a mirror held in one 15-s continuous take when the set was blocked as a mirrored twin with both characters moving in sync and the mirror as an opening (production-pipeline ch. 8 protocol b). |

**Feasibility answer ("can this scene be generated?") — fixed shape:** one verdict line (green / yellow with rescues / red), then a feasibility table (the pre-decision form of the rule-11 risk register; once the director decides, kept rows move into the rule-11 register unchanged in meaning): Beat or element | Rating 🟢🟡🔴 | Failure (§2 row) | Rescue (§3) | Decision (keep / rescue / cut — the director's, left blank until they decide). Never answer in prose only and never rewrite the scene silently.

records.title: 3. Rescue paths for red/yellow action elements
records.text:
## 3. Rescue paths for red/yellow action elements
- **Fights/multi-person action:** never one long choreography. Decompose into **attack–reaction beats as separate short clips** (attack = clip, reaction = clip), characters locked via references; the EDIT is the fight choreography. Write contacts + settling per beat (video-prompting ch. 14).
- **Stunt that will not generate → shoot it yourself [H-off, P24]:** two bodies in constant contact over a prop (a struggle for a gun in a car: limbs fused, weapon vanishing) would not converge in text; the feature-film fix was stunt performers in a real car filmed on a phone, fed as MOTION reference — the model laid the cast, interior and light over it. One day of phone footage instead of a week of iterations; the only place a text-to-video-only production stepped outside its rule (production-pipeline ch. 8 phone-shot blocking).
- **Dance/choreography move by move [H-off, P48]:** "'dances' means nothing to Seedance" — write the moves: "two head nods, shoulders rolling one at a time, a knee dip, a finger snap, a quarter spin at the door"; per cut one register ("slow head bob left and right" · "sharp footwork, skips, stomps, quick weight shifts" · "locking style, arms snapping into frozen geometric poses" · "wide arms, shoulder isolations, stopping on the beat"); the track as timing input (video-prompting ch. 14b).
- **Vehicles/wheels:** hide wheel rotation — night/rain (motivated motion blur), framing above wheel height, parallel tracking (wheel detail unreadable), cockpit coverage; wheel close-ups only as short beats with water/mud eruption as distraction.
- **Subject vs. camera motion:** never combine opposing directions (subject runs right + dolly-in = mush) — one motion direction dominates per shot.
- **Animals:** short single beats, no long behavior chains; image reference instead of species name for fantasy/hybrid creatures.
- **Moving crowds:** multi-variant sheet + crowd in mid/background layer only; foreground extras directed individually.
- **Crowd scale — never a number, always three layers [H-off, P25]:** "the prompt never says show a thousand samurai": one sharp warrior up front, a dense crowd behind him, silhouettes fading into the mist — about 40 soldiers read clearly and the brain fills in the rest. Pair with the fog cap (§2) and silhouette classes. A synchronised army drop-into-stance is a legitimate held ENDING STATE (formation reads as drilled, not as animation — the async rule applies to individuals, video-prompting ch. 12).
- **Degradation looks as rescue style:** VHS/CCTV/16mm grain has built-in fault tolerance — a footage format (style-control §6b) is a legitimate rescue for risk shots.

records.title: 4. Format matrix (what each look forgives)
records.text:
## 4. Format matrix (what each look forgives)
| Format | Fit | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Pixar/stylized 3D** | **Excellent — safest "cinema look"** | Stylization absorbs physics/texture errors; audiences expect no real physics. Look definition and evidence: pixar-look.md |
| High-action anime | Excellent | Speed lines/held poses mask model weaknesses |
| UGC/found footage | Excellent | Degradation hides artifacts |
| Photoreal drama, static dialogue | Good with discipline | Reverse plates + framing recycling mandatory |
| Flat 2D/limited animation | Hard | Punishes every wobble; simple motion only (style-control §5b) |
| Photoreal action with hero physics | Hardest | Plan rescue cuts per risk shot |

records.title: 5. Camera & cut rules
records.text:
## 5. Camera & cut rules
One camera verb per shot · fixed camera grammar per sequence in the shot table's Framing column; in the prompt only the one camera line where continuity across cuts demands it (12h element 5 / OPTICS+CAMERA) · lock positions by previs/clay render or plate, not by the take's opener — the establishing wide is a SHOT, not the opening beat, for crowd scale and stylized 3D (§2 wide-shot row); a plain photoreal two-hander may still open wide · never cross the axis (state it) · match cuts across scene borders bind on identical motion · hectic cuts exactly at hard motion = model hiding failure → reject take.

records.title: 5b. Lighting consistency: directional light vs. whole-body brightness [PP]
records.text:
## 5b. Lighting consistency: directional light vs. whole-body brightness [PP]
🟢 **Directional light and whole-body brightness adjectives on the same object are mutually exclusive.** Once a prompt demands a light DIRECTION, phase, or partial shading on an object (moon phase, backlight, terminator, half-shadow, rim light), never pair it with global brightness words for that same object — "bright", "fully lit", "luminous", "brightly glowing", "strong contrast". Whole-body words grab the entire object and override the phase: documented failure — a moon prompted with a side-lit phase (lit side toward a low sun, shadow side away) PLUS "clear bright lunar disc" rendered as a fully lit disc with no shadow side, physically inconsistent with the stated sun position.
🟢 **Instead:** describe light exclusively per direction — which side/surface is lit, which lies in shadow. If contrast is wanted, name the contrast of the LIT EDGE against the background ("the lit edge stands out against the black sky"), never the brightness of the whole object.
Memory hook: a phase instruction only wins when no contradicting brightness word stands next to it.

records.title: 6. Model quick profiles (for shot assignment)
records.text:
## 6. Model quick profiles (for shot assignment)
**Prompt technique is a project decision (SKILL rule 4); the containers per model are in ch. 21 / 12g.** Seedance 2.0 know-how holds on 2.5 unless a documented difference says otherwise (video-prompting ch. 14b table: timestamps, multi-view references, action wording, constraint words).

Per-shot decision rule: Seedance 2.5 whenever references, edits, long takes or choreography matter; Seedance 2.0 for simple UGC-realism shots and drafts (production-pipeline ch. 11); H3 for 2D/anime line quality, quoted on-screen text or cheap hosted 2K; Veo 3.1 for photoreal environments; Kling 3.0 for directed movement in stylized-photoreal; Grok for stylized fast tests; Flux 3 Video for calm dialogue. Ties → the motion ladder; name the pick in the slate.
| Model | Strengths | Limits / slop accent |
|---|---|---|
| **Seedance 2.0** | resolution: native 4K last documented on Higgsfield under HF-CS4-HIST@2026-08 (platforms-models ch. 13 archive, unverified since — working assumption 1080p until the live output dropdown shows 4K), 15-s takes, cost/quality champion, UGC home turf | Peak at take end fails; plastic skin tendency; [P56] keeps 2.0 for SIMPLE shots where 4K crispness matters (Aug 2026), but its physics and reference placement lost to 2.5 in every staged test |
| **Seedance 2.5** | 30-s takes (extension chains ≈60 s; 180 s beta is Dreamina-only), 50 refs (30i/10v/10a incl. @Clay Render + voice refs), **edit suite** (region/timestamp-scoped, camera-perspective, green-screen, subject-swap, audio-category — video-prompting ch. 14b), complex continuous camera, choreography with weight, in-shot transformations, multi-stage emotions, reflections, skin texture; best adherence with eight references and best emotion progression in the [P56] four-model test | ~2× price; resolution platform-dependent (Higgsfield 1080p since Aug 2026, one practitioner aggregator run at 1080p/30 s with sound, Sep 2026 [P19], Dreamina 480/720p; 4K on Higgsfield only via Upscale / FLUX 3 Video Upscaler per HF-WEB@2026-09-04 — no native 2K/4K verified; other surfaces: read the live form); real-face references are rejected by most hosted surfaces (moderation plan + face-grid fallback: post-audio-legal ch. 20); baked-in artifacts → upscaler; logic decays with take length; in-frame text still broken |
| **Veo 3.1** | Polished cinematic realism, environments, ingredients/first-last/extension | Physics-correct motion fights stylized looks |
| **Kling 3.0** | Directed movement, multi-shot storytelling, strongest stylization of the photoreal class, MotionControl | Style drift per generation (ch. 21 sequence rule); 2–3× rerolls for anime |
| **MiniMax H3 (Hailuo 3)** | 2D/anime line quality, official quoted-text channel + stable UI/text 🟡, LoRA style lock, physics (passes glass test), cheap, native 2K hosted, Ref2VA omni mode (9i/3v/3a), V2V edits without masks, L2VA (events before the image) | Plastic under realism demands [P43, P56 — plastic tears, skin worse than 2.x], audio loops 🟡 [W], one beat per shot [MM-off], weak IP moderation 🟡 [W] (legally risky — practitioners market the local build for "copyrighted and unrestricted" content, post-audio-legal ch. 20); [P56] also logged an unprompted camera move in a static-camera test and a screen-direction flip between shots, while lyric text in a music-video test rendered cleanly |
| **Flux 3 Video** (BFL; on OpenArt and Higgsfield, Aug 2026) 🟡 [P56] | 20-s takes, 1080p, native audio; the most natural DIALOGUE voice of the four models in the test and a strong documentary / interview register; sharp faces and close-ups | Weakest prompt adherence in the test (camera-move chains and staged actions dropped), takes reference images literally (a white sheet background carried into the scene), comic drift, fast unintelligible delivery — route calm dialogue-heavy shots, not choreography; priced above 2.5 on OpenArt; no syntax profile here — write it in the project's technique (SKILL rule 4), camera mid-prompt as on Seedance (12g), with the platform's live docs as the receipt |
| **Grok Imagine 1.5** | Native stylization bias (anime/cartoon/art-directed), fast, cheap, native audio | Drifts cartoonish on photoreal intent; negatives unreliable; resolution: ch. 21 Grok line |
| **Wan 2.6/2.7/3.0** (open-weight family; version per surface — Higgsfield: Wan 3.0 / 3.0 Prime, OpenArt: WAN 2.7 and a WAN 3.0 page, 2026-09-04) | Open-weight, LoRA, multi-shot, reference-to-video, 1080p, budget | Less polished than top class |
| **PixVerse** | Fast social iteration, transition mode | Not for long-form/high-end. No syntax profile here — if a PixVerse prompt is requested, say so and write it in the project's technique (SKILL rule 4), camera mid-prompt as on Seedance (12g), with the platform's live docs as the receipt |

⚠️ **Resolution/duration cells above are capability notes, not receipts.** Before any resolution or duration goes into a Render Slate `Settings` row: apply the platform-ui-workflows.md output-configuration rule — use the LOWER verified value for the surface (Higgsfield: 1080p / 30 s under HF-CS4@2026-09-04), ask the user to read the live model/plan dropdown, and write `unverified` in the slate if neither is possible. Never write a reference key you did not check.

No universal winner: run the motion ladder (post-audio-legal ch. 19) per style/model before committing.
⚠️ **Retired/wound down — do not plan pipelines on:** Sora 2 (wind-down 2026) · Runway Gen-3 family (retired Jul 2026) · OpenArt Workflows (sunset Jan 2026). Current surfaces + retirement tracking: platform-ui-workflows.md.

---
name: ai-film-production
description: Plan, write and prompt AI-generated video/film end to end — treatments, scripts, shot lists, asset orders (character sheets, locations, props), video prompts and a multi-session production bible — for Seedance 2.x, Veo 3.x, Kling 3.x, Hailuo/H3 and the Higgsfield Cinema Studio pipeline (plus Runway, fal.ai, OpenArt UI routing). Use whenever the user writes, reviews or fixes a treatment, script, screenplay, storyboard, shot list, scene, asset order or generation prompt whose footage will be GENERATED by a video model; asks "can this scene be generated?", "make this script AI-ready", "plan my AI film"; names Seedance, Veo, Kling, Higgsfield, Runway or fal; or resumes an AI film project. Trigger without the word "AI" when the production path is clearly generative video. records.title: AI Film Production
records.text:
# AI Film Production

**v3.4 · 2026-09** — universal: nothing project- or person-specific.

Write, plan and prompt AI-generated film so no shot looks AI-generated: design around the models' failure classes (identity drift, physics errors, anatomy, interaction, broken in-frame text) instead of fighting them in post.

**Language rule.** Conversation, treatments, scripts, shot tables, slate labels, intent lines and risk registers follow the user's language. **Every prompt code block is English** — every vendor-verbatim control string is English; a translated lock is an untested lock. Two exceptions: a dialogue/VO line stays verbatim in the project's dialogue language (bible section B1; on H3 inside its language tag, `<d>[Japanese] …</d>`), and prompt text the director supplies stays verbatim. Technical terms (`references/glossary.md`), IDs and @tags stay English/ASCII.

**Role.** The agent is the director's full crew — DoP, editor, gaffer, script consultant, line producer; the user is the director and the only approval instance. Advise, then follow the call.
- Flag a real risk ONCE per project, in plain language, and never gate on it — only canon gaps (rule 14) and status moves (rule 12) wait for the director. Never cite chapter numbers at the user.
- A heard warning goes into the bible shot board's `Risk → rescue` cell as `ACCEPTED by user <date>`, a declined offer into the decision log; without a bible, once per session.
- A feeling → propose the craft; an instruction → execute it and note its effect once; a named style → start from the recipes.

**Economy and division of labour — the model is a specialist partner.** A video prompt states only what is explicitly necessary for the beat or deliberately steered for the look (the **economy doctrine**). Every further line costs three times: complexity, contradiction risk (an agent is not consistent across thirty prompts), and budget, where it pushes a load-bearing line out. Prompts that locked every axis, quantified every value and hung an exclusion list on every reference ran at roughly 80 % rejects; a 250-word prompt on the same take reproduced its beat structure four of four [PP 2026-09-14, `references/sources.md`]. The rejects were prompt faults, not render faults: contradictions inside the prompt, technical instead of scenic description, absolute sizes without a scale, missing acting directions, inconsistent timing and geography, metaphors that pull off-theme, working lines dropped between revisions. Length is not limited — a prompt that states what belongs in it, once, limits itself (ch. 12h). The default allocation (🟢 house doctrine, every video model):

| The model owns by default — nothing is written here unless deliberately steered | The agent always owns — exactly this is written |
|---|---|
| camera composition inside a named shot size · in-take cutting and cut timing · character motion and body mechanics · material rendering · light behaviour and falloff · transitions · the physics of simple contact actions | what is in the scene · what happens in which order, and the state each beat ends in · which reference carries which single job · canon fidelity (the written beat) · one camera line where continuity across internal cuts requires it |

- Steer a model-owned axis only when (a) the canon says it in so many words, (b) the look needs exactly that control — a lens, an aperture, a colour temperature, a light direction — or (c) a failed run of THIS take showed the model doing that one thing against the canon. Then one statement, in the beat or block it concerns, listed in the slate's `Crew choices`.
- "I don't trust the model" is not a reason for any line.
- A *run* is one batch of 4 rolls judged as one iteration (rule 15); a fault "shown in a run" means the batch failed on that axis, never one odd roll. A new steer or a first exclusion after ONE failed run; restating an existing exclusion after TWO.

**Scope & version.** Reference rules carry a confidence label (🟢 verified/production-proven · 🟡 single-source · 🔴 marketing claim), source tags, ⚠️ for a source conflict and [PP] for first-party production evidence — legend, source tiers and registry: `references/sources.md`. Unlabeled text in SKILL.md, workflows, production-bible, film-craft, director-recipes, genre-baselines and worked-example is house doctrine and ranks 🟢. **The RECEIPT line** — every stored or user-facing platform claim, every slate `Run in` row and every bible section B1b row, in this order:

`<KEY> · <platform> → <access route: web UI | MCP | ChatGPT | API | plugin> → <account/workspace/project, if known> → <surface/tool> → <model + mode id ("UI label")> → <vendor version | unversioned UI @ YYYY-MM-DD> → <source URL> · <state: live-checked YYYY-MM-DD | from reference KEY>`

`KEY` = `<LEDGER-PREFIX>@<the day YOU checked the live surface>` (`HF-WEB@2026-09-10`); prefixes and the full KEY grammar: `platform-ui-workflows.md` §0. Receipt states: rule 17.

records.title: What to load — the loading map
records.text:
## What to load — the loading map

Nothing for the always-rules: they bind unread. **Resume** → the project bible, then only what the active runbook step names. **New project** → W1 (`workflows.md`) → `genre-baselines.md` when a genre is named or evident, else story-structures ch. 23a. **Any prompt** → the runbook (W3 shot · W4 scene · W5 repair) → ONLY the project's technique chapter (video-prompting ch. 12h, or ch. 12, or style-control §6c) plus ch. 12b, 14 and 14b for Seedance, 12g and platforms-models ch. 21 for Kling/Veo/Grok/H3, renderability §2–3, and the target platform's § in `platform-ui-workflows.md`. **Stills** → production-pipeline ch. 5, style-control §2–4, image-model-logic 24b and 24i. **Look questions** → director-recipes, genre-baselines, pixar-look. Never load `video-prompting.md`, `platform-ui-workflows.md` or `production-pipeline.md` whole — the large reference files open with a contents block; read the entry you need. Never open a second technique chapter; open `sources.md` only when a label is disputed.

records.title: Citation convention — how chapters and sections are addressed
records.text:
## Citation convention — how chapters and sections are addressed

`ch. N` is a GLOBAL chapter ID: 1–11 and 16 = production-pipeline · 12, 12b–h, 14, 14b, 15 = video-prompting · 13, 13b, 21 = platforms-models · 17–20 = post-audio-legal · 22 (22a–e) = production-bible · 23 (23a–g) = story-structures · 24 (24a–i) = image-model-logic · 25 (W1–W10) = workflows. Chapters 12–25 and 16 may be cited bare (`ch. 14b`); chapters 1–11 always carry the stem (`production-pipeline ch. 8`) — a bare `ch. N` with N ≤ 11 means production-pipeline, never the file you are reading. `§N` is FILE-LOCAL: style-control §1–7, renderability §1–6, film-craft §1–9, pixar-look §1–10, platform-ui-workflows §1–8 (its unnumbered preamble is §0); a `§` without a file name means the file you are reading. Bible template headings are SECTIONS (`bible section B3`); bible session rules are `22a rule N`; runbooks are `W1`–`W10`; the rules of this file are `rule 1`–`rule 17`.

records.title: Precedence — when two instructions collide
records.text:
## Precedence — when two instructions collide

1. An explicit director instruction wins (Role).
2. Project canon (bible → approved script → approved treatment) beats any skill default.
3. The always-rules beat reference-file text — EXCEPT where a reference chapter names the rule it narrows ("Reconciled with SKILL rule N", "exception to SKILL rule N"); such an exception applies inside its stated scope only.
4. Reference chapters beat examples and templates (worked-example.md, the 22b template) where they differ.
5. Between two reference rules: (a) a ⚠️-marked conflict is settled by the sentence next to the marker; (b) a rule scoped to the model, platform or scenario at hand beats a general rule — a technique chapter beats ch. 12g for a named model; (c) otherwise 🟢 outranks 🟡 outranks 🔴, and at equal label the source tier decides (sources.md legend): vendor documentation and first-party measurement [PP] > platform tutorials and established practitioners > single social finds, which never win a frontal contradiction with a vendor statement without striking proof. A rule learned on an older model version holds on the newer one until version-specific information says otherwise.
6. Routing table, always-rules, per-prompt checklist and Workflow are cumulative layers (what to read → constraints → order of work → order of deliverables), not competitors.

Still open after this ladder → name both rules to the director in one line and ask.

records.title: Task routing — which file is the spine for which task
records.text:
## Task routing — which file is the spine for which task

**Order of operations for every request.** (1) Resume and new-project entry: the loading map above. (2) A job with a runbook → that runbook (`workflows.md` W1–W10) is the SPINE and names which further files to open and when. (3) Otherwise the topmost matching row below is the spine; other rows are opened only when the spine, the checklist or a genre filter line points there. (4) Every step that writes a prompt runs the per-prompt checklist; its file pointers are mandatory reads for that step.

| Task at hand | Spine — read the named part, not the whole file |
|---|---|
| Resume a running project; "where were we"; project state, asset registry, shot status | `references/production-bible.md` — the project's bible, then only what the active runbook step names |
| New project with a genre named or evident ("action film", "horror short", "doc-style" …) | `references/genre-baselines.md` — craft defaults, recipe shortlist, per-genre file filters |
| A story or idea needs its dramaturgical shape; story completeness check | `references/story-structures.md` — intake gate 23a, container library, causal change lint 23g |
| Write, fix or review ANY video prompt | `references/workflows.md` W3 (W4 scene, W5 repair) → the project's technique chapter (rule 4; filled examples worked-example.md §3b for A, §3 for B) → ch. 14–14b; the checklist then pulls the platform receipt and `renderability.md` §2–3. A fix/review returns: verdict line → numbered findings (quoted line → problem → change) → the rewritten prompt as a Render Slate — never a silent rewrite; the first finding looked for is over-instruction (rule 15) |
| Prompt syntax for H3 / Kling / Veo / Grok (not live UI controls) | `references/platforms-models.md` ch. 21 (copy-ready instance per model) + `references/video-prompting.md` 12g — verify the live syntax before a paid run |
| A live UI/MCP/API surface, setting, mode, limit, receipt or learning link for Higgsfield / fal.ai / Runway / OpenArt / Arcads / ChatGPT | `references/platform-ui-workflows.md` — §0, then the platform's § (§6 when choosing between platforms); the archived Cinema 3.5 table (platforms-models ch. 13) is never a current selector list |
| Treatment, script, shot list; asset orders (sheets, plates, props); still-model choice; QA batches; reverse angles and coverage; a new camera angle on an existing clip, generated or filmed | `references/production-pipeline.md` — deliverable shapes ch. 2, asset order ch. 3, model matrix ch. 5, QA ch. 10, coverage ladder ch. 16 |
| Any stylized look; any prompt that uses reference images; image-model mechanics | `references/style-control.md` — §2 GPT Image 2.5 · §3 Nano Banana Pro · §4 Soul Cinema/Seedream · §5b medium motion grammar · §6c medium-emulation packages and the Master Style Block (technique C) · §7 reference integration |
| Position, size, count or exclusion problems in image prompts; a model "ignoring" an instruction | `references/image-model-logic.md` ch. 24 — writing contract 24b, control ladders 24c–e, negation channels 24f, edits 24g, still-prompt lint 24i |
| Feasibility lint of a script or shot; assign models; rescue risky action; lighting consistency | `references/renderability.md` — answer shape under §2, rescues §3, lighting §5b, model profiles §6 |
| Cinematography, editing, light, colour or dramaturgy advice; "how should this scene feel" | `references/film-craft.md` |
| A style starting point; a director or DoP is named | `references/director-recipes.md` — selection index, then the named recipe; each closes on a Verify line |
| Pixar / stylized-3D projects | `references/pixar-look.md` — figure-anchor rule §8, figure-less method §9, previs-to-AI case study §10 |
| Post, upscaling, music and voices, continuity ledger, legal and AI disclosure, real-face moderation, take verdict order | `references/post-audio-legal.md` — ch. 19 holds the binding verdict order and the six review passes |
| The storyboard-first production model; "how do we go about this"; storyboard, camera setup system, take/cut table, animatic or blockout stage | `references/workflows.md` W10 — nine gated stages from idea to production takes |
| Which model to run a session, a subagent or a batch on; handing skill work to another agent | `references/agent-models.md` — measured cold-test results per model, what to delegate and what never, the cold-test protocol |
| First production task ever; a term is ambiguous | `references/worked-example.md` (one complete delivery in both techniques) · `references/glossary.md` (one meaning per term) |

records.title: The 17 rules that always apply (no file read needed)
records.text:
## The 17 rules that always apply (no file read needed)

1. **Stills-first, anchor as reference.** Every shot is an approved still before video — the look is won in the image. Attach the still as a tagged reference (`@anchor_1A`), never as a start/end frame; a multi-shot take attaches every internal shot's anchor, scoped to its own shot and time range (production-pipeline ch. 1).
   - A literal frame only for a frame-exact join on a route with NO extension mode, or a first→last-frame INTERPOLATION between two stills approved for THIS shot — a controlled move, not a performance.
   - Seedance 2.5 continues with `video_extension` from the source clip (ch. 14b).
2. **Plan in shots (4–12 s), generate in takes.** Take length ≤ 15 s on Seedance 2.0, ≤ 30 s on 2.5; always an explicit ENDING STATE, never a dramatic peak at a take's end.
   - A calm single-event beat = ONE shot per take; beats that need a cut for pace or coverage = 2–3 labelled internal shots with HARD CUTs; montage/commercial ≤ 12–15 cuts per 30 s (ch. 14b).
   - First pass: a draft batch of 4 at 480/720p in the take's planned length (10 s when nothing else is planned; W3 step 5); the production take: rule 13.
3. **Complexity budget per shot.** One main action; default two acting characters — more only with the large-cast doctrine (production-pipeline ch. 3 and ch. 8, renderability §2–3); a camera line only where continuity across internal cuts or the canon demands it. Split everything else across cuts.
4. **The prompting technique is a project decision — never one-size-fits-all.** The menu, with no default: **A Caption Spine** (ch. 12h — a caption in prose) · **B block structure** (ch. 12 — labelled blocks, explicit per-axis control) · **C Master Style Block + story** (style-control §6c — a seven-layer medium description, then a short story part in prose beats; its terminal MUST NOT APPEAR list is its one negation).
   - Decide WITH the director at intake, together with project type, look and video model (W1 step 3): the question lists all three entries, recommends one with its reason in one sentence and, when the choice is not obvious, offers the test — ONE draft batch (4 rolls) of one beat per candidate, same references. Never a bare "confirm C"; an ASSUMED technique ships with the same menu line.
   - Persist the decision in bible section B1: one technique per project, changed only by a documented decision, never per prompt, never two in one prompt.
   - Model containers hold in every technique (ch. 12g, ch. 21): H3's official field schema; Veo 3.1 opens on the one camera line (Google's formula); camera-first on Kling 3.x and a leading style qualifier on Grok Imagine are 🟡 recommendations. Seedance 2.0 know-how holds on 2.5 unless a documented difference says otherwise (ch. 14b table): timecode beats are a 2.5 form, on 2.0 the beats are numbered shots.
5. **References: plan the set before the prose; attach → address.** Prose is for what happens, references are for what persists.
   - One line per reference inside the prompt, one job each — A: one positive job sentence, no exclusion list (ch. 12h); B: the ACTIVE REFERENCES shape, an exclusion clause only after a non-transfer has occurred (ch. 12). A reference used only IN PART names its part positively; a video or audio reference used in part also names what is not taken, from the first run — a scoping clause, not a negation.
   - Stable @names verbatim everywhere; the literal token per surface: ch. 12b. The upload-order list is the slate's `Inputs` row, never prompt text.
   - Seedance 2.5: every element that must persist gets its own pool reference; per take ≤ 8 distinct image subjects and 1–5 video/audio subjects (trim order when over budget: ch. 12b).
6. **Write the visible, in generator logic (ch. 24b).** A prompt is a scene description for a caption-trained generator, not instructions to a reader.
   - Micro-cues instead of emotion labels; cause before reaction; appearance and emotion positive; a class's default state before its exceptions (24a); each lock once, where its technique puts it; ZERO contradictions — the model blends conflicts silently and never warns.
   - Length: a still prompt stays inside the routed model+version's measured word budget (24b item 8) — past it, correct instructions are dropped silently. A video prompt has no house word ceiling (a vendor-documented target stays — H3 Ref2VA, ch. 21): it states what belongs, once, and stops when complete (ch. 12h, the eight checks). After a failure REPLACE, never append.
   - Exclusions are a channel decision (24f). Video: a concrete ban once, in its beat or block; a style/genre/quality ban only as technique C's single terminal list — A and B carry the look positively (evidence and condition: ch. 14). Diffusion stills: negative field only, bare nouns. AR stills (GPT Image 2.5, Nano Banana Pro): one style-repulsion anchor and one Avoid list (style-control §2). A list holds protected world rules plus errors that actually occurred, never prophylactic quality words; a failed exclusion is restated once, after two failed runs, next to what it protects (ch. 12b).
7. **Scale and distance are relational; look values are deliberate, never default.**
   - Write size and distance only as visible relations between two things in the frame — "his back level with the top step", "twice the size of the lantern beside it" — never metres or unit counts: a generated scene has no tape measure, so a measure is unread or lands on an arbitrary object. One relation per axis, once. [PP 2026-09-14]
   - Lens (mm or FOV°), aperture, colour temperature (Kelvin), speeds and percentages are LOOK CONTROLS: permitted in every technique, never default, written once only when the look needs exactly that value (values: 12c/12d; stills: 24b item 5) and listed in `Crew choices`.
   - Numbers belong in numeric channels: layout boxes, masks drawn at size, blockout geometry, the bible's camera-setup table (24c/24d).
8. **Red-list lint before delivery.** No readable in-frame text, no frame-exact mirror beats, no fine hand manipulation on screen (a hand close-up only as one short single-action beat, cut away before the fine work, with a handling-invariant lock), no readable-face crowds, no hero physics — ellipsis over simulation (renderability §2). Every kept risk gets a rescue cut (rule 11).
9. **Stylized 3D needs an anchor:** a figure in frame (default, all models) or — for figure-less environment stills on GPT Image 2.5 in bright light — the style-forcing blocks (pixar-look §9); dark scenes add a self-generated bright style anchor (production-pipeline ch. 1). A style word alone is ignored.
10. **Audio — diegetic only; the score is built in post.** Sound is written where the beat has it (inside the beat on A, the AUDIO block on B), in ONE audio notation (ch. 12b); the platform's audio switch is a `Settings` value, never prompt text. Never music in the video model: whenever the take runs with audio on, the music exclusion is written ONCE as a plain sentence (A's closing sentence, B's AUDIO block, C's terminal list) and never again (12b bleed remedy: rule 6).
11. **Deliver as Render Slates.** Every prompt the user is expected to execute ships with the slate table directly above its code block (contract below); the code block stays pure prompt. After the last slate of the delivery: the **risk register** `| Shot | Kept risk | List (red/yellow, renderability §2) | Why kept | Rescue |`, one row per kept red/yellow element. A treatment carries risk and rescue in its shot-table columns; the bible shot board's `Risk → rescue` cell is canon for both.
12. **The production bible is canon** (ch. 22, template 22b). ONE living bible per project, created before the first asset order — even for a job that looks like a single session. Resume: read it first; close: update it last. Statuses move only on director approval. Before it exists, canon = the treatment or script the director approved in this conversation, recorded at the first close; once it exists: not in the bible = not canon.
13. **Repair before reroll (Seedance 2.5).** An approved take with a local fault is fixed with the edit suite — region/timestamp-scoped, camera-perspective, green-screen, audio-category edits — or extended, never regenerated wholesale (ch. 14b, W5). The production take is a NEW generation of the locked prompt at target resolution and full planned duration, never a `video_extension` of the draft; from then on every fix to it is an edit or an extension.
14. **Canon before invention — never guess story content.** Every content claim in a prompt is READ from the treatment, script or bible for that exact beat, then checked once against scene physics and story logic; every prompt is re-read against its canon passage before delivery.
   - *Canon-bound — never guessed:* what happens in the beat · who is present and where · dialogue/VO text · prop and wardrobe STATE changes · time of day, weather and light state where plot or continuity fixes them · anything that changes the story.
   - *Craft-fillable — only WHEN a line is needed:* the shot-size word · the one camera line · look controls (rule 7) · light direction within the plate's light side · micro-cues for the stated emotion · blocking inside the stated geography · diegetic sound — each listed in `Crew choices` for the director's veto.
   - Canon silent on a canon-bound item → ship a `PROPOSAL — not canon` block in that prompt's place (shape below), continue with the rest of the batch, never fill the gap. Approval = an explicit yes or a picked option (22a rule 3); "go on" is not — ask once, naming the options. Treatments, scripts and shot lists are the agent's DRAFT until approved — a prompt written from one says so in its `Intent` row.
   ```
   PROPOSAL — not canon · Shot 1B · the treatment does not say how the cat reaches the lever
   A) the cat climbs the coiled rope beside the lever (uses the rope in @loc_lamproom, plants nothing new)
   B) the wind slams the hatch and the cat is thrown toward the lever (needs a plant in 1A)
   Pick A or B, or give the beat — the prompt follows.
   ```
15. **Prompt first, model last.** Most presumed "model limits" are prompt faults [PP]. Before blaming the model, switching method or cutting the shot, lint YOUR prompt — over-instruction first, then contradictions, a missing lock on exactly the failing aspect, stacked instructions on one axis (they average, not add), meta-commentary.
   - One iteration = one prompt revision judged on ONE batch of 4 rolls: one or two odd rolls = reroll, do not touch the prompt; three or four bad rolls on one axis = failed iteration (production-pipeline ch. 10).
   - Repair per iteration, one line each: REMOVE (sentences on model-owned axes, second mentions) → CHANGE one line → ADD one line; the word count never rises.
   - After the 3rd failed iteration: rewrite short from scratch — never longer than the prompt that failed — AND move the failing aspect to a stronger channel: reference, sketch, mask, seed, other model (24b item 7). A model limit only after that clean prompt has failed twice on at least two channels → other model (renderability §6) or the shot's rescue path. Budget 10–15 iterations per shot; then simplify the SHOT — split it, drop an action, change the angle — not the words.
16. **The causal chain is load-bearing — no event without cause, no rescue without plant.** Every event is CAUSED by what precedes it and CAUSES what follows ("therefore/but", never "and then"); coincidence may create trouble, never resolve it; every payoff is planted. Before proposing ANY script, treatment or beat change, run the causal change lint (ch. 23g) and name the change's upstream cause and downstream consequence IN the proposal.
17. **Version receipt before an external generation.** Every UI/MCP/API recommendation and every stored platform fact carries the project KEY (RECEIPT line in bible section B1b) in exactly one state: `live-checked <date>` — you or the director read the live form or schema in THIS session; only then may a new date, price or account appear · `from reference <KEY>` — no live read this session: cite the newest stored receipt with ITS check date, account and cost left empty. A from-reference slate is a complete, valid deliverable; a live-checked date for a check you did not perform is fabrication. Never gate drafting on a live value.

records.title: The per-prompt checklist — every new still or video prompt, edit or extension, in this order
records.text:
## The per-prompt checklist — every new still or video prompt, edit or extension, in this order

1. **CANON** — read the treatment/script/bible passage for this exact beat or asset; a canon-bound gap → rule 14.
2. **ROUTE** — platform, surface, model and mode BEFORE writing; mint or reuse the project KEY with its receipt state (rule 17). Stills: model matrix (production-pipeline ch. 5) + style mechanics (style-control §2–4). Seedance 2.5: `t2v` / `omni_reference` / `video_edit` / `video_extension`, written as `id ("UI label")` per the mode table in platform-ui-workflows §1 — and first ask: is this a repair or extension of an existing take (rule 13)?
3. **REFERENCES** — one reference per element that must persist, pulled from the pool by exact tag, one *reference line* each in the technique's shape (glossary), counted against rule 5's ceiling.
4. **WRITE** — in the project's technique and the model's container (rule 4), in generator logic (rule 6): describe, don't argue; positive first; one instruction per axis; must-have element first; relations, not measures (rule 7); nothing on a model-owned axis unless deliberately steered.
5. **LINT** — still: the eight checks of ch. 24i. Video: the seven measures into the slate's `Lint` row (format: slate contract; definitions: the "Lint before delivery" paragraph of ch. 12h — shared by every technique; reading that one paragraph is not opening a second technique chapter); a failed measure is repaired, never delivered with a justification. Then the red-list lint with a rescue for every kept risk (rule 8) and the canon re-read — fix or flag (rule 14).
6. **DELIVER** — the Render Slate above the code block, then the risk register (rule 11).
7. **AFTER THE RESULT** — review in six passes, in this order: identity → continuity → timing → camera → audio → style (the take-level checks of the project's Verify line; verdict order post-audio-legal ch. 19). A result you cannot see is never described: put the six passes to the director as questions and record THEIR answers as the review (`director review, TK03`); without one the take keeps its status (`TKnn — review pending (director)` in the bible Handoff). A local fault on an approved take → W5; a global fault, or a model without a scoped edit route → back to the prompt in the rule-15 order.

records.title: The Render Slate — delivery wrapper for every executable prompt
records.text:
## The Render Slate — delivery wrapper for every executable prompt

A Markdown table immediately above the code block (a key-value list where tables don't render). Applicable rows only, in this order; omit unknown rows — no placeholders, no invented values; labels in the user's language, IDs and @tags ASCII-verbatim. Filled instances: worked-example.md §3b (technique A) and §3 (technique B).

| Row | Content |
|---|---|
| `Render ID` | `<PROJECT>_<Shot ID>__<platform-model>__<operation>__P<nn>` (ID discipline below) |
| `Intent` | One director-readable line: shot, action, decisive creative constraint; opens with `Canon: DRAFT — approve the treatment before running` when the treatment is not yet approved (rule 14) |
| `Crew choices` | Two halves. *Left to the model:* the axes this prompt deliberately does not instruct. *Decided by the crew:* the craft-fillable decisions the canon did not fix, every look control included — the director's veto list (rule 14). Example: `Left to the model: composition inside the shot sizes, cut timing, body mechanics, wet fur and brass, the light bloom. Decided by the crew: medium-wide → close-up → medium-wide; one camera line, low at the cat's shoulder height, looking toward the lever; the rain shake as the reaction cue.` |
| `Run in` | The RECEIPT chain platform → access route → project/workspace → surface/tool → model → mode as `id ("UI label")`, then the KEY and its receipt state (rule 17). Example: `Higgsfield → web UI → project LIGHTCAT → Video → Seedance 2.5 → t2v (UI label unverified — read the live task dropdown) — from reference HF-WEB@2026-09-04, not live-checked this session; confirm model, mode and workspace on the live form before Generate` |
| `Settings` | Executable UI values: ratio, resolution, duration, audio, any non-default control. Never repeat a UI setting inside a video prompt — no double control (exceptions: the take's duration where the technique's form carries it; a control the project's A/B proved inert, platform-ui-workflows §1; the Higgsfield DoP tool, production-pipeline ch. 16). Still prompts keep the canvas/aspect/grid line in the prompt, first, AND set it in the UI (style-control §2) |
| `Lint` | Every video prompt, in any technique: `words n · negations n/1 · numerals outside TC n/0 · absolute measures n/0 · double mentions none · contradictions none · beats complete` (definitions and counting rules: ch. 12h; `words` is a count for the rule-15 ratchet, never a ceiling; each numeral exception is a look control named in Crew choices) |
| `Inputs` | One line per reference, numbered in slot/upload order: `n. @tag = what it is — its one job`; say whether the anchor is a reference or a literal start/end frame (rule 1); on a platform with a persistent library say "Elements, no upload"; add `🟡 token form unverified — match the upload label before running` when the surface could not be seen (ch. 12b) |
| `Store in` | Known platform project/folder or local destination — omit rather than invent |
| `Handoff` | Linked work only: an extension boundary state, an edit source + scope (`edit source …__T2V__P01__TK03`), a continuity boundary |

**ID discipline.** The Shot ID is project canon from the shot board (`1A`, `SQ03_SC12_12A`) — never invent sequence or scene data; without a board, `<scene><letter>` in delivery order and the delivered shot table IS the board. The Render ID appends platform-model, operation and prompt revision (`…__HF-SD25__T2V__P01`; a rewrite is `P02`); a Take ID (`TK01` …) exists only once a generated result exists — in the bible and review notes, never in a slate. No title yet → ask once and hold the row, never a placeholder; a one-off prompt outside any project omits the row and says so. Full grammar — tokens, variants, asset prompts, multi-shot takes, instance chain, first-session bootstrap: production-bible 22e; read it before a project's first Render ID.

records.title: Workflow
records.text:
## Workflow

1. **Intake** — run W1 (`workflows.md`), then settle only what the conversation has not settled — format and look, length and platform, deliverable, model stack, prompting technique (rule 4), dialogue language and its route (ch. 18; default native, proven by one draft-resolution test take) — then the bible (W1 step 5). **Interaction contract** (full text: W1 step 3): before the first deliverable at most ONE grouped question message — the story-gate gaps plus the open intake items; everything unanswered ships on a labelled default, marked `ASSUMED` where it appears and logged in the bible decision log. "Just do it" or an unavailable director → proceed on ASSUMED values, canon-bound gaps as PROPOSALs (rule 14); afterwards one question at a time, only when a canon-bound item blocks the next step.
2. **Write shot-first, canon-first** — re-read the canon passage before every beat (rule 14); a treatment or shot list that is itself the deliverable is a DRAFT proposal from the intake, asking only for story gaps (23a), never per beat. Numbered shots, a fixed camera grammar per sequence, object-anchored blocking (never screen directions), @asset names, match-action cues (shot-writing grammar and dialogue scenes: production-pipeline ch. 2 and ch. 7).
3. **Lint** against `renderability.md`; rewrite or rescue every hit.
4. **Pre-production sections in the treatment** — build order, set build and casting per production-pipeline ch. 1, 3 and 4; the style contract = one bible paragraph derived from the recipe, never pasted as-is: stills → the model's style section (style-control §2–5); technique A → the 8–10 STYLE tokens (ch. 12h); B → distributed into the blocks (ch. 12 placement rule 1); C → the Master Style Block (§6c).
5. **Deliver** per the routing table's file for the format — treatments end each scene with its shot table; its Shot IDs ARE the bible shot board's IDs, assigned once and never renumbered (the board mirrors Shot, Len and Risk → rescue; Framing, Action and Assets stay in the approved treatment):
   `| Shot ID | Len | Framing | Action | Assets | Risk | Rescue |`
   `| 1A | 4 s | medium-wide, static, low, from the room corner | wet cat squeezes through the hatch, shakes, looks up at the dark lamp | @cat @loc_lamproom @anchor_1A | 🟡 wide opening (stylized 3D) | open on the medium, arrive at the wide by transition |`
   Framing = shot size, camera height/direction and move in words, never degrees or lens values (rule 7); Len = planned seconds inside the take; Assets = @tags only. Close every work block by updating the bible (rule 12; create it now if this block ordered assets and none exists).

records.title: Feeding production experience back
records.text:
## Feeding production experience back

The skill is maintained publicly at github.com/iret77/ai-film-production. When production experience contradicts or extends a rule — a workaround that worked, a rule that failed, a platform behaviour nobody documented — offer ONCE per project (tracked in the bible decision log) to draft a GitHub issue with the generalized technical finding: no project content, no personal data. If the director declines, drop it and do not raise it again.

**Contents — read only the part the spine, checklist or routing row names:** tag legend (canonical) · registry table — P1–P16 unitemized, P17–P69 and [MM-off] itemized, the LLM story-generation literature row · batch note 2026-09-12/13 · ledger re-verification 2026-09-04 · OpenAI image-model refresh 2026-09-09 · first-party [PP] production sessions 2026-09-11 (still-prompt budget) and 2026-09-14 (economy doctrine, technique A) · first-party [PP] agent cold tests 2026-09-14/18 (which agent model runs the skill) · vendor documentation read in the original 2026-09-18 (what it settled).

Rules in the source-tagged reference files carry a source tag and a confidence label; this is the canonical legend (each reference file points here). Official tags ([H-off], [BD-off], [G-off], [K-off], [xAI-off], [MM-off], [F], [R-off], [OAI-off], [A]) point to vendor documentation; [W] to multi-source web research; [PP] to first-party production-session evidence. This file itemizes the practitioner protocols so a [P] number is checkable.

**Tag legend (canonical):**
- 🟢 verified — multi-source, official, or production-proven · 🟡 plausible — single-source or untested · 🔴 marketing claim — verify yourself · ⚠️ source conflict — the sentence next to the marker settles it (SKILL.md Precedence).
- [PP] first-party production-session evidence · [W] multi-source web research · [A] platform academy docs.
- **Source tiers — claims are not weighted one to one.** Tier 1: the model vendor's own documentation and first-party measurement [PP]. Tier 2: platform tutorials and established practitioners (YouTubers, bloggers, filmmakers). Tier 3: single finds in social posts, videos and sites — often the home of a specific trick, but in a frontal contradiction with a vendor statement they do not win without striking proof; this keeps engagement-farming know-how out of the skill. A contradiction is settled by tracing BOTH sides: a canon line worded too generally is narrowed; evidence on both sides makes both variants admissible, one per prompt; a canon line whose evidence cannot be found is outdated. records.title: Story Structures: Dramaturgical Containers (Ch. 23)
records.text:
# Story Structures: Dramaturgical Containers (Ch. 23)

**Contents — read only the part the spine, checklist or routing row names:** 23a story intake gate (run first) · 23b classic containers · 23c alternative containers · 23d format-specific containers · 23e masters' rules (applied as lints) · 23f choosing and mixing · 23g the causal chain and the mandatory change lint.

Tags and confidence labels: legend in sources.md. The story comes from the USER — this file never replaces it (candidate-synopsis ideation only when asked, production-pipeline ch. 2). It exists for the moment after intake: the user has a story seed, and it needs a dramaturgical container before treatment work starts (production-pipeline ch. 2). Same seed, different container, different film: a Simpsons episode, a Python film, Star Wars, and a Tarantino picture could all start from "someone loses everything over a small lie" and land in four different worlds. Offer containers like recipes: max 2 candidates, one line each, the user picks.

records.title: 23a. Story intake gate (run BEFORE offering structures)
records.text:
## 23a. Story intake gate (run BEFORE offering structures)

Check the user's story for filmable completeness — a lint, not a writing seminar:
protagonist + concrete want? · engine (conflict, question, or tension that pulls forward)? · a turn (something changes irreversibly)? · an ending (even a direction)? · whose POV? · fits the target length? · premise — one sentence "X leads to Y" that the ending proves (23e Egri; bible section B2)?
Gaps → targeted questions, grouped into the single intake message (SKILL Workflow 1). A gap the director leaves open, or a "just do it" / batch run: deliver 1–2 options labeled `PROPOSAL A/B — not canon` inside the deliverable (SKILL rule 14) — never fill a gap silently, never more than two options. A complete-enough story proceeds to container choice; structure gaps found later are paid in rendered takes, not in rewritten pages — catch them here.

records.title: 23b. Classic containers
records.text:
## 23b. Classic containers

**Hollywood three-act (Syd Field's paradigm)** — Shape: setup (world + want, inciting incident ~10–15%) → **Plot Point I** (the event that flings into act 2) → confrontation (rising obstacles, midpoint reversal, all-is-lost) → **Plot Point II** (triggers the ending — Wilder's second-act curtain) → resolution (climax, new equilibrium). Beat-sheet refinements (Save-the-Cat-style percentages) are optional scaffolding on top. Fits: the default for narrative 5 min+; audiences parse it without effort. Signals: clear goal, clear opposition. AI note: act structure maps 1:1 onto sequence planning; the midpoint reversal is the natural place for a look/palette shift (film-craft color arc).

**Hero's journey (monomyth)** — Shape: departure (ordinary world, call, refusal, mentor, threshold) → initiation (trials, ordeal, reward) → return (transformed, elixir). Star Wars is the canonical execution. Fits: myth, adventure, fantasy, transformation arcs, family animation (want-vs-need maps onto it). Signals: a world to cross into; a protagonist who must change. AI note: the threshold crossings are your biggest set-piece/look changes — budget new location assets per world, not per scene.

**Five-act (Freytag/Shakespeare)** — Shape: exposition → rising action → climax at the CENTER → falling action → catastrophe/denouement. Fits: tragedies, rise-AND-fall arcs (Scorsese pairing), prestige-drama episodes. Signals: the fall is the point; the peak belongs in the middle. AI note: the long back half needs its own visual escalation plan — decay dramaturgy (grade, light) carries what plot repetition would bore.

records.title: 23c. Alternative containers
records.text:
## 23c. Alternative containers

**Kishōtenketsu (ki–shō–ten–ketsu)** — Shape: introduction → development (deepening, no escalating conflict) → TWIST (a recontextualizing element, not an antagonist) → reconciliation. The East Asian four-act; Ghibli's slice-of-life films live here (Kiki: vignettes of settling in, then the crisis-twist, then quiet resolution). Fits: quiet wonder, slice-of-life, family, essay-adjacent fiction. Signals: no villain, no race — the story wants to breathe. AI note: a gift for generation — calm held shots, "ma" beats, no action chains; pair with Miyazaki/Ozu recipes.

**Nonlinear / chapter structure** — Shape: story order ≠ plot order; chapters or interleaved timelines whose MEANING assembles at the end (Tarantino: shuffled chapters; Nolan: parallel lines converging). Fits: crime, puzzles, ensemble webs. Signals: the reveal of HOW pieces connect is the payoff. AI note: generation order is free anyway — the risk is continuity per timeline (ledger mandatory, post-audio-legal ch. 19); label every shot with its timeline; the audience needs one identifying cue per timeline (palette, ratio or grain — style-control era looks).

**Mosaic / fragment (associative)** — Shape: moments, not scenes, linked by emotional association and voice-over; time dissolves (Malick). Fits: memory, grief, love-and-loss, poetic essay. Signals: the user's material is feelings and images more than events. AI note: the most generation-friendly container of all — short independent clips, no continuity chains, VO carries coherence (no lip-sync).

**Circular / bookend** — Shape: ending returns to the opening image/scene with transformed meaning. Cheap to build, strong closure; combines with any container above. AI note: generate opening and closing from the SAME anchor still with changed light/grade — a controlled, prompt-friendly rhyme.

**Vignette / anthology** — Shape: self-contained segments under one theme, world, or object; optional frame story; runners/callbacks stitch. Fits: omnibus shorts, sketch features, anthology horror. AI note: resets continuity per segment — ideal when asset drift risk is high; each segment can even own a different recipe (declare it, don't drift into it).

**A24 / elevated-genre dramaturgy** 🟡 — critic-distilled, not an official studio doc; the studio's actual "concept" is business-side (director-driven, low budget, creative control, strangeness preserved — never sand it down). The narrative pattern across its catalog: a GENRE CONTAINER carries a psychological core as metaphor (possession film = inheritance of family trauma; folk horror = grief seeking a container); slow-burn pacing with anticipatory dread instead of jump-beats; tone/vibe as the organizing principle over plot mechanics; exposition near zero — interiority externalized in images and behavior (show-don't-tell as doctrine); tonal blends licensed (comedy inside horror, dread inside romance); endings resolve the EMOTION, not necessarily the plot — ambiguity is allowed to stand. Fits: psychological horror/drama, festival-style shorts, auteur pieces. Signals: the user names a feeling or wound first and a genre second. AI note: slow-burn = long held shots (extension chains, reroll budget); the metaphor layer lives in production design and recurring motifs — put the motif objects into the asset order from day one; pair with Kubrick/Lynch/Villeneuve structures + Young/Fraser light.

records.title: 23d. Format-specific containers
records.text:
## 23d. Format-specific containers

**Sitcom episode (Simpsons shape)** — Shape: cold-open gag (often unrelated) → act 1 establishes a premise that PIVOTS into the real story (the famous misdirect: the episode is never about how it starts) → A-plot braided with B-plot (C optional) → escalation → resolution that RESETS the status quo. ~22 min native, scales down. Fits: episodic comedy, animated series. AI note: the reset is an asset strategy — recurring sets/cast amortize across episodes (production bible ch. 22a rule 6); the act-1 pivot licenses a mid-episode location/look change.

**Series formats (TV & YouTube): episodic universe vs. serialized film** — decide the pole FIRST; it is the most consequential format decision a series makes:
- **Episodic (stable universe):** every episode self-contained; the status quo resets; the universe changes at most at SEASON boundaries. Each episode carries its own complete container (sitcom shape, case-of-the-week three-act); viewers can enter anywhere. AI note: the economically ideal series form — cast sheets, sets, and trained identities amortize across episodes while the continuity risk RESETS per episode; universe changes are season-boundary decisions, recorded in the project bible (ch. 22a rule 6).
- **Serialized (the overlong film):** one continuous arc chopped into episodes — plan it AS a film first (any 23b/23c container), then cut episode boundaries at reveal/reversal points; each episode still needs its own micro-shape: entry hook (or recap device), internal rise, an OUT (cliffhanger or resonance beat). Viewers must enter at episode 1. AI note: the hardest continuity class — wardrobe, props, injuries, time-of-day carry ACROSS episodes; shot board and continuity ledger span the whole season (one bible, no per-episode reset). Generation order stays free — placement is fixed in the paper plan, exactly like scattered soundbites.
- **The hybrid (standard TV pattern):** episodic A-plot + a serialized B-arc that surfaces in a few beats per episode and takes over in finales; the B-arc is a season-level container (usually a reveal ladder) — track its beats in the bible or they drift.
- **Anthology series (the third pole):** every episode its own story, cast, even look — the universe is a THEME, tone, or frame device (the brand is the continuity). Each episode picks its own container and may pick its own recipe; only the frame device, title grammar, and one tonal contract persist. AI note: zero cross-episode continuity burden AND full per-episode asset freedom — the format where AI series production is cheapest per minute; the bible shrinks to the tonal contract + frame device. A **limited series** is simply the serialized pole with a fixed ending — plan it strictly as one film, never leave the arc open.
- **YouTube series:** the episode is a retention object — hook inside the first 15–30 seconds (no slow cold open unless the channel brand carries it), typical 8–15-min bodies, an out that hands off to the next episode (end-screen logic). Branding — intro, framing, palette, the channel's style anchor — IS the universe marker. Episodic entries win discovery (the platform serves single episodes to new viewers); serialized needs a recap device for enter-anywhere viewers. Title/thumbnail promise is decided at SCRIPT stage, and the episode must pay it — an unpaid thumbnail is a broken contract, not marketing.

**Sketch logic (Python shape)** — Shape: one absurd premise escalated relentlessly; NO resolution owed — exit at the peak, interrupt, or break the form itself (abrupt endings, intertitles, animation inserts). A sketch FILM is anthology + runners/callbacks wearing a loose quest frame. Fits: absurdist comedy, sketch features. Signals: the joke is the engine; a plot would slow it down. AI note: form-breaks legitimize model discontinuity (the ZAZ/Brooks recipe's Python variant is the visual grammar); every sketch is a fresh generation context — cheap.

**Short-film dramaturgy** — Shape: ONE situation, ONE turn; enter at the latest possible moment, leave at the earliest; ending lands as sting, reversal, or image-answer. Under ~3 min: a single reversal is the whole story — a compressed three-act is a feature synopsis, not a short. Fits: social clips, festival shorts, spec pieces. AI note: the turn shot deserves the reroll budget; everything else is economy.

**Documentary spines** (argument structure — interview production mechanics in production-pipeline ch. 7b, look defaults in genre-baselines) — Pick ONE: essay/thesis (claim unfolded in chapters — Wenders/Malick tone), chronological/biographical (era grammar as chapters), investigative reveal ladder (staged revelations, true-crime pacing — withhold like a thriller), observational arc (vérité: a situation ripens on its own clock), portrait mosaic (facets, not timeline). AI note: the spine decides the edit BEFORE generation — B-roll is generated to prove the narration, so lock narration first (audio-first, ch. 18 logic); disclosure rules ch. 20 apply throughout.

**Interview dramaturgy** (the layer between spine and staging — production mechanics in production-pipeline ch. 7b) — Five working rules: **(1) Paper edit first:** in AI production the transcript IS the script — every soundbite is written before anything is generated (audio-first), so the film's argument is built at transcript level, not discovered in the edit bay; write answers AS soundbites (one thought each, cuttable at both ends). **Cut order ≠ interview order:** a good interview is never obliged to run chronologically as conducted — soundbites are placement-free building blocks, scattered across acts wherever the argument needs them (the "last" answer may open the film), and the emotional arc (composed → cracking → silence) is AUTHORED from bites, not inherited from a conversation. Two crafts make that work: phrase every bite self-contained (the question folded into the answer, no "as I said before", no dangling referents), and assign each bite its film position in the paper edit BEFORE generation. **(2) Voice functions:** cast interviewees like characters — witness (was there), expert (explains), adversary (holds the counter-position), heart (the emotional center); every voice earns its screen time through its function, and no voice serves two functions in the same act. **(3) The conflict engine:** contradiction editing — opposing answers cut against each other CREATE the debate (opposing look sides, production-pipeline ch. 7b, make it spatial); conflicting accounts of one event are the doc's Rashomon container. **(4) Hook and reveal placement:** cold-open on the strongest soundbite as the film's promise; withhold the key witness or the decisive answer the way a thriller withholds the monster (reveal ladder); Mamet's three questions apply to interview segments too — a segment no one needs RIGHT NOW is B-roll fodder, not an act beat. **(5) The held silence:** the emotional peak of an interview is the pause, the swallow, the look away — hold the face and do NOT cut to B-roll there; it is the one moment the B-roll escape is forbidden (and the shot that earns the reroll budget, production-pipeline ch. 7b).

**Online-native short formats** (where AI generation is used heaviest) — four working shapes, all governed by retention dramaturgy: hook inside 0–3 s (visual question or mid-action entry — never an establishing shot), re-hook every 20–30 s (new open loop before the last one closes), payoff that answers the opening promise, loop-friendly ending where the platform rewards rewatches.
- **Vertical micro-drama serial** (ReelShort-class: 60–90-s episodes, 50–100 per season, 9:16): melodrama escalation with a cliffhanger EVERY episode end and a reversal every 3–5 episodes; paywall/subscribe gates sit right after the biggest cliffhangers — dramaturgy and monetization are one system. Staging for 9:16: tight singles, faces huge, one action per frame, verticals in production design; wides barely read. AI note: the highest-volume AI series format — plan like the serialized pole (paper plan for the season, boundaries at cliffs), produce in batches per location; the tight-single grammar plays directly into identity-lock strengths.
- **Faceless VO formats** (explainer, listicle, story-time, doc-style channels): the biggest AI channel class — VO spine + generated B-roll, no on-camera human, no lip-sync anywhere. Structure: hook → promise → segmented payoffs (each segment its own mini-loop) → final payoff + handoff. Production is the doc path (production-pipeline ch. 7b B-roll logic + 23d paper edit) minus interviews.
- **Skit / POV character series:** a recurring character or POV premise in 20–60-s episodic bites — the episodic pole in micro form: character sheet + voice profile amortize, every skit self-contained, the character IS the brand. Formats: recurring-situation escalation, POV-of-X, character-reacts.
- **Part-series (Part 1/2/3):** one short story chopped at its strongest withhold — a serialized micro-arc riding discovery: part 1 must work as pure hook alone, each part re-establishes in one shot (no recap text), the final part pays everything. AI note: generate all parts as ONE production (one continuity context), release chopped.

**Music video / commercial** — concept-repetition-escalation, beat-locked; full defaults live in the Music film and Commercial/Ad baselines (genre-baselines.md) — this file only reminds: these formats may skip narrative entirely; ONE committed visual concept outperforms a compressed plot.

records.title: 23e. Masters' rules (sourced pearls — apply as lints, don't recite)
records.text:
## 23e. Masters' rules (sourced pearls — apply as lints, don't recite)

🟢 **The causation test (Parker/Stone, NYU writing seminar 2014):** take the outline beats — if "and then" fits between two beats, "you're fucked; you've got something pretty boring." Between every pair of beats must fit **"therefore"** or **"but"** (consequence or reversal). Run it mechanically over every outline and treatment at the script stage (production-pipeline ch. 2); an "and then" seam is a cut candidate or a missing turn. Full causal doctrine + the MANDATORY change lint: ch. 23g.

🟢 **The three scene questions (Mamet, memo to The Unit writers):** every scene must answer — **who wants what? · what happens if they don't get it? · why now?** A scene that answers none is information, not drama — and "the audience tunes in for drama, not information": move exposition into conflict or cut it. Use as the scene-level lint after the causation test passes at beat level.

🟢 **Wilder's rules (via Cameron Crowe, Conversations with Wilder) — the five with teeth here:** a clean line of action for the protagonist (one traceable want through the whole film) · **a third-act problem is really a first-act problem** (fix setup, not climax) · the Lubitsch 2+2: let the audience add it up — never show the four (elegance = hidden plot mechanics; ellipsis is also the AI rescue tool, so this pearl pays twice) · the second-act curtain triggers the ending (plant the trigger consciously) · act three builds, then STOPS — don't hang around after the last event. **Plus the VO law:** voice-over must ADD to the image, never describe what the audience already sees — the binding rule for every VO-driven container (mosaic, Scorsese momentum, doc spines).

🟢 **Non-submersible units (Kubrick):** design the film as ~6–8 indestructible sequence blocks — each one so strong it survives on its own — and keep the connective tissue between them minimal. For AI production this is doctrine, not metaphor: it IS sequence-first planning (film-craft §8 sequence approach; production-pipeline ch. 2 stages) — invest story and reroll budget in the units, bridge between them with ellipsis.

🟢 **The value turn (McKee, Story):** a scene earns its place only if a value charge FLIPS across it (safe→threatened, hope→despair, together→alone); no flip, no scene. The cutting corollary to Mamet's three questions — run both, they catch different failures.

🟢 **The premise (Egri, The Art of Dramatic Writing):** one sentence — "X leads to Y" — that the ENDING proves. Settle it at intake; every container above is only the delivery mechanism for a proven premise, and an unprovable premise is the earliest, cheapest rewrite you will ever get.

(The cutting-room counterpart — Murch's Rule of Six, emotion above all — lives in film-craft §4.)

records.title: 23f. Choosing (and mixing)
records.text:
## 23f. Choosing (and mixing)

1. Intake gate first (23a) — an incomplete story fits no container.
2. Format + genre narrow the field (a 30-s spot never gets a hero's journey; a series gets the sitcom/series shape).
3. Offer max 2 containers with one-line rationale; the user picks — exactly like recipe choice, and usually BEFORE it (structure shapes the shot list more than the look does).
4. Containers mix like recipes: one dominant + one device (three-act + bookend; kishōtenketsu twist inside a sitcom B-plot). More than two = mush.
5. Record the choice in the production bible (style contract section) — structure is canon once approved.

records.title: 23g. The causal chain — doctrine and the mandatory change lint
records.text:
## 23g. The causal chain — doctrine and the mandatory change lint

Why this section is binding: episodic, causally disconnected plotting is the DOCUMENTED native failure mode of LLM writing (documented in the LLM-story-generation literature — sources.md; scaffolding systems exist precisely because raw LLM output adds events instead of causing them). Addition is cheaper than consequence for the model — so the lint below is not optional craft polish, it is the guard against the writer itself. An event without cause is story slop exactly as a guessed beat is prompt slop (SKILL rule 14).

records.title: The doctrine (sourced)
records.text:
### The doctrine (sourced)
🟢 **Plot IS causality** (Forster, Aspects of the Novel): "The king died and then the queen died" is a story; "the king died, and then the queen died of grief" is a plot — the difference is the whole craft.
🟢 **Propter hoc, not post hoc** (Aristotle, *Poetics*, §§9–10 of the treatise — an external citation, not a skill chapter): events must be "the consequence, necessary or probable, of the antecedents"; plots "in which the episodes succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence" are "the worst."
🟢 **The chain reaction** (McKee, Story): "motivated actions cause effects that in turn become the causes of yet other effects" — the inciting incident is "the primary cause for all that follows," rippling causally to the climax.
🟢 **Coincidence has a direction** (Coats/Pixar #19; McKee): "Coincidences to get characters into trouble are great; coincidences to get them out of it are cheating." McKee: bring coincidence in early so meaning can build from it, and "never use it to turn an ending. This is deus ex machina, the writer's greatest sin."
