(2) **Smart Edit** — clip → "Edit", or model Seedance 2.5 → mode "Smart Edit": rectangle/brush/arrow/text/eraser/mark annotations, each "Add to chat" with its instruction, reference images inline; several edits (remove ×2, replace, add) succeeded in ONE submission with reflections and ground patterns held, slight degradation at 720p — but the AUDIO of a removed subject stayed (footsteps): pair every visual removal with an audio-category edit. Dreamina also exposes a reference-weight slider (unverified, [P35]).
🟢 **Music track as timing input [H-off, P48, Seedance 2.0 on Higgsfield]:** "add the music track as an input and have the hero dance in time with its beat" — the track is loaded as an audio reference beside the prompt and every move landed on the beat; a TIMING reference, not generated score (rule 10 holds). Choreography still needs move-by-move language (renderability §3).

🟢 **Plan the reference set BEFORE the prose [BD-off].** Official capacity: 30 images + 10 video + 10 audio per generation; ByteDance: "a larger volume and wider variety of references can better capture the user's intent." The agent's duty at shot-brief time: walk the shot's element list and give EVERY element that must stay consistent its own reference — characters (4-view sheet, one view a strong expression), wardrobe, key props, location plates, style still, motion clips, voice/audio, clay blockout. **Prose is for what happens; references are for what persists** — an element controlled only by text will drift. Reference-maximal ≠ reference-dump: stability ranges: the 12b budgets [X-ext]; one deliberate reference per element beats a cluttered set [H-off]. Selection stays per-scene (casting pool, ch. 14) — but the POOL is built out maximally as a project asset (production-pipeline ch. 1).
⚠️ 🟡 **Single-view images per subject instead of one sheet [P58, sponsored, ~$2,000 of tests]:** with 30 image slots one practitioner stopped attaching collage sheets on 2.5 and gives ONE subject four face angles plus four body angles as separate single images, declared together as one distinct subject in the casting block ("more context per subject"); products get six single-view angles the same way. Conflicts with the feature-film sheet doctrine (production-pipeline ch. 3, [P24], 🟢, proven on 2.0 with headless sheets); the ByteDance ">5 subjects → single-view images" rule points the same way for cameos. ByteDance settles the scope [BD-off]: on 2.5 single-view AND multi-view inputs are supported for 1–5 subjects; above 5, single views are more stable and several views go into separate images, never one combined image; on 2.0 multi-view images are not recommended at all (headshot + full-body instead). Treat it as a legitimate 2.5 alternative for the 1–3 leads when the slot budget allows: the identity source is still ONE clean face, now spread over several single-view files instead of panels; the ten-of-ten stress test decides between the two formats, not the format itself.

🟢 **The four reference classes and their default jobs [BD-off]:** `@Image` = identity/appearance · `@Video` = **motion/pacing by default, not identity** — say so explicitly when you mean otherwise · `@Audio` = voice/dialogue/ambience/music via a role line ("@Audio 1 defines <character>'s voice") — voice consistency across scenes is an official capability, and audio refs drive lip-sync performance · **`@Clay Render`** = staging (official ByteDance reference class): a textureless 3D blockout carries "camera movement, pacing, shot-size transitions, subject trajectory, and blocking"; 2.5 derives physically plausible LIGHTING (source direction, colour temperature, shadow projection) from its spatial info on its own — but the lighting JOB is assigned to an image reference's role line, never to the clay render's ("Refer to @Clay Render 1 for camera movement… @Image 2 for character design, scene, materials, lighting, color" is the official pattern; production-pipeline ch. 8 role split). Coarse vs. fine blockout discipline: ch. 14 (strip path lines, axes, camera frustums — they render as content). On Higgsfield, attach the Blender viewport render/recording as a normal reference (Blender plugin, platforms-models ch. 13). **The clay render is also the hard SIZE and staging control for props/creatures** — the video-side answer to image-model-logic ch. 24d.

🟢 **Voice channel per character — text half always, reference half by surface:** the verbatim voice-conditions block (12b) is the TEXT half and goes into every take where the character speaks. The REFERENCE half is exactly one of, in this order: (1) a saved/cloned platform voice where the surface offers one (post-audio-legal ch. 18); (2) an `@Audio` reference — one compilation of the character's approved generated lines, combined <30 s, uploaded as an AUDIO file, role line "@Audio N defines <character>'s voice — timbre and manner only, do not reuse its words" (the audio-slot form of the ch. 18 P17 harvest); (3) the surface takes video but no audio references: the ch. 18 P17 black-screen MP4 as `@Video`, role line "@Video N carries <character>'s voice only — it is not a motion, pacing or framing reference" (the exclusion is mandatory: @Video defaults to motion). Never attach the same compilation as both @Audio and @Video; never list a voice reference for a character who has no line in the take (12b tag rule).
🟡 **Deriving the text half from a sample [P52]:** upload a real recording of the intended voice to the text LLM and ask for a voice prompt (pitch, timbre, cadence, energy, accent); freeze the result verbatim per 12b. Generated lines from a TTS service can serve as the reference half where the surface takes audio or black-screen video references (post-audio-legal ch. 18) — consent and licence terms of that voice apply (ch. 20).
🟡 **A third `@Audio` job — diegetic playback [P57]:** beside voice and timing input, an attached track can be the sound source INSIDE the scene: `@Audio 1 is the song playing on the car radio — the characters hear it and react`; two listeners nodded to the beat and called the song "fire", a driver sang along to a track that "played through the radio". Pool ceiling 30 s combined; the model also invented a radio-host intro line around the track (12b invented-dialogue risk — lock the spoken text). One class per audio file: never voice and music in one upload [P58].

🟢 **The edit suite — repair before reroll.** An approved take is never regenerated for a local fault. All official [BD-off], all invoked as prompts (Higgsfield's Video page exposes no mask/annotation editor as of 2026-08-31 — describe the region in words; 🟡 a draw-over tool was sighted in Cinema Studio's Edit → Advanced on 2026-09-01, platform-ui-workflows §1):
- **Region edit:** `[what] + [change] + [effective time range]` — "repaints just that region, no full regeneration, no seed lottery" [H-off]. Always time-scope (ch. 14 edit format).
- **Camera-perspective edit = a B-camera pass on an approved performance:** "Edit @Video 1. Keep the characters, actions, and visual style unchanged. Adjust only the camera movement." + a segmented camera plan per time range (official worked prompt). Coverage tool: production-pipeline ch. 16 rung 2.
- **Green-screen relocation** (runs as `omni_reference` with the source clip attached): moves a performance into a new environment; the model adapts cloth flutter, hair, gait rhythm, and lighting interaction to the new scene.
- **Subject swap:** Timeline Inheritance clause mandatory (ch. 14).
- **Audio-category edits:** dialogue, spoken language, voice, BGM, SFX edit independently ("Remove only the original background music. Keep the character dialogue, lip sync, ambience, and action sound effects").
Constraints [X-ext]: edit source ≤20 s recommended, 1–5 accompanying refs; **an edit bills the source's FULL duration on Higgsfield** — the saving is fewer attempts, not per-run price. Consequence: **draft at the take's planned length (10 s by default); once the beats lock, regenerate the locked prompt as a fresh full-length take at target resolution (never extend the draft — extension is for building length PAST a full take, next paragraph); from then on every fix is an edit.** ⚠️ **Edit-round ceiling — by analogy, no 2.5-specific evidence yet:** treat chained video edits like image edit chains (style-control §2, image-model-logic ch. 24g multi-turn collapse): after 3 edit rounds on one source, stop chaining. Export the best intermediate as .mov (ModelArk item above), register it as the new `@Video 1` source, and continue edits from that file; if the remaining fault is global, regenerate from the original references instead (W8 / production-pipeline ch. 1 review loop). Log each edit round as a Take ID.

🟢 **Extension chains [BD-off]:** 4–30 s per round, forward or backward; carries main characters, environment, narrative pacing, audio continuity. **Chain ceiling ≈60 s** (30 s source + one 30 s extension) — beyond that, re-anchor a NEW generation from the original references instead of extending an extension (degradation compounds). Boundary-frame contract every round: forward — "the first frame of the extended segment directly continues from the last frame of @Video 1" (the last clean frame — boundary-frame source, ch. 14); backward — write the source's first frame as the extension's explicit END state and declare which materials must not appear early ("then connect to the source video" is the documented failure; ch. 14 extension rules). Restate the continuity list each round. 180 s single-flow is a Dreamina-only beta, not a Higgsfield plan (⚠️ [P58] reported a 180-s option on the Higgsfield surface in Aug 2026 — "six 30-s videos stitched from one 5,000-character prompt" — same mechanism, same verdict: not for held scenes; read the live form). 🟡 **Copy-ready extension wording that held without extra references [P57]:** forward — `Extend @Video 1 forward, directly continued from its last frame, matching the subject's pose, position, background, camera angle, lighting and motion direction. New action: …`; backward — `Extend @Video 1 backward: before the video starts, …` (a 19-s prequel cut cleanly against the source's first 5 s). 🟡 **Video-as-reference continuation drifts geometry [P52]:** "continue from @Video 1" with the clip attached as a reference (omni-style, not an extension) changed a prop's size between clips; extension or last-frame chaining holds geometry better — if omni continuation is used, attach the prop as its own reference.
🟡 **One location per take for narrative intercuts [P28, Seedance 2.0 evidence]:** do not prompt A/B parallel action inside one generation (hero ship ↔ enemy ship); generate one take per location and cut in the NLE — the complexity budget (SKILL rule 3) applied to locations. Montage/commercial takes (next line) are exempt: they may span locations because no parallel action is implied. ⚠️ Scope [H-off, P66]: the rule holds for text-only prompting; a continuous JOURNEY through several locations (street → corridor → kitchen → casino, 30 s) held on 2.5 when a clay render carried the route (production-pipeline ch. 8 protocol c) — parallel intercuts stay one-location-per-take, a travelled route with a blockout does not.
🟡 **Montage ceiling and the missing agent [P38]:** commercials/montages are the exception to the 2–3-shot drama budget — cap at **12–15 cuts per 30-s take** ("so it can focus on each cut"; an LLM's first draft had far more). Name the ACTOR of every action: "onions are chopped" rendered a kitchen with no hands in frame — write "the chef's hands chop". 🟢 **Everything unreferenced goes static — write background life explicitly [P39, P41; H-off, P69]:** with ~9 references the composite held but crowd and sky froze; the vendor's harbour scene had "NPC crowds staring into space" until the prompt forced every background person to be mid-action in every frame — write it ("people moving in the beach bar", "every passer-by mid-stride") or get a ghost town. The same vendor fix for a beat that over-shot (a shoulder bump rendered as a hug): write the physical mechanics — shoulders hit, suitcases swing, momentum carries them half a step past, planted feet turn — "when the collision becomes physics, the romance feels natural" (ch. 14 cause before reaction).
🟡 **Write the boundary state from harvested frames [P22]:** before prompting an extension, frame-harvest the source's first/last frame plus 2–3 keyframes, and let the agent write the continuation FROM those stills — who stands where, what each hand holds, where the light comes from — so positions, hand contact and eyeline are held verbatim ("his hand stays on the side of the washing machine"). A well-anchored extension cut together with its source was reported seamless.

🟢 **Timestamp control is a documented channel at generation AND edit time [BD-off]:** the three ch. 14 timing forms (range / exact point / relative) hold at edit time too; every timed segment ends on an explicit end state. Still budgets, not frames — "timestamps allocate proportion, not frames" [F]: never demand events inside one second, never plan frame-accurate hits (precision limits, ch. 14).
🟢 **Beats inside a declared single shot — settled by version [BD-off; H-off P47 vs P49 for 2.0]:** Seedance 2.5 takes integer-second stamps inside one continuous take — a stamp is an event budget, never a cut point, and the official examples stamp a "single continuous take … no cuts". What produces unrequested cuts is an overfilled window (ch. 14 timing patterns): give each window one main event, or use relative timing. Seedance 2.0 does not respond to timestamps — numbered shots or relative timing; the two conflicting Higgsfield observations (per-second beats worked / "forcing Seedance to do cuts") are 2.0 behaviour and stay version-dated.

Read that file for ANY stylized-look task and whenever writing prompts that use references.

records.title: Worked Example: 20-Second Spot, End to End
records.text:
# Worked Example: 20-Second Spot, End to End

**Contents — read once end to end on first use; afterwards only the part a pointer names:** §1 canon → shot plan · §1b route receipt · §2 assets · §3 sequence take S1 in technique B (block structure, for comparison) · §3b the same take in technique A (Caption Spine — the technique this project chose) · §3c production take of S1 · §4 sequence take S2, extension round · §5 QA and log.

A compact walkthrough applying the pipeline to a fictional brief — read once to see how the chapters connect; every deliverable below is in the form the rules require (per-prompt checklist steps 1–7, Render Slate, risk register, bible rows). Style: Pixar-adjacent stylized 3D (in a real project the style is picked via the director-recipes selection index — here fixed for brevity). Model path: Nano Banana Pro (figure-anchored anchor plate, sheets) → GPT Image 2.5 (derived empty plate, reverse plate) → Seedance 2.5 on Higgsfield (motion). Project slug: `LIGHTCAT`. Element tags (Higgsfield Elements, verbatim everywhere — tag token rule, video-prompting ch. 12b): `@cat`, `@loc_lamproom`, `@loc_lamproom_rev`, `@prop_lever`, `@anchor_1A`, `@anchor_1B`. On a Dreamina/ModelArk surface the same prompts would carry `@Image 1…n` by upload order. Sequence take S1 is shown in BOTH prompt shapes on the same canon: §3b is the Caption Spine — the technique this example project chose at intake (SKILL rule 4; read this one first) — and §3 is the same take in the block structure, for comparison; the extension round (§4) is in the Caption Spine. Both carry the same Render ID: the technique is a project constant, not a prompt variant.

records.title: 1. Canon → shot plan (SKILL rule 14, production-pipeline ch. 2)
records.text:
## 1. Canon → shot plan (SKILL rule 14, production-pipeline ch. 2)
Canon comes from the director's treatment — never from the agent. Treatment excerpt (the passage every canon-bound claim below is read from): "Sc. 1, night, rain. The keeper's cat slips through the hatch into the dark lamp room, shakes off, rears up and pushes the brass lever with its whole body. The lamp ignites; the cat sits and watches the beam." Canon is silent on where the cat enters from → delivered as `PROPOSAL — not canon` ("hatch at the left wall"), approved by the director before it entered any prompt. Camera height and light direction are craft-fillable (rule 14) — decided by the crew and listed in each slate's `Crew choices` row; the lens, the composition inside the named shot size and the cut timing are left to the model by default (SKILL.md Economy and division of labour), and the `Crew choices` row says so. Intake decision (SKILL rule 4): technique A, Caption Spine — a calm single-event beat with clear canon and a look the anchors carry; no draft takes were needed. Recorded in the bible frame (section B1).
Renderability pass: paw-level object manipulation 🟡 (renderability §2 hands row) → rescue: whole-body push (big motion, no finger-class precision); rescue cut if it fails: lever-only insert + reaction MCU. Both takes contain a cut for coverage; a calm single-event beat would be ONE shot in one take (production-pipeline ch. 2).

Shot table (SKILL.md Workflow step 5 schema; these Shot IDs ARE the bible shot board's IDs):
| Shot ID | Len | Framing | Action | Assets | Risk | Rescue |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1A | 4 s | medium-wide, static, low, from the rear-left corner | wet cat squeezes through the hatch, shakes, looks up at the dark lamp | @cat @loc_lamproom @anchor_1A | 🟡 wide opening (stylized 3D) | open on the medium, arrive at the wide by transition |
| 1B | 6 s | close-up insert on the lever, then back to 1A's setup | cat rears up, pushes the lever with its whole body; lamp ignites; cat settles | @cat @prop_lever @anchor_1B | 🟡 paw manipulation | whole-body push; cut to lever insert + reaction MCU |
| 1C | 4 s | medium, static, same position | cat blinks in the warm light, breathes out | @cat | — | — |
| 1D | 6 s | wide, low, counter-angle | the beam starts to rotate; the sweep crosses the cat's face | @cat @loc_lamproom_rev | — | — |
Sequence takes (SKILL rule 2): S1 = 1A + 1B (10-s `t2v` take, three internal shots: 1A → 1B insert → return to 1A's setup) · S2 = 1C + 1D (10-s `video_extension` of S1's production take, counter-angle as internal shot 2 after the HARD CUT). A multi-shot take carries the Render ID of its FIRST internal shot; every internal shot's board row points to it.

This example project chose technique A (§1); the same take in the block structure shows what B costs and buys: every axis is steered explicitly — camera, optics, light, continuity — which a project picks when it deliberately wants that control (SKILL rule 4). Canon, route and Render ID are identical to §3b.

| Intent | The wet cat enters the dark lamp room and pushes the lever with its whole body; the lamp ignites — three internal shots, medium-wide → lever insert → medium-wide |
| Crew choices | Left to the model: the cat's body mechanics, wet-fur and brass rendering, the light bloom, the cut timing inside the declared ranges. Decided by the crew — the look controls technique B steers deliberately, each a paid line: medium-wide 63° / close-up 47°, window key 8500K, lamp key 3200K, camera height and distance as relations, the two-shake rain shed as the reaction cue |
| Run in | Higgsfield → web UI → project LIGHTCAT → Video → Seedance 2.5 → t2v (UI label unverified — read the live task dropdown) — from reference HF-WEB@2026-09-04 (checked 2026-09-04), not live-checked this session; confirm model/mode/workspace on the live form before Generate |
| Settings | 16:9 · 720p (draft tier) · 10 s · audio on · no Cinema Studio controls (Video page) |
| Lint | words 467 · negations 1/1 (the AUDIO music exclusion — once per governing block) · numerals outside TC: 63°, 47°, 8500K, 3200K — deliberate look controls listed in Crew choices · absolute measures 0/0 · double mentions none (ENDING STATE restates the last frame by contract, ch. 14) · contradictions none · beats complete |
| Inputs | 1. `@anchor_1A` = approved still 1A — opening composition of SHOT 1 and SHOT 3 (reference, not start frame) · 2. `@anchor_1B` = approved still 1B — opening composition of SHOT 2 from the HARD CUT (reference, not start frame) · 3. `@loc_lamproom` = lamp-room master plate — set only · 4. `@cat` = cat sheet, wet state — identity only · 5. `@prop_lever` = lever detail, state down — prop only (all five are Higgsfield Elements addressed by name; no upload) |
| Store in | Higgsfield project LIGHTCAT / SC01 |

```
SCENE CONTEXT: Night, rain, lamp room of a lighthouse. @cat has just slipped in through the hatch and will push the brass lever to relight the dark lamp above.
ACTIVE REFERENCES: @anchor_1A is the opening composition of SHOT 1 (0.0–4.0 s) and of SHOT 3 (7.0–10.0 s); the take opens already in motion. @anchor_1B is the opening composition of SHOT 2, from the HARD CUT at 4.0 s onward. @cat controls only the cat — small grey tabby, wet clumped fur, white chest patch, green eyes, one notch in the left ear. 100% matches the reference. @loc_lamproom controls only the set. 100% matches the reference. @prop_lever controls only the lever — shape, state: down. 100% matches the reference.
LOCATION MAP: foreground wet floorboards; midground the brass lever on the right wall, the hatch on the left wall; background rain-streaked windows, the dark lamp above centre. Camera in the rear-left corner of the room.
FIRST FRAME/BLOCKING: the cat mid-squeeze through the half-open hatch, body toward frame centre, gaze up at the lamp.
FORMAT MODE: sequential cuts, three shots, 10 s total — Shot 1 0.0–4.0 s, Shot 2 4.0–7.0 s, Shot 3 7.0–10.0 s.
OPTICS: Shots 1 and 3 medium-wide at 63°; Shot 2 close-up at 47°; soft rounded rendering.
CAMERA: Shots 1 and 3 static, lens at the height of the cat's shoulders; Shot 2 static, lens level with the lever and close enough that the lever fills the frame's height.
ACTION: SHOT 1 (0.0–4.0 s): the cat lands on the floorboards, shakes rain off in two shakes — droplets catch the window light — then looks up at the lamp. HARD CUT; the cat's pose at the end of Shot 1 exactly matches its start in Shot 2. SHOT 2 (4.0–7.0 s): the cat rears up and pushes the brass lever with both forepaws and its whole body weight; the lever tips up with one heavy clunk; only then a warm glow blooms from above. HARD CUT. SHOT 3 (7.0–10.0 s): the cat settles onto its haunches in the amber light, eyes widening, ears rising, and goes still.
LIGHTING: Shot 1 one cold key from the windows screen-right, 8500K, low exposure, the cat's far side in shadow; from the ignition in Shot 2 a warm 3200K top light, brighter than the window key, contact shadows under the cat.
AUDIO: <rain on glass, continuous> <two wet shakes> <one heavy metallic clunk at 6.0 s> <low warm hum from the lamp from 6.0 s> No music, no BGM — room tone and effects only.
ENDING STATE: cat seated on its haunches facing the lit lamp, lever up, room in warm amber, rain continuing on the glass.
STYLE: stylized 3D animated-feature look, matte rendered materials, soft global illumination; clean, grain-free image.
POSITIVE LOCKS: exactly one cat in every frame.
```
The attachment list lives in the slate's `Inputs` row, never inside the prompt (SKILL rule 11).

The same canon as §3, written for a specialist model: the agent states what is in the scene, what happens in which order and where each beat rests, gives each reference one job and writes one camera line for the return cut; composition inside the shot sizes, cut timing, the cat's body mechanics, wet fur, brass and the light bloom are the model's. Three references (identity, opening composition, insert framing) — the anchor stills stay references, not start frames (rule 1).
| Row | Content |
|---|---|
| Render ID | `LIGHTCAT_1A__HF-SD25__T2V__P01` (multi-shot take S1 = 1A+1B) |
| Intent | The wet cat enters the dark lamp room and pushes the lever with its whole body; the lamp ignites — medium-wide → insert on the lever → medium-wide |
| Crew choices | Left to the model: camera composition inside the named shot sizes, the cut timing around the insert, the cat's body mechanics, wet-fur and brass rendering, the light bloom. Decided by the crew: shot-size words per beat; one camera line (low, looking toward the lever, holding still — continuity of the return cut); the rain shake as the reaction cue; window light cold / lamp light warm, as words |
| Run in | Higgsfield → web UI → project LIGHTCAT → Video → Seedance 2.5 → t2v (UI label unverified — read the live task dropdown) — from reference HF-WEB@2026-09-04 (checked 2026-09-04), not live-checked this session; confirm model/mode/workspace on the live form before Generate |
| Settings | 16:9 · 720p (draft tier) · 10 s · audio on · no Cinema Studio controls (Video page) |
| Lint | words 256 · negations 1/1 · numerals outside TC 0/0 · absolute measures 0/0 · double mentions none · contradictions none · beats complete |
| Inputs | 1. `@cat` = cat sheet, wet state — identity only · 2. `@anchor_1A` = approved still 1A — exact background and opening composition (reference, not start frame) · 3. `@anchor_1B` = approved still 1B — exact framing of the lever insert (reference, not start frame) (all three Higgsfield Elements addressed by name; no upload) |
| Store in | Higgsfield project LIGHTCAT / SC01 |

```
Create a 10-second stylized 3D animated short inside the dark lamp room of a lighthouse on a rainy night.
STYLE: matte rendered materials, soft global illumination, cold window light, wet reflective floorboards, shallow depth of field, hushed mood, slow deliberate motion, room-tone sound.
@cat is a small grey tabby cat with wet clumped fur, a white chest patch, green eyes and a notch in its left ear. Keep the cat visually consistent throughout.
@anchor_1A is the exact background and the opening composition: the brass lever on the right wall, the half-open hatch on the left wall, rain-streaked windows and the unlit lamp above. @anchor_1B is the exact framing of the lever insert.
Camera: low, at the height of the cat's shoulders, looking across the floorboards toward the lever; the camera holds still.
0–4 s, medium-wide: the cat drops from the hatch onto the floorboards, shakes the rain off and looks up at the lamp; the lever stays down; rain drums on the glass.
4–7 s, close-up on the lever: the cat rears into frame and pushes the lever with its forepaws and its whole body until the lever tips up with a heavy clunk, and a warm glow blooms from above.
7–10 s, medium-wide: the cat settles onto its haunches and looks up at the lamp; its ears rise and it goes still; a low hum joins the rain.
End with the cat seated and still beneath the lamp, the room warm amber.
No dialogue, no subtitles, no text, no music. Maintain the same look throughout.
```
What is deliberately NOT in this prompt, and why: no OPTICS/FOV, no camera distance, no Kelvin, no PHYSICS block, no POSITIVE LOCKS — those axes are the model's (Division of labour); the lever's start state and the return to the medium-wide are each said once, inside the beat they belong to; the anchors carry the geography, so the beats never re-describe the room; the only negation is the closing sentence. If a run pushes with the head instead of the flank, the first repair step is still REMOVE (is anything on the push stated twice, or on an axis the model owns?), the second changes the half-sentence in beat two ("pushes the lever with its flank"), only the third adds one (SKILL rule 15).

**Risk register** (SKILL rule 11 — one table after the last slate of the delivery; covers §3 and §3b):
| Shot | Kept risk | List (red/yellow, renderability §2) | Why kept | Rescue |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1B | object manipulation (lever push) | yellow | it is the story beat; whole-body push, no toes/fingers visible | paws morph → cut to lever-only insert (`@prop_lever` state pair) + reaction MCU |
| 1A | wide opening in stylized 3D | yellow | single-room interior at close range | positions locked by `@anchor_1A`; if scale breaks, open on the medium and arrive at the wide by transition (pixar-look §10) |

records.title: Workflows: The Typical Jobs, as Runbooks (ch. 25)
records.text:
# Workflows: The Typical Jobs, as Runbooks (ch. 25)

**Contents — read only the runbook the task names:** W1 new project · W2 asset & reference-pool build-out · W3 produce one shot · W4 build a scene/sequence · W5 repair a faulty take · W6 new angle / coverage · W7 define & lock a style · W8 a generation keeps failing · W9 session open & close · W10 storyboard-first production model (nine gated stages).

Named, ordered procedures for the recurring jobs of an AI-film production. They add NO new rules — they chain the existing chapters into the order that has proven to work, so a session never improvises the sequence. Every step that writes a prompt runs the per-prompt checklist (SKILL.md); every workflow ends by updating the production bible (SKILL rule 12). Every external generation/edit first receives a RECEIPT line (SKILL.md Scope & version; state per SKILL rule 17) in that bible. Pick the workflow by trigger; if two apply, run the earlier-numbered one first — except W10, which is a production MODEL: when a project runs storyboard-first, W10 is the spine and calls W1–W3 and W7 at the stages it names. Citations: `production-pipeline ch. N` for chapters 1–11, `<file> §N` for section-numbered files (SKILL.md citation convention).

records.title: W1 — New project (trigger: a new film/short/ad/social video begins)
records.text:
## W1 — New project (trigger: a new film/short/ad/social video begins)
1. Genre named or evident? Read `genre-baselines.md` FIRST — it pre-answers craft defaults and names the files THIS project type needs.
2. Story intake gate (story-structures ch. 23a): the story comes from the user; offer a dramaturgical container before any craft settles.
3. Settle the intake items of SKILL.md Workflow step 1 (format/look · length & platform · deliverable · model stack · prompting technique, rule 4 — put as the menu line with all three entries, the recommended one and its reason, from the technique-menu preface of `video-prompting.md`; when unclear, offer ONE draft batch of one beat per candidate · dialogue language + route: native in-model, audio dub or video dub with lip-sync, post-audio-legal ch. 18) under the interaction contract.
   **Interaction contract (full text; SKILL.md Workflow step 1 carries the short form).** Before the first deliverable, at most ONE grouped question message: the story-gate gaps plus the open intake items. Everything unanswered ships on a labelled default — craft per `genre-baselines.md`, model stack per renderability §6 and production-pipeline ch. 5, dialogue in the user's language, technique as the recommended menu entry — marked `ASSUMED` where it appears and logged in the bible decision log as `<date> — ASSUMED: <item> = <value> — confirm`. "Just do it" or an unavailable director (batch or subagent run) → proceed on ASSUMED values and ship canon-bound gaps as `PROPOSAL A/B — not canon` (SKILL rule 14). Afterwards one question at a time, only when a canon-bound item blocks the next step.
4. Style direction: user names a director/DoP or a mood → W7.
5. Create the production bible (ch. 22, template 22b) BEFORE the first asset order — every project, even one that looks like a single session (SKILL rule 12); register the decisions above as canon. The bible's Verify-line row is never left empty: with a recipe, copy its Verify line; without one, write a DEFAULT VERIFY LINE of three binary checks derived from the style anchor and the genre baseline defaults, e.g. "palette = anchor palette? · key light from the stated side and motivated? · sequence camera grammar as planned?" — label it DEFAULT so W7 can replace it if a recipe is chosen later.
Exit: bible exists, container chosen, look decided, model stack named (Render-ID tokens fixed in bible section B1), prompting technique recorded (section B1), Verify line present.

records.title: W2 — Asset & reference-pool build-out (trigger: project has a bible, no approved assets yet; or a new character/location/prop enters)
records.text:
## W2 — Asset & reference-pool build-out (trigger: project has a bible, no approved assets yet; or a new character/location/prop enters)
1. Order of build per the production-pipeline ch. 1 build-order rule — case (a) default: location plates → characters → props → composite stills; case (b) stylized 3D/Pixar: character sheets first, figure-anchored plates, then derived empty plates (pixar-look §8); case (c) any project with a blockout stage (W10): sheets → blockout → plates.
2. Per character: minimal sheet (or animation variant: 1 pose + 8 expressions), defensive anatomy locks, one-face rule, iterated to the anchor standard (production-pipeline ch. 3). Persistent state changes = NEW state sheets, never prompt adjectives. Each order ships as a Render Slate + still prompt (asset order shape, production-pipeline ch. 3).
3. Per location: master wide + 2–3 detail plates at ONE exposure; decide reverses UP FRONT (production-pipeline ch. 4 / ch. 16 — late reverse plates are the most expensive single mistake; in a storyboard-first project the camera setup system of ch. 2 IS this decision). Location needs counter-angles (dialogue, cross-room action)? Produce the plates NOW: with a master plate and no layout map, start with the empty-location walkthrough (production-pipeline ch. 4 — rung 2, one cheap video); go to rung-3 tools when the walkthrough fails the reverse test or a layout map already exists — a purpose-built angle tool IF the live Higgsfield shell has one (production-pipeline ch. 16 tool section: undated, verify in the tool picker and mint a fresh receipt first) or GPT Image 2.5 WITH the layout map or master plate as input, never free-text "same scene from behind" — and reverse-test against the master (anchors, openings, light side, palette; production-pipeline ch. 16 rung 3, platforms-models ch. 13b). The coverage ladder of W6 is for angles needed on an EXISTING take; it does not delay planned plates.
4. Build the reference POOL as a deliverable (ch. 14b) = the bible's asset registry (section B3): wardrobe details, prop stills, style stills, motion clips, voice/audio refs, clay blockouts — one reference for every element that must stay consistent anywhere, each row carrying its reference class (@Image / @Video / @Audio / @Clay Render).
5. Register everything as named elements with EXACT tag names (@hero, @loc_x, @anchor_1A); a name mismatch silently unbinds (production-pipeline ch. 5b; token form per surface: video-prompting ch. 12b) — and so does a missing one: the handle must stand as its literal `@token` in the prompt TEXT; an attached image referred to as "the reference image" does not bind, slot or no slot (style-control §7 Rule 0b).
6. Lock gate per LEAD asset (recurring characters, hero locations, hero props): ten-of-ten stress test (production-pipeline ch. 3 — ten generations with the sheet attached, varied pose and light, recognisable in ten of ten; run as image-model stills at draft tier — the cheap form — a fail means the description/sheet is wrong, not the model: fix and re-run). Only after it passes may the bible status move approved → locked (user approval still required, bible rule 3); cameos, extras and one-scene props stop at approved. The motion ladder is the STYLE/model gate and runs once per model in W7 step 4, not per asset.
Exit: every element the script needs exists as an approved, tagged reference; leads have passed the lock gate; bible asset registry updated.

records.title: W3 — Produce one shot (trigger: a numbered shot needs its first take)
records.text:
## W3 — Produce one shot (trigger: a numbered shot needs its first take)
1. CANON: read the beat in treatment/script/bible (rule 14: canon-bound vs craft-fillable content) — content before platform, same order as the per-prompt checklist.
2. ROUTE RECEIPT: mint or reuse the project KEY and write its RECEIPT line (SKILL.md Scope & version) in one of rule 17's two states — `live-checked <date>` when you or the user read the live form in THIS session, else `from reference <KEY>` with the stored key's own date. A from-reference receipt (rule 17) is enough to draft; live confirmation is the Generate-time gate, done by whoever has the form open. Do not choose controls until the receipt exists.
3. Lint the shot against `renderability.md` (red list §2, rescues §3) — rewrite or attach a rescue BEFORE spending a render.
4. Stills-first: generate the shot's still (per-prompt checklist; style mechanics per style-control §2–4 for the routed model) → user approves → register as `@anchor_<shot>`.
5. Draft batch — a BATCH OF 4 draft takes at draft resolution (480/720p, the take's planned length — 10 s by default; the motion test of production-pipeline ch. 1; ch. 10 batch protocol — watch all four fully: one odd take is a roll, four are the prompt) with the anchor attached as a tagged reference, take opening in motion (start-frame slot only for rule 1's two cases — say which path in the slate), the prompt in the project's technique (SKILL rule 4, from the bible frame) with its `Lint` row (video-prompting ch. 12h); judge with the project's Verify line (recipe's, or the default line from W1 step 5) + shot criteria (review loop, production-pipeline ch. 1; verdict order post-audio-legal ch. 19). When the agent cannot view the result, the director answers the six passes (SKILL checklist step 7). No bible (one-off prompt) → put the rule-4 menu to the director in one line, or ship `ASSUMED: technique = A` per the interaction contract and say so in the Intent row.
6. Production take only after the draft batch sits: target resolution, full duration — a new generation of the locked prompt (same Render ID, new settings row), not an extension of the draft take. The route decides what the target can be: over the Higgsfield API Seedance 2.5 renders 480p and 720p only (`HF-API@2026-09-18`) — a 1080p production take needs the web UI or an upscale (post-audio-legal ch. 17). **Exception to SKILL rule 13 (🟡 [PP]):** when the target-resolution generation loses scale or structure the draft had, route draft → scoped `video_edit` / upscale (W5, post-audio-legal ch. 17) instead of rerolling — a new Take ID (bible rule 3); offered, never forced, and draft pixels never go into the final. A defect accepted at the still stage propagates — surface that trade-off, the user decides.
Exit: approved take; anchor + statuses + render/take log rows in the bible.

records.title: W4 — Build a scene/sequence (trigger: several shots of one scene; anything longer than one take)
records.text:
## W4 — Build a scene/sequence (trigger: several shots of one scene; anything longer than one take)
1. Plan in shots (4–12 s), generate in takes: 1–3 internal shots per take (single shot for calm single-event beats, 2–3 only where a cut is needed for pace or coverage — production-pipeline ch. 2), every internal shot's anchor attached and time-scoped (production-pipeline ch. 1), explicit ENDING STATE, never a dramatic peak at a take's end (SKILL rule 2, ch. 14).
2. Chain takes with state chaining: each take's prompt begins from the previous ENDING STATE ("continue forward, do not replay"). Pick ONE join mechanism per model, never both for the same join: Seedance 2.5 → `video_extension` (30 s base + ONE extension round ≈60 s, boundary-frame contract each round from the last CLEAN frame of the raw export, then re-anchor a NEW generation from the original references — ch. 14b; no cold stitching, no harvested start frame; harvest the source's last frame only to WRITE the boundary state); models without a native extension mode (Seedance 2.0; check renderability §6 for others) → harvest the final frame as the next take's start frame — the chain case, rule 1's case (a) — case (b), the two-still interpolation, is the other; outside chained continuation the anchor is a reference, not a start frame (production-pipeline ch. 1).
3. Dialogue scenes: shot/reverse-shot with the multi-plate set + 180° lock (production-pipeline ch. 7; multi-plate set platforms-models ch. 13b); strongest lock = 3D blockout path (production-pipeline ch. 8). No recipe overrides the in-take axis lock (director-recipes header).
4. Assemble; the score is built in post — never in the video model (rule 10).
Exit: scene cut together from approved takes; continuity ledger (bible section B7) updated (ch. 19).

records.title: W5 — Repair a faulty take (trigger: a take that passed the hard rejects and won its batch by emotion — post-audio-legal ch. 19 verdict order — has a local fault)
records.text:
## W5 — Repair a faulty take (trigger: a take that passed the hard rejects and won its batch by emotion — post-audio-legal ch. 19 verdict order — has a local fault)
Seedance 2.5: never reroll an approved take for a local fault (rule 13) — route by the table. Other models: use the last three rows (Genjutsu on Higgsfield · no scoped edit route · global fault).
| Fault | Fix |
|---|---|
| Wrong object/face/detail in a region or time window | `video_edit`, region description + explicit time scope (ch. 14b/14) |
| Right performance, wrong camera | camera-perspective edit — segmented camera plan, everything else locked (ch. 14b); [PP]-unproven, one test, then rung 3 of W6 |
| Right performance, wrong environment | green-screen relocation via `omni_reference` (ch. 14b) |
| Wrong subject, right timeline | subject swap + Timeline Inheritance clause (ch. 14) |
| Audio only (music/voice/language/SFX) | audio-category edit — never touch pixels (ch. 14b) |
| Too short / scene continues | `video_extension` with boundary-frame contract (ch. 14b) |
| Wrong object, prop, wardrobe or location in an existing clip, any model's output, on Higgsfield | **Genjutsu — Object Swap** (Video → model selector → Genjutsu; one clip ≤30 s + up to 30 reference photos, output ≤1080p; `HF-WEB@2026-09-04`, changelog 2026-09-01) — untested here [🟡]; confirm the live form and treat the result as a new Take ID |
| Model/surface has no scoped edit route for this fault (Seedance 2.0, Kling, Veo, Grok; check the model's quick profile, renderability §6, and the surface in platform-ui-workflows — Runway = Aleph 2.0 Edit Studio, H3 = V2V edit) | harvest clean 2–4 s as coverage (production-pipeline ch. 10), fix the weakest instruction in the rule-15 order (remove → change → add), regenerate; `extend` only where the model offers it (Veo 3.1, Seedance) |
| Fault is global (style, light, physics everywhere) | back to the prompt in the rule-15 order — REMOVE first (every line on an axis the model owns and every second mention of a thing), CHANGE one line second, ADD only third; the word count never rises — then regenerate (production-pipeline ch. 1 review loop) |
Constraints (ch. 14b): source ≤20 s recommended, 1–5 refs; edits bill the source's full duration; ≤3 edit rounds per source, then branch from the best intermediate .mov export as the new @Video 1 (ch. 14b edit-round ceiling). Every edit result is a new Take ID (bible rule 3).
Exit: fixed take approved; its RECEIPT KEY and render/take log row noted in the bible.

records.title: W6 — Get a new angle / coverage (trigger: a reverse, insert, or B-camera view is needed on an EXISTING take, an approved still set or a filmed clip; planned reverse plates for dialogue/cross-room sets are pre-production → W2 step 3)
records.text:
## W6 — Get a new angle / coverage (trigger: a reverse, insert, or B-camera view is needed on an EXISTING take, an approved still set or a filmed clip; planned reverse plates for dialogue/cross-room sets are pre-production → W2 step 3)
Climb the ladder, exhaust each rung (ch. 16):
1. New angles as internal shots of the SAME take (cheapest, most reliable).
2. Harvest frames from an existing successful generation as references (last frame + "continue forward, do not replay"); or ONE camera-perspective edit on the approved take (B-camera pass — [PP]-unproven, budget one test only, bills the source's full duration; ch. 16 rung 2, ch. 14b). A filmed clip takes the same two routes — edit keeps its timing, reference re-creates the scene (ch. 16 rung 2). A failed single test → rung 3, not a second edit.
3. Still needed as a STILL: a purpose-built angle tool IF the live Higgsfield shell has one (production-pipeline ch. 16 tool section: undated, verify in the tool picker and mint a fresh receipt first) or GPT Image 2.5 WITH a layout map — never free-text "same scene from behind". Reverse test: anchors, openings, light side, palette against the master plate.
4. Nothing pins → geometry inputs: 3D blockout/clay render (production-pipeline ch. 8; video-prompting ch. 14b).
Exit: coverage that passes the reverse test.

records.title: W7 — Define & lock a style (trigger: user names a director/film/mood, or the look drifts)
records.text:
## W7 — Define & lock a style (trigger: user names a director/film/mood, or the look drifts)
1. User names a direction → `director-recipes.md` selection index; cap = ONE director recipe + at most ONE DoP signature (two packages, one dominant); two directors named → synthesis (selection index step 6), never two recipes side by side.
2. Build the project style anchor (the style-contract paragraph) from look-defining references via LLM reverse-engineering (style-control §7), or from the vocabulary packages (style-control §6) — plus its look tokens (8–10 for a Caption Spine, 4–8 for the block structure, none in technique C — SKILL.md Workflow step 4).
3. Stylized 3D: figure anchor or style-forcing blocks (SKILL rule 9; pixar-look §8/§9).
4. Validate on ONE still + one motion-ladder test per model before rolling out (style-control §5b); the recipe's Verify line becomes the standing reroll gate (replacing a DEFAULT line from W1 step 5).
5. Write the final style anchor + look tokens into the bible (section B2); from then on it is canon, distributed into every prompt per SKILL.md Workflow step 4.
Exit: style anchor + look tokens + Verify line in the bible + a passing verify still.

records.title: W8 — A generation keeps failing (trigger: one prompt has failed on the same axis on a full batch of 4, or two iterations in a row)
records.text:
## W8 — A generation keeps failing (trigger: one prompt has failed on the same axis on a full batch of 4, or two iterations in a row)
1. Suspect the PROMPT first (in first-party production sessions [PP, 🟡 heuristic, not a measured statistic] roughly 8 of 10 presumed model limits were prompt faults, SKILL rule 15): **for a STILL prompt count the words against the routed model+version's budget BEFORE reading the text** — past the budget, instructions that are present and correct are dropped silently, which is the single cheapest fault to miss (ch. 24b item 8; a video prompt has no house word ceiling) — then suspect OVER-instruction first (economy doctrine): read the seven `Lint` measures off the failed prompt and strip every sentence on an axis the model owns (SKILL.md Division of labour) and every second mention before anything else — then lint for internal contradictions, missing positive lock on the failing axis, stacked instructions on one axis, meta commentary (ch. 24b). Stills: run the eight-check lint (ch. 24i).
2. Count and repair per SKILL rule 15 (iteration = batch of 4 · remove → change → add · 3 failed iterations = short rewrite + channel change · 2 clean failures = model limit · 10–15 iterations = simplify the shot); routes: other model renderability §6, rescue §3, kept risk into the register (rule 11).
Exit: working result, or a documented model limit with a rescue.

records.title: W9 — Session open & close (trigger: every working session in an existing project)
records.text:
## W9 — Session open & close (trigger: every working session in an existing project)
Open: load the production bible FIRST (rule 12) — its frame decisions (model stack, look, prompting technique: rule 4) are the session's constants; read only the files the active runbook step names; revalidate the RECEIPT line (SKILL.md Scope & version; state per SKILL rule 17) for every active generation route before relying on a control.
Close: run the `[edit]`-tagged assembly checks of the project's Verify line on the assembled cut (director-recipes; they never gate a reroll); then update the bible LAST — add each actual generation/edit's KEY and render/take log row (section B4b) to the shot board and the delivery's Render Slates; statuses only on user approval, decisions as canon, open risks into the shot board's Risk → rescue cell (copied from the delivery risk registers); reviews the agent could not perform as `TKnn — review pending (director)` in Handoff; nothing outside the bible is canon. Offer ONCE per project (bible decision log: `feedback-to-skill offer: made / declined`) to feed genuinely new production findings back to the public skill (generalized, no project content — SKILL.md closing section).

records.title: W10 — Storyboard-first production model (trigger: a new project adopts the storyboard-first model; "how do we go about this"; any project with more than one camera axis per location, vertical geography, or a documented geography drift between takes)
records.text:
## W10 — Storyboard-first production model (trigger: a new project adopts the storyboard-first model; "how do we go about this"; any project with more than one camera axis per location, vertical geography, or a documented geography drift between takes)
Nine gated stages (stage 4, the animatic, is optional — the director may skip it on a short single-axis project; record the skip in the decision log). Each stage names its **Deliverable**, its **Gate** (what must exist before the next stage starts — a gate not passed means the next stage does not start) and its **Reads** (the only files opened in that stage). W10 adds no rules of its own: every rule it applies lives in the chapter it cites (production-pipeline ch. 1 build order, ch. 3 anchor standard, ch. 8 blockout trigger, ch. 9 storyboard roles, ch. 2 deliverable shape; production-take exception W3 step 6); W10 fixes the ORDER in which W1–W3 and W7 run and inserts the three planning artefacts (camera setup system, take/cut table, timed animatic) the later stages consume.

1. **Idea & brainstorming** — the director brings the idea; the agent moderates (story intake gate story-structures 23a, container offer 23f, causal change lint 23g). Reads: `genre-baselines.md` if a genre is named, `story-structures.md` 23a/23f/23g. Deliverable: logline + beat chain as a DRAFT proposal (SKILL rule 14), every beat written cause→effect (rule 16). Gate: the director confirms the logline AND the beat chain; an unconfirmed beat is not drawn in stage 3.
2. **Project briefing / bible** — create the bible (production-bible 22b) with story, look contract (W7 if a style is named), character/location/prop list (names + planned statuses), format, length, platform, model stack (W1 steps 3–5). Reads: `production-bible.md` 22a/22b, `renderability.md` §2–3, W1. Then the **renderability lint of the briefing**: classify EVERY beat against the renderability §2 rows — in particular "Physics as hero", "Tiny hero object", "Dark, figure-less macro", "Continuous approach over distance", "Cut back onto the same emissive object", "Long continuous camera moves", "Wide shots". Every red beat receives an ellipsis or still rescue (renderability §3) or is cut — BEFORE the storyboard. Why: these beat classes are the documented time-eaters; a storyboard that draws them plans shots that never come out. Deliverable: bible B1–B3 filled, beat-level risk register (SKILL rule 11 shape; the director's decision is written into `Why kept`). Gate: bible exists; no beat is red without a decided rescue.
3. **Storyboard = shot planning** — deliver the STORYBOARD of production-pipeline ch. 2, all four parts: (1) camera setup system per location, (2) look-free panels with setup tags and a/b pairs, (3) take/cut table with the state ladder, (4) layout map — and the ranking stated there (setup system + table + ladder + anchors bind; panels are the director's checking view). Reads: `production-pipeline.md` ch. 2 (shape, rules, export schema), ch. 4 (the setup system IS the reverse decision), ch. 8 (layout map), ch. 9 (storyboard roles; grey sketch template); `film-craft.md` for coverage grammar. Tool: **FilmFlow Pro** (`FILMFLOW-WEB@2026-09-07`, platform-ui-workflows ledger) is the recommended environment for stages 2–3 IF (a) its frames stay look-free (sketch/clay, no rendered look) and (b) it yields an agent-readable export in the production-pipeline ch. 2 schema; otherwise a Markdown shot board + grey image-model sketches. Gate: director sign-off on all four parts; the storyboard is linked in bible section B3b with version and sign-off date. From here every prompt is written from panel + setup line + take row — never from prose.
4. **Animatic — timing & montage simulation (OPTIONAL, before the sheets)** — play the storyboard as a TIMED reel to test montage, order, rhythm, causality and per-shot duration BEFORE any consistency asset is built. Each panel (or a/b pair) is held for its take-table `Len`; scratch audio (VO + temp music + timing markers) sets the true minimum durations — dialogue length is only real once spoken (SKILL rule 2: the take's `Len` is where this locks). Why HERE, before the sheets: the animatic needs NO final designs — only the load-bearing aspects of figures and locations sketched, i.e. the look-free panels stage 3 already produced (production-pipeline ch. 9 storyboard roles). Running it first is a GATE that kills, merges, reorders or shortens shots before sheet and render budget is spent on them — and the R3 rung below doubles as the earliest warning system for exactly the red-list beats (fast motion, hero physics, `Physics as hero`) flagged in stage 2, the beats most expensive to fix late. **Fidelity ladder — chosen PER BEAT (not per project); escalate only as far as the beat's open question demands:**
   - **R1 — held still + scratch audio:** order, duration, dialogue timing. Zero cost, the default rung.
   - **R2 — deterministic camera on the still** (Ken Burns push/pan/zoom, dissolves; or a first→last-frame interpolation between two panels of THIS shot — the SKILL rule 1 controlled move, not a performance): tests camera timing, reveals, cut rhythm. Deterministic, no drift, no model cost, re-editable (NLE / ffmpeg `zoompan`).
   - **R3 — sub-shot panels** (higher temporal resolution of one shot: several drawings per shot, played flip-book): tests action/motion timing for fast or complex beats — does the beat fit its seconds, or must it be split/elided (renderability §3). Three interchangeable ways to produce the in-betweens, all feeding the same reel: hand- or AI-drawn intermediate panels (deterministic, no model); cheap image-gen in the same rough sketch style; or a cheap low-res tween (480p, an old video model) / interpolation between two panels.
     - **R3 discipline (binding):** the in-betweens illustrate the ACTION PROGRESSION and TIMING only — never the performance, the optics, or the identity. Read duration and beat-fit; discard the model's specific motion. Letting a cheap tween's motion become canon plans the shot against motion the production model will not reproduce (a timing test laundered into false canon).

   Reads: `production-pipeline.md` ch. 2 (take/cut table + state ladder — the animatic PLAYS this), ch. 9 (storyboard roles; panels stay look-free); `film-craft.md` (editing, rhythm, coverage grammar); `renderability.md` §2–3 (the red beats the R3 rung stress-tests). Tool: FilmFlow Pro (`FILMFLOW-WEB@2026-09-07`, platform-ui-workflows ledger) already binds panels to shots with animatic playback and per-shot timing and fits R1/R2 directly (the same surface used for stages 2–3); otherwise an NLE or ffmpeg `zoompan`. For an R3 tween a cheap video route at 480p — mint a receipt first (SKILL rule 17). Deliverable: a timed animatic reel + a **revised take/cut table** — `Len` values locked or corrected, internal-shot counts decided (SKILL rule 2: calm beat = 1 shot; dynamic/dialogue = 2–3 cuts), continuity/causality flags raised (rule 16). Gate: director sign-off on the reel; the corrected `Len` and cut points are written back into the storyboard (B3b) and the take/cut table (B4) BEFORE the sheets start. The animatic never becomes a look reference and its R3 motion is never canon — it corrects timing and cut points, nothing else.
5. **Character & prop sheets (Elements)** — BEFORE the blockout: build-order case (c) of production-pipeline ch. 1 (the blockout needs the proportions; body length is the scale unit of the layout map — a numeric channel (SKILL rule 7); in prose scale stays a relation). W2 steps 2, 5 and 6 per character; prop sheets and state pairs per the state ladder (production-pipeline ch. 4). Iterate every sheet to the **anchor standard** (production-pipeline ch. 3: exact, never "good enough"). Reads: `production-pipeline.md` ch. 1 (order), ch. 3–4, `style-control.md` for the routed still model, W2. Gate: sheets approved (leads through the W2 step-6 lock gate), scale written as object relations in B3 (production-pipeline ch. 4).
6. **3D blocking / blockout** — the production-pipeline ch. 8 blockout, run as a stage under the **blockout trigger rule** (production-pipeline ch. 8: optional for one axis + flat geography, mandatory for vertical geography, several axes, or documented drift): one scene per location, every panel placed as a camera on it; viewport render per the production-pipeline ch. 8 blockout-video requirements (24 fps, overlays off, 3–5 s per move, ≈30 s reference budget) as the `@Clay Render` staging reference — role split blockout = camera/blocking/timing, images = look (production-pipeline ch. 8 mandatory companions). Tool-neutral (production-pipeline ch. 8 evidence tiers; Blender + Bridge MCP `HF-BRIDGE-MCP@2026-09-04` is the documented baseline). Reads: `production-pipeline.md` ch. 8, `video-prompting.md` ch. 14b (reference budgets, @Clay Render role line). Gate: blockout frames match the panels (framing, position, gaze direction); a mismatch is fixed in the blockout or marked on the panel — the panel is never redrawn to match the blockout.
7. **Location anchors** — plates AFTER the blockout (production-pipeline ch. 1 case (c)): the blockout frame or the layout schematic is the geography reference of the plate prompt, the look comes from the style contract (B2); light openings described as geometry per production-pipeline ch. 4. W2 step 3 and production-pipeline ch. 4 per location, one plate per setup that needs its own view. Storyboard panels never enter a generation (production-pipeline ch. 9 storyboard roles). Reads: `production-pipeline.md` ch. 4, `style-control.md`, W2 step 3. Gate: anchors exact (anchor standard, production-pipeline ch. 3) — light direction, scale, geography match the layout map.
8. **Draft takes at draft tier (720p)** — per take W3 steps 1–5: canon from panel + take row, receipt, lint, still anchor, batch of 4 at 720p; rule-15 iteration count. Reads: W3, W4 (chaining), W8 (failing), `video-prompting.md` ch. 12h / ch. 12 / style-control §6c per the project's technique (bible B1), ch. 14. Gate: the STRUCTURE of the take holds — cuts land on the take-table timecodes, continuity states in and out match, identities hold. Polish is not judged here.
9. **Production takes (1080p / 4K)** — W3 step 6: a new generation of the locked prompt at target resolution by default; its documented exception (draft → `video_edit` / upscale when the reroll loses scale or structure) applies as written there. Never cut draft pixels into the final: the draft cut fixes structure, not pixels. Then picture lock → audio → grade as dated stages (post-audio-legal ch. 17/18; dates in B6, state in B8). Reads: W3 step 6, W5, `post-audio-legal.md` ch. 17–19.
Exit: storyboard, setup system and take/cut table in the bible as canon (B3b, B4 columns filled); every shot at status ≥ take; picture lock dated.

**W10 house rules** (each lives in the chapter named; listed here so a session sees them together):
- Anchor standard — iterate until exact, deadline pressure does not lower it (production-pipeline ch. 3).
- A post-state needs a visible cause in frame — break point, debris, crack — or it reads as placed (state ladder, production-pipeline ch. 2; state pairs, production-pipeline ch. 4).
- Continuity between takes = the join mechanism of W4 step 2 (keeper's end frame per rule 1) + a position lock over all internal shots + one axis (production-pipeline ch. 6 position lock).
- Scale only as object relations, never adjectives (production-pipeline ch. 4; image-model-logic 24b).
- Light openings as geometry; light-geometry words generate rays (production-pipeline ch. 4).
- Actions as two states; an uninvolved object or a gaze direction is written only when the canon demands it or a run of this take has shown it drifting (production-pipeline ch. 6 position lock).
- Panels from an image model are independent inventions — consistency comes from the setup system on paper and the blockout in geometry; the storyboard says WHAT must stay the same, the blockout says HOW (production-pipeline ch. 9 storyboard roles).
- A storyboard without a camera setup system is unusable — free camera positions per panel produce the perspective inconsistency that later shows up in the takes (production-pipeline ch. 2).
- A storyboard is canon only when linked in the bible (section B3b); a document beside the bible is ignored by the next session.

records.title: SKILL
records.text:

name: ai-film-production

records.title: AI Film Production
records.text: Write, plan and prompt AI-generated film so no shot looks AI-generated: design around the models' failure classes (identity drift, physics errors, anatomy, interaction, broken in-frame text) instead of fighting them in post.

records.title: AI Film Production
records.text: **Language rule.** Conversation, treatments, scripts, shot tables, slate labels, intent lines and risk registers follow the user's language. **Every prompt code block is English** — every vendor-verbatim control string is English; a translated lock is an untested lock. Two exceptions: a dialogue/VO line stays verbatim in the project's dialogue language (bible section B1; on H3 inside its language tag, `<d>[Japanese] …</d>`), and prompt text the director supplies stays verbatim. Technical terms (`references/glossary.md`), IDs and @tags stay English/ASCII.

records.title: AI Film Production
records.text:
**Role.** The agent is the director's full crew — DoP, editor, gaffer, script consultant, line producer; the user is the director and the only approval instance. Advise, then follow the call.
- Flag a real risk ONCE per project, in plain language, and never gate on it — only canon gaps (rule 14) and status moves (rule 12) wait for the director. Never cite chapter numbers at the user.
- A heard warning goes into the bible shot board's `Risk → rescue` cell as `ACCEPTED by user <date>`, a declined offer into the decision log; without a bible, once per session.
- A feeling → propose the craft; an instruction → execute it and note its effect once; a named style → start from the recipes.

records.title: AI Film Production
records.text: **Economy and division of labour — the model is a specialist partner.** A video prompt states only what is explicitly necessary for the beat or deliberately steered for the look (the **economy doctrine**). Every further line costs three times: complexity, contradiction risk (an agent is not consistent across thirty prompts), and budget, where it pushes a load-bearing line out. Prompts that locked every axis, quantified every value and hung an exclusion list on every reference ran at roughly 80 % rejects; a 250-word prompt on the same take reproduced its beat structure four of four [PP 2026-09-14, `references/sources.md`]. The rejects were prompt faults, not render faults: contradictions inside the prompt, technical instead of scenic description, absolute sizes without a scale, missing acting directions, inconsistent timing and geography, metaphors that pull off-theme, working lines dropped between revisions. Length is not limited — a prompt that states what belongs in it, once, limits itself (ch. 12h). The default allocation (🟢 house doctrine, every video model):

records.title: AI Film Production
records.text:
| The model owns by default — nothing is written here unless deliberately steered | The agent always owns — exactly this is written |
|---|---|
| camera composition inside a named shot size · in-take cutting and cut timing · character motion and body mechanics · material rendering · light behaviour and falloff · transitions · the physics of simple contact actions | what is in the scene · what happens in which order, and the state each beat ends in · which reference carries which single job · canon fidelity (the written beat) · one camera line where continuity across internal cuts requires it |

records.title: AI Film Production
records.text:
- Steer a model-owned axis only when (a) the canon says it in so many words, (b) the look needs exactly that control — a lens, an aperture, a colour temperature, a light direction — or (c) a failed run of THIS take showed the model doing that one thing against the canon. Then one statement, in the beat or block it concerns, listed in the slate's `Crew choices`.
- "I don't trust the model" is not a reason for any line.
- A *run* is one batch of 4 rolls judged as one iteration (rule 15); a fault "shown in a run" means the batch failed on that axis, never one odd roll. A new steer or a first exclusion after ONE failed run; restating an existing exclusion after TWO.

records.title: Precedence — when two instructions collide
records.text: ## Precedence — when two instructions collide

records.title: Precedence — when two instructions collide
records.text:
1. An explicit director instruction wins (Role).
2. Project canon (bible → approved script → approved treatment) beats any skill default.
3. The always-rules beat reference-file text — EXCEPT where a reference chapter names the rule it narrows ("Reconciled with SKILL rule N", "exception to SKILL rule N"); such an exception applies inside its stated scope only.
4. Reference chapters beat examples and templates (worked-example.md, the 22b template) where they differ.
5. Between two reference rules: (a) a ⚠️-marked conflict is settled by the sentence next to the marker; (b) a rule scoped to the model, platform or scenario at hand beats a general rule — a technique chapter beats ch. 12g for a named model; (c) otherwise 🟢 outranks 🟡 outranks 🔴, and at equal label the source tier decides (sources.md legend): vendor documentation and first-party measurement [PP] > platform tutorials and established practitioners > single social finds, which never win a frontal contradiction with a vendor statement without striking proof. A rule learned on an older model version holds on the newer one until version-specific information says otherwise.
6. Routing table, always-rules, per-prompt checklist and Workflow are cumulative layers (what to read → constraints → order of work → order of deliverables), not competitors.
