| Headroom/lead room | Comfort norms | Break them (crowded headroom, no lead room) for unease |
| Depth layering | Immersion, scale | Always name FG/MG/BG (ties into location plates) |
| High vs. low horizon | Sky = fate/freedom; ground = weight/burden | Establishings, emotional wides |
| Balance/imbalance | Stability vs. tension | Tilt/dutch and asymmetry signal "something is wrong" |
**Aspect ratio is a meaning choice, not a delivery spec:** 2.39:1 = landscape/scope/fate · 1.85/16:9 = neutral human · 4:3/1.19 = portrait pressure, intimacy, past · 9:16 = phone-native presence. Choose per story before production (master strategy: post-audio-legal ch. 17); a mid-film ratio change is a legitimate marked device (memory, constriction).
**Combination logic:** pick ONE dominant compositional idea per shot; a second one only in service of the first. Composition changes across a scene should track the emotional arc (ordered → fragmented as a situation degrades).

records.title: 3. Camera: position, angle, movement, lens
records.text:
## 3. Camera: position, angle, movement, lens
**Height/angle:** eye level = neutral/human · low angle = power, monumentality, threat · high angle = weakness, overview, fate · overhead/top-down = pattern, godview, death · dutch = instability. Child/creature worlds: camera AT the character's eye height turns sets monumental (write the height as a relation — "lens level with the child's eyes"; a specific FOV only as a deliberate look control, ch. 12d).
**Distance is intimacy:** EWS context → WS body language → MS conversation → CU emotion → ECU obsession/detail. Move closer as stakes rise; a scene's tightest framing should land on its emotional peak.
**Movement grammar (motivate every move):**
| Move | Reads as | Motivated by |
|---|---|---|
| Static/locked | Observation, tension, dignity | Letting performance play; dread (what moves inside the frame?) |
| Pan/tilt | Attention shift | Following gaze or subject |
| Dolly in | Rising importance, realization | Emotional intensification (slow) or threat (fast) |
| Dolly out | Abandonment, context reveal, ending | Loss, punchline reveals, closing shots |
| Tracking/lateral | Accompaniment, parallel life | Walk-and-talks, journeys |
| Crane/rise | Overview, transcendence, epilogue | Openings/closings, scale reveals |
| Handheld | Presence, nervousness, documentary truth | Subjectivity, chaos — dose it, don't default |
| Orbit | Inspection, disorientation, iconization | Hero moments, revelations; expensive — earn it |
| Zoom (vs dolly) | Artificial attention, period flavor | 70s look, crash-zoom comedy/doc |
| Crash zoom in / out | Shock, sudden realisation, comic emphasis (in); absurd context reveal, punchline (out) | A discovery or a gag beat — the 70s / Kill Bill register [P59] |
| Snorricam / body mount | Panic, intoxication, dissociation — the head locked, the world lurching | Subjective crisis; the worn-product shot (video-prompting 12e) [P59] |
| Earth zoom-out · infinite zoom · tilt-shift | From one human moment to the whole world · surreal reveal · model-world detachment | Openings, closings, dream and scale devices — cheap in AI, dose them [P59] |
**Lens psychology:** wide = space dominates, distortion near the lens, energy · normal = human truth · tele = compression, surveillance, intimacy-from-distance, isolated subject on creamy BG. Depth of field: deep = the world matters; shallow = only the subject matters. (Degrees per video-prompting ch. 12d — a deliberate look control, never a default; by default the lens is the model's and the psychology is written as words: SKILL rule 7.)

records.title: 4. Editing
records.text:
## 4. Editing
**Cut types & when:**
| Cut | Function |
|---|---|
| Hard cut on action | Invisible continuity — cut mid-movement, the motion hides the seam |
| Match cut (graphic/motion) | Poetic linkage across space/time; scene transitions |
| Cut on look (eyeline) | Question → answer: face looks, next shot shows what they see (Kuleshov: the pairing CREATES the emotion) |
| J-cut (audio leads) | Pulls forward, smooth scene entry — sound of the next scene starts under the current one |
| L-cut (audio trails) | Reaction room — we watch listeners while the speaker continues |
| Jump cut | Time compression, nervous energy, comedy of repetition |
| Smash cut | Violent contrast (loud→silent, calm→chaos); comedy and shock |
| Cutaway/insert | Detail emphasis, tension objects, hiding continuity errors |
| Cross-cutting | Parallel action = suspense engine; alternate locations, tighten intervals toward collision |
| Ellipsis | Skip the unfilmable/boring; the audience's mind bridges (also the AI rescue tool, renderability) |
| Scene transitions | Sound bridge (audio crosses the cut — the workhorse) · match dissolve (time passing, memory) · hard black (chapter weight) · whip/wipe (playful momentum, period flavor) — pick ONE transition language per film |
**Rhythm:** shot length is tempo. Long takes = immersion, dread, dignity; short = urgency, chaos. The classic suspense curve SHORTENS shot lengths toward the climax, then holds one LONG shot at the peak. Cut on motion, breath, or beat; in dialogue, cut on the reaction, not the line end — the listener's face usually carries the scene. **Editing dramaturgy:** every cut must answer a question the previous shot raised, or raise a new one; if neither, the cut (or the shot) is redundant.
🟢 **Murch's Rule of Six (In the Blink of an Eye) — the cut-decision priority ladder:** Emotion (51%) > Story (23%) > Rhythm (10%) > Eye-trace (7%) > Planarity/stage-line (5%) > 3D spatial continuity (4%). Never sacrifice a higher item for a lower one; when forced to choose, spatial continuity is the FIRST thing to give up and emotion the last — "if the emotion is right, the audience tends not to notice lower-order problems." AI corollary: this is the license the whole skill runs on — a take with a minor continuity artifact but the right emotion BEATS a technically clean take that feels wrong; pick takes by the ladder, top down. **Scope:** the ladder ranks only takes that have already passed the hard rejects (slop tell, identity failure — post-audio-legal ch. 19 verdict order); "minor continuity artifact" means a ledger-level detail repaired in the edit (workflows W5), never a rendering tell or a lost identity.

records.title: 5. Light
records.text:
## 5. Light
**Systematics:** key (main source, sets direction) · fill (controls shadow depth) · rim/back (separation, halo). **Key-to-fill ratio is mood:** low contrast/high fill = open, safe, comedic, corporate · high contrast/low fill (chiaroscuro) = drama, secrecy, noir. **High-key** (bright, few shadows): comedy, romance, ads. **Low-key** (dominant shadow): thriller, noir, horror.
**Direction:** front = flat/honest · side = texture, inner conflict (half-lit face) · back = silhouette, mystery, sanctity · top = judgment, interrogation, shadowed eyes · under = wrongness, campfire horror.
**Motivation:** every light needs an in-world source (window, lamp, fire, moon) — unmotivated light reads artificial; stylization may exaggerate a motivated source but not invent sourceless light (Calahan doctrine, pixar-look §4).
**Quality & color:** hard light (small source) = edges, drama, harshness · soft light (big/diffused) = beauty, youth, calm. Warm↔cool contrast on one subject = inner conflict/decision point; the practical-in-frame (visible source) anchors realism and is the single strongest atmosphere tool.
**Time of day as meaning:** golden hour = nostalgia/hope · midday hard sun = exposure, mercilessness · blue hour = melancholy, threshold states · night+practicals = intimacy or danger by ratio.

records.title: 6. Color
records.text:
## 6. Color
**Schemes:** complementary (orange-teal: energetic, commercial) · analogous (harmony, calm) · monochrome+accent (control; the accent color becomes narrative) · triadic (playful, comic-book). **60/30/10** distribution keeps schemes readable.
**Color as arc, not decor:** define per act/sequence a palette temperature AND saturation; shifts must track the story (desaturation with loss; a new color entering with a new force). A recurring "signature color" bound to a character/idea pays off when it transfers (the antagonist's color creeping into the hero's world).
**Meaning is contextual, not absolute:** red = passion/danger/power, blue = distance/calm/sadness, green = nature/poison/uncanny, yellow = warmth/madness, white = innocence/void, black = authority/death — the FILM defines the code by consistent use; establish it early, then exploit it.
**Grade discipline:** one grade concept for the whole film (post-audio-legal ch. 17); scene-level deviations only as marked story beats (flashback, other world).

records.title: 7. Timing & pacing
records.text:
## 7. Timing & pacing
**Scene micro-rhythm:** enter late, leave early — start the scene at the last possible moment, cut before the energy dies. **Beat = smallest unit of change** (a want meets an obstacle, something shifts); a scene without a turn is a cuttable scene.
**Tension mechanics:** suspense = audience knows MORE than the character (show the bomb under the table) · surprise = knows less · dramatic irony sustains whole sequences. Delay is the engine: the cutaway before the door opens, the pause before the answer. **Silence and stillness are beats,** not gaps — the held look after bad news IS the content (the post-flashback processing rule generalizes: after every heavy beat, give 1–2 s of visible processing before new information).
**Payoff economics:** every setup pays off (Chekhov), every payoff was set up; the gap between them is proportional to the payoff's weight.

records.title: 8. Dramaturgy
records.text:
## 8. Dramaturgy
**Macro:** the container is chosen in story-structures ch. 23 (23b three-act, 23e non-submersible units = sequence blocks, 23d short-film); one sequence = one production block.
**Scene level:** every scene has an owner (whose scene is it?), a want, an obstacle, and a turn; write the audience question the scene asks and make the last shot answer or sharpen it.
**Openings:** cold open on motion/question; establish the WORLD-rule of the film in the first 30 s (tone, style, what kind of film promises what kind of ending). **Endings:** the final image is the thesis — plan it first, shoot toward it.
**Blocking & staging (the director's invisible language):** blocking = who stands/moves where; staging = the whole frame's orchestration around it. Working vocabulary: **crosses** (a move across the space = energy shift, re-anchors attention) and **counter-crosses** (opposed movement = conflict made spatial) · **levels** (sitting/standing/elevated = power dynamics without a word) · **foreground shift** (moving a character forward = agency claimed; backward = retreat) · **grounding props & business** (props and small physical tasks ground performances and motivate pauses) · **stillness as statement** (the one who does NOT move owns the scene) · distance between bodies = the relationship's current temperature; who turns their back = the scene's verdict. Blocking also sets TEMPO: movement accelerates a scene, stillness forces the audience to sit in it. Plan blocking on a floor plan before framing — the frame then selects from truthful movement instead of inventing it (in AI production this IS the layout-map/3D-blockout layer, production-pipeline ch. 8).
**Character in shots:** want vs. need readable in behavior, not dialogue; props as externalized inner state.

records.title: 9. Combining the elements (the DoP conversation)
records.text:
## 9. Combining the elements (the DoP conversation)
Decision order per scene: (1) whose scene + what feeling → (2) the ONE dominant device carrying that feeling (a move? a light state? a cut pattern? a color shift?) → (3) all other elements set to NEUTRAL-supporting so the dominant device reads → (4) plan the scene's arc as a change in exactly that device. Everything-loud = nothing-loud: a scene that changes lens grammar, light, palette, AND rhythm at once reads as style soup. Across scenes, contrast is the tool: after loud comes quiet, after tight comes wide — the alternation IS the film's breathing.
When the user gives a concrete instruction, execute it and state (once, briefly) what it will do to the audience; when the user gives a feeling, propose the device stack via this file; when the user names a style, start from `director-recipes.md` and adapt.

records.title: Genre Baselines: Entry Points & Skill Filters
records.text: # Genre Baselines: Entry Points & Skill Filters

records.title: Genre Baselines: Entry Points & Skill Filters
records.text: The FIRST file to read when a project's genre is known. Per genre: the audience contract, craft defaults (vocabulary from film-craft.md), subgenre shifts, a recipe shortlist (director-recipes.md), AI-production notes, and a **skill filter** — which files belong in context for this project type. Baselines are starting points the user bends, never rules — and look decisions, not prompt boilerplate: a default enters a prompt only where the beat needs it and is listed in `Crew choices` (economy doctrine, SKILL rule 7).

records.title: Genre Baselines: Entry Points & Skill Filters
records.text: Tags and confidence labels: legend in sources.md. **Always in context regardless of genre:** SKILL.md (routing + always-rules). Add per the filter lines below (SKILL.md Task routing, operation 3, opens them only via this filter line, the spine runbook, or the per-prompt checklist); load video-prompting.md when prompts are actually being written.

records.title: Genre Baselines: Entry Points & Skill Filters
Action
records.text:
## Action
**Contract:** kinetic clarity — the audience must always know who, where, and what's at stake mid-chaos. **Defaults:** sequence-approach structure (setpieces as mini-films) · escalating setpiece scale · geography established BEFORE chaos (one orienting master per beat) · shot lengths shorten into impacts, one long "oner" showpiece per act · wide-to-tight lens pattern, low angles on heroes · hard motivated light, high contrast · desaturated base + heat accents · impacts on the cut, silence before the biggest hit. **Subgenres:** martial-arts (longer takes, full bodies in frame, choreography readable) · car/chase (parallel cross-cutting, cockpit inserts, wheel rules) · disaster (scale reveals, crowd logistics) · superhero (icon poses as held frames). **Recipes:** Greengrass × Kamiński / Kurosawa × Kamiński (combat realism — verité chaos or ensemble motion and weather) · Nolan × Hoytema (engineered setpieces at monumental scale) · Leone × Storaro (standoff tension in operatic hue) · Wachowskis/Pope (wire-fu techno-noir; house signature, no DoP). **AI notes:** fights = attack–reaction beats cut in the edit (renderability §3); vehicles/wheels rescue paths; crowd rules; blockout path for complex camera chains (production-pipeline ch. 8). **Filter:** renderability.md (critical) · production-pipeline.md · film-craft.md §3–4.

records.title: Spy / Espionage
records.text:
## Spy / Espionage
**Contract:** controlled paranoia — information is the weapon, watching is the action. **Defaults:** cross-cut parallel operations · surveillance grammar (long-lens compression, foreground occlusion, observation patterns — video-prompting ch. 12e) · immaculate wides for glamour variants, gray realism for le-Carré variants · practicals in offices/safehouses, faces half-lit · steel blue/gray + amber interior pockets · quiet tension, sudden violence in short bursts. **Subgenres:** glamour spy (anamorphic gloss, location-spectacle establishing shots, tux-and-neon) · bureaucratic/le Carré (static frames, fluorescent light, silence, paper) · action-spy (borrow Action defaults for setpieces only). **Recipes:** Fincher (surgical watching; house signature, no DoP) · Nolan × Hoytema (mechanism at sober scale) · Hitchcock × Willis (suspense grammar in institutional darkness). **AI notes:** observation patterns are copy-ready (ch. 12e); dialogue-heavy → reverse plates + 180° lock mandatory; in-frame documents/screens = post-compositing. **Filter:** film-craft.md §4/§7 (suspense mechanics) · renderability.md · platforms-models.md if multi-model.

records.title: Horror
records.text:
## Horror
**Contract:** dread before shock — the audience imagines worse than you can show. **Defaults:** withholding as system (off-screen space, negative space, what the frame does NOT show) · slow static or creeping camera; handheld only in panic peaks · low-key light, single motivated sources, pools in darkness · underexposure trusted · desaturated cold base, one signal color · long silence, sound-before-source, held shots past comfort · the monster in fragments until the latest possible reveal. **Subgenres:** found footage (UGC recipe wholesale — device logic, four-tell rule) · supernatural/haunted (Kubrick geometry, Lynch wrongness) · slasher (POV shots, Hitchcock look-triads) · body horror (macro detail, texture emphasis) · folk horror (daylight dread — inverted: bright wides, wrongness in openness). **Recipes:** Kubrick (fate geometry; house signature, no DoP) · Lynch / Hitchcock × Young (faces must stay readable) or × Willis (unreadable eyes are the point) · Ridley Scott (layered-atmosphere dread; house signature, no DoP). **AI notes:** darkness hides model artifacts (advantage); found footage = highest artifact tolerance; gore is a content-policy boundary — imply via reaction and aftermath (also better craft). **Filter:** film-craft.md §5/§7 · renderability.md §3 · style-control.md §6b (footage authenticity).

records.title: Thriller
records.text:
## Thriller
**Contract:** the audience knows more than the character (suspense) or exactly as little (mystery) — pick per scene, mostly the former. **Defaults:** bomb-under-the-table cross-cutting · delay engines (cutaways before doors, pauses before answers) · tightening framings as the net closes · clean controlled camera drifting ever closer · low-key motivated light, venetian/architectural shadow patterns · cool desaturation, sickly practicals · relentless even pacing, no wasted scene. **Subgenres:** psycho-thriller (subjective camera, unreliable frames, Lynch borrowings) · conspiracy (70s grammar: zooms, long-lens voyeurism, Willis darkness) · survival (geography as antagonist, wide isolation frames). **Recipes:** Fincher (the genre default; house signature, no DoP) · Hitchcock × Willis (grammar source in moral darkness) · Villeneuve × Fraser (slow-dread variant — texture alive in deep shadow). **AI notes:** dialogue discipline (production-pipeline ch. 7) carries most scenes; suspense = editing structure, cheap to generate — the craft is in the cut order, not the pixels. **Filter:** film-craft.md §4/§7 (core) · renderability.md · post-audio-legal.md ch. 19 (continuity ledger — thrillers punish continuity errors hardest).

records.title: Crime
records.text:
## Crime
**Contract:** procedure meets morality — solving as narrative spine, milieu as texture. **Defaults:** scene-of-crime grammar (detail inserts, top-down pattern shots) · interview/interrogation coverage (two-sided reverse plates, table geometry) · milieu realism in light (available, unglamorous) · muted palette with era/city identity · measured pacing with discovery beats · voiceover legitimate (noir lineage). **Subgenres:** noir (hard keys, blinds, night-wet streets, fatalist VO) · Scandinavian (gray daylight, institutional interiors, silence) · heist (mechanism structure — Nolan cross-cut planning/execution, playful tempo) · cozy/whodunit (warm palette, ensemble tableaus, Anderson-adjacent order). **Recipes:** Fincher (procedural) · Gilligan (slow-burn empire/corrosion) · Scorsese (kinetic rise-and-fall) · Willis (dynasty darkness) · Nolan (heist mechanism) · Anderson (cozy variant). **AI notes:** interrogations = the dialogue-scene discipline verbatim; evidence close-ups (documents!) = in-frame-text rules; crime scenes = still-heavy, cheap to produce. **Filter:** film-craft.md §4/§8 · renderability.md §2 (text!) · production-pipeline.md ch. 7.

records.title: Drama
records.text:
## Drama
**Contract:** emotional truth — the audience watches people change. **Defaults:** performance first: coverage that protects acting (longer takes, reaction-side cutting, L-cuts for listening) · camera restraint (static/slow, moves only on emotional shifts) · naturalistic motivated light, window-side modelling · palette tracks the emotional arc (color script discipline) · scenes enter late/leave early but BREATHE inside · silence and processing beats as content. **Subgenres:** chamber (Bergman wholesale) · family/generational (Ozu stillness, seasons) · social realism (the Dardenne/Arnold recipe: following handheld, available light, no score) · romance (two-shot intimacy, warm practicals, Wong Kar-wai for longing variants) · coming-of-age (Malick fragments, golden memory). **Recipes:** Bergman × Nykvist (chamber — the face fully modelled) · Ozu × Nykvist (family stillness, tenderness) · Wenders × Müller (road and available light) · Malick × Lubezki (memory fragments in natural light) · Wong Kar-wai × Doyle (longing in neon smear) · Sciamma × Mathon (the exchanged gaze by flame and dusk) · Dardenne/Arnold (social realism — available light IS the signature, no DoP). **AI notes:** THE hardest genre for AI — everything hangs on face performance: multi-stage emotion formulas (ch. 14), acting micro-cues per the ch. 14 emotion formula, expression sheets; budget rerolls on emotional peaks. **Filter:** video-prompting.md ch. 14 (emotion formula) + the project's technique chapter (12h or 12) · film-craft.md §7–8 · pixar-look.md only if stylized.

records.title: Comedy
records.text:
## Comedy
**Contract:** timing is the content — the frame and the cut ARE the joke. **Defaults:** wider framings than drama (bodies + spatial relationships carry gags) · flat/even "sitcom-bright" light unless the joke needs mood · static camera lets comedy play; the pan/push-in AS punchline · hold after the gag (deadpan air) · rhythm: setup–beat–punch, rule of three, callback economy · reaction shots are the laugh multiplier. **Subgenres:** deadpan (Anderson wholesale: symmetry + metronome) · slapstick/physical (full bodies, longer takes, choreography readable — animation's home turf) · dark comedy (drama light + comedy timing, the collision is the tone) · rom-com (warm high-key, two-shot chemistry, montage sequences) · mockumentary (UGC/doc grammar + straight-face interviews). **Recipes:** Anderson (the precision pole) · ZAZ/Brooks (parody deadpan) · Allen lineage (master-shot talk) · Wright (comedy in the cut) · Boyle (kinetic-comedy energy) · UGC (mockumentary). **AI notes:** comedy timing lives in the EDIT — generate reaction coverage deliberately; slapstick choreography is written beat-by-beat — who does what in which order and the state each move ends in, never the body mechanics of a move (Division of labour), one main action per shot (SKILL rule 3) — never "he stumbles funny"; animation formats forgive and amplify physical comedy. **Filter:** film-craft.md §4/§7 (rhythm!) · director-recipes (Anderson) · production-pipeline.md ch. 2.

records.title: Biopic
records.text:
## Biopic
**Contract:** a life shaped into meaning — truth-adjacent, dramaturgically honest. **Defaults:** era grammar as system (period-correct palette, film-stock look, production design — style-control §6b era looks) · structure choice UP FRONT: cradle-to-grave vs. decisive-window vs. mosaic — decisive-window by default (one want, one turn); cradle-to-grave only at feature length; mosaic when the material is images and feelings more than events (23c) · archive-style inserts (era-matched footage grammar) as texture · restrained camera dignity, documentary borrowings for authenticity beats · one signature visual motif tied to the person. **Subgenres:** artist/musician (performance recreations — see Music film) · political (institutional grammar, Willis/Hoytema sobriety) · sports (training montage + event coverage grammar). **Recipes:** Spielberg (classical dignity) · Fincher (procedural lives) · Malick (memory-mosaic variant) + Kamiński (testimony). **AI notes:** REAL PERSONS = the legal boundary — likeness/voice only with documented consent, AND test platform acceptance of the face before casting a licensed likeness (moderation plan, post-audio-legal ch. 20); fictionalized-inspired characters are the safe route; era looks are cheap style wins. **Filter:** post-audio-legal.md ch. 20 (critical, first) · style-control.md §6b · film-craft.md §8.

records.title: Documentary (style)
records.text:
## Documentary (style)
**Contract:** credibility — the form must read as witnessed, not staged. **Defaults:** interview grammar (eyeline just off-lens, motivated window/practical light, shallow-focus environment context) · B-roll logic (cutaways that PROVE the narration) · handheld observational restraint, zoom-and-refocus honesty · available light doctrine · lower-third/archive conventions (post!) · VO or interview audio as spine, ambience beds. **Subgenres:** nature doc (long-lens patience, macro grammar, Attenborough pacing) · true crime (reenactment style: soft-focus anonymity, moody reconstruction light) · essay film (Wenders/Malick contemplation) · vérité (no interviews, pure observation). **Recipes:** Wenders (essay) · Greengrass (vérité energy) · UGC (raw witness) + Lubezki (nature-poetic). **AI notes:** AI-generated "documentary" of real events is a disclosure minefield (ch. 20 EU AI Act) — fictional subjects or clearly-labeled reconstruction; the doc LOOK itself is low-risk and artifact-tolerant; interview talking-heads = lip-sync quality gate — build them via the interview path (production-pipeline ch. 7b: audio-first, B-roll escape, coverage convention). **Filter:** production-pipeline.md ch. 7b (interviews) · post-audio-legal.md ch. 18/20 · style-control.md §6b · renderability.md.

records.title: Anime (as genre dramaturgy)
records.text:
## Anime (as genre dramaturgy)
**Contract:** heightened emotion made visible — inner states externalized as visual events. **Defaults:** emotion beats get HELD poses and full stops (sakuga economy: spend motion on peaks, hold between) · impact frames, speed lines, smears at action peaks · monologue-under-action convention legitimate · tournament/escalation arcs, named-attack beats · scenery pause shots (Ghibli "ma") as breathing · music-synced emotional crescendos. **Subgenres:** shōnen action (escalation ladders, power-up reveals) · slice-of-life (Ozu-adjacent stillness, seasonal markers) · mecha (scale grammar: human cockpit ↔ machine wide) · isekai/fantasy (establish world-rule early, travel montages). **Recipes:** Miyazaki (the humanist pole) · Leone (standoff DNA — anime inherited it) · Boyle (music-drive) + anime vocabularies (style-control §6). **AI notes:** high-action anime is a documented model SWEET SPOT (renderability §1); flat 2D punishes wobble — style-control §5b anti-3D rules; held poses are cheap AND correct here. **Filter:** style-control.md §5b/§6 (critical) · renderability.md · film-craft.md §7.

records.title: Family Animation ("Pixar/Disney" as dramaturgy, not look)
records.text:
## Family Animation ("Pixar/Disney" as dramaturgy, not look)
**Contract:** two audiences at once — sincere emotional core for everyone, wit layered for adults; the ending EARNS its warmth. **Defaults:** want-vs-need spine (hero pursues the want, discovers the need) · sidekick as externalized inner voice · villain-as-mirror or system-as-antagonist · gag-per-page density WITHOUT breaking sincerity · setpiece + heart-beat alternation ("laugh, laugh, gut-punch") · the all-is-lost beat before the truth · physical comedy choreographed like action · color script tracks the emotional arc explicitly (pixar-look §3). **Subgenres:** buddy/road (two-hander chemistry, Wenders structure in bright colors) · fish-out-of-water (world-rule comedy) · fairy-tale musical (see Music film for numbers). **Recipes:** Spielberg (wonder grammar) · Miyazaki (quiet pole) · Anderson (deadpan variant) + pixar-look.md as the visual bible when the look is also Pixar. **AI notes:** the format's error tolerance is the strategic reason to choose it (renderability §4); figure-anchor rule governs all stills; squash-and-stretch motion must be prompted or physics-correct models flatten the comedy. **Filter:** pixar-look.md (critical) · style-control.md · film-craft.md §7–8 · renderability.md.

records.title: Music Film / Musical
records.text:
## Music Film / Musical
**Contract:** emotion exceeds speech and becomes performance — the audience accepts the world singing. **Defaults:** numbers as setpieces with their own visual identity each · cut ON the beat, move WITH the phrase (audio-first workflow: track before image — post-audio-legal ch. 18 score logic inverted) · wide enough to prove the choreography, inserts for accents · light shifts mid-number legitimate (reality bends) · saturated palette jumps per number · between numbers: drama defaults apply. **Subgenres:** backstage/band story (doc grammar + performance setpieces) · dance film (full-body framing law, longer takes, floor visible) · concert film (coverage grammar: master + roaming + crowd + detail) · jukebox/montage (Boyle needle-drop structure) · music video (3–5-min single-track piece: ONE visual concept committed fully, any recipe legitimate, beat-cut discipline — the format with the widest stylistic license). **Recipes:** Boyle (music-cut DNA) · Wong Kar-wai (mood-music fusion) · Anderson (choreographed-frame numbers) + Storaro (number-per-color ideology). **AI notes:** audio-to-video path (music as timing skeleton, production-pipeline ch. 9) and beat-synced choreography prompting (audio reference as timing input — video-prompting ch. 14b [H-off, P48]); instrument fingering stays yellow (frame around it); song RIGHTS come first — ch. 18 licensing before any number is built. **Filter:** post-audio-legal.md ch. 18 (first!) · film-craft.md §4/§7 · production-pipeline.md ch. 9.

records.title: Commercial / Ad
records.text:
## Commercial / Ad
**Contract:** one message, remembered — every second earns its place; the product is protagonist or payoff, never wallpaper. **Defaults:** format dramaturgy by length (6 s: one gag/one image · 15 s: setup–payoff · 30 s: mini-arc · 60 s+: short-film grammar with brand restraint) · product-hero grammar (tabletop: macro detail, controlled highlights, slow orbital/reveal moves) · ONE polish position chosen up front: commercial sheen (Ridley Scott ad lineage — atmosphere, backlight, surface control) OR deliberate UGC authenticity — never both · light default for product/lifestyle spots: soft even daylight from the camera side, bright and clean — no backlight, no shadow-side framing [H-off, P48] (the 12c shadow-side default is drama doctrine) · end-card discipline: logo/claim/pack shot as designed graphics in post, never generated (renderability §2) · platform aspect ratios and casting decided before the first still. **Subgenres:** product/tabletop (food, cosmetics, tech — macro + slow moves, physics-risky pours/steam) · lifestyle/performance (people using it — drama/comedy defaults apply) · UGC-style ad (creator-camera authenticity; disclosure rules!) · brand film (60 s+, essay/doc grammar). **Recipes:** Ridley Scott (polished atmosphere) · Anderson (deadpan product tableaus) · Boyle (energy cut) · UGC (authenticity pole) + any genre recipe when the ad borrows or parodies one (ZAZ logic). **AI notes:** product geometry must match reality (legal!) — lock with reference images; food/liquid macro needs a physics lint on pours, steam, condensation; AI-disclosure duties per market (post-audio-legal ch. 20). **Filter:** renderability.md §2 (critical) · style-control.md (reference integration for the product) · post-audio-legal.md ch. 20 · platforms-models.md (per-platform deliverables).

records.title: How to use a baseline (agent instructions)
records.text:
## How to use a baseline (agent instructions)
1. Genre known → read this file's section → open the filter files through their contents blocks and read only the parts the runbook step or the task names (a bare file name in a filter line means "relevant for this genre", never "load it whole" — SKILL loading map) → state the defaults to the user as the working assumption in TWO sentences, not a lecture.
2. Baseline + user wishes → concrete craft plan; deviations from baseline are normal and the user's call.
3. Subgenre named → apply the shift on top of the base genre.
4. Genre mix ("horror comedy") → one genre owns STRUCTURE, the other owns TEXTURE; say which, ask only if truly ambiguous.

records.title: Glossary — the terms every rule uses (one meaning each)
records.text: # Glossary — the terms every rule uses (one meaning each)

records.title: Glossary — the terms every rule uses (one meaning each)
records.text: House doctrine (ranks 🟢, SKILL.md Precedence). Read this file when a term in a rule, slate or asset order is ambiguous — every term below has exactly one meaning in this skill; where a word carries several (anchor, sequence, lock, state), the qualified form is the one to write.

records.title: Glossary — the terms every rule uses (one meaning each)
records.text:
- **Shot** — planned unit, 4–12 s, one row of the shot table/board. **Take** — one generated video result (`TK01`…). **Draft take** — one roll of the batch of 4 at draft tier (480/720p, the take's planned length — 10 s by default; W3 step 5); the batch is the motion test of production-pipeline ch. 1 and, when it decides the technique, the rule-4 test. **Sequence take (`S<n>`, bible B4 `Seq. take`)** — the planned generation unit of 1–3 internal shots (rule 2, ch. 14); its generated results are Take IDs `TKnn`, never `S<n>`; **sequence (story)** — a run of scenes / the "sequence approach" (film-craft); say which when ambiguous.
- **Plate** — an approved still of a location (master wide or detail plate) used as a location reference; figure-less by default, but stylized/Pixar projects build **figure-anchored plates** first and derive the empty plate (production-pipeline ch. 1). **Reverse plate** — the same location generated from the counter-angle for shot/reverse-shot (production-pipeline ch. 4/16). **Sheet** — a character reference still set (turnaround/expressions, neutral light); **state sheet** — a new sheet for a persistent state change (wet, wounded, costume change).
- **Anchor still / `@anchor_<shot>`** — the approved still of a shot, registered as an element and attached as a reference (rule 1); bible asset Type "anchor" means only this. **Reference line** — the ONE line a reference gets in a prompt (SKILL rule 5): the *job sentence* in a Caption Spine (12h), the ACTIVE REFERENCES line in the block structure (its identity segment is 12b's *anchor line*), the *role line* of an @Audio/@Clay Render (14b); bible B3 column `Job line`. **Anchor line** — the one-line identity text after an @tag (ch. 12b), the identity segment of a block-structure reference line. **Style anchor** — the project's style-contract paragraph in the bible (section B2), carried per the project's technique (SKILL rule 4, Workflow step 4: STYLE line in A, distributed blocks in B, the Master Style Block in C) — never a bare keyword prefix. **Figure anchor** — a character placed in frame to force a stylized render (rule 9, pixar-look §8). **Anchor object** — the fixed prop in a location all staging is tied to (production-pipeline ch. 4). **Anchor composition** — a locked composition (camera setup + framing) that recurs across acts so that change reads as difference inside an identical frame (production-pipeline ch. 2 STORYBOARD). **Grounding props & business** — acting term: props/tasks that ground a performance (film-craft).
- **Lock (prompt)** — a positive sentence protecting one attribute (inside the beat it protects in a Caption Spine; in POSITIVE LOCKS in the block structure); **180° lock** — the axis-of-action rule for coverage; **locked (status)** — bible asset status after user approval (draft → approved → locked); **style lock** — W7, fixing recipe + style anchor + verify line.
- **Prompting technique** — the project-level choice of prompt shape from the SKILL rule-4 menu, taken with the director at intake and persisted with the frame decisions; never one-size-fits-all, never tied to a model version. **A — Caption Spine** — prose without a word ceiling: title sentence · STYLE line · character line(s) · optional location-style line · optional single camera line · timecode beats · "End with …" · one closing prohibition sentence (video-prompting ch. 12h). **B — Block structure** — the ch. 12 blocks SCENE CONTEXT … POSITIVE LOCKS for explicit per-axis control. **C — Master Style Block + story** — a 200–400-word physical-medium description opening the prompt, beats underneath (style-control §6c). **Economy doctrine** — a prompt states only what is explicitly necessary or deliberately steered; nothing twice, no contradictions, nothing out of distrust; look values (lens, aperture, Kelvin) are deliberate controls, never defaults. **Division of labour** — the SKILL.md default allocation, every video model: the model owns camera composition, cutting, body mechanics, material, light, transitions and simple contact physics unless the agent steers one deliberately; the agent always writes scene content, beat order and end states, one job per reference, canon, at most one camera line. **Relation (scale)** — the only admissible form of a size or distance in a prompt: a visible comparison between two things in the frame (rule 7); a **measure** (metres, degrees, millimetres, body-lengths, unit counts) is never written in prose.
- **ENDING STATE** — the last-frame description a take ends on and the next begins from (the "End with …" paragraph on the Caption Spine); **state** otherwise = an asset's persistent condition (state sheet).
- **Channel** — the control path an instruction travels by: prose, reference image, sketch, mask, seed, clay render, model choice (ch. 24b contract item 7). **Axis** — one controllable aspect of the output (size, count, position, light…); "three failures on one axis" = same aspect, unrelated to the 180° axis.
- **`@Clay Render`** — Seedance 2.5 reference class: a textureless 3D blockout video that carries camera movement, pacing, shot-size transitions and blocking (ch. 14b). **Style donor** — the reference declared to give its rendering style to the other references (style-control §7, pixar-look §10).
- **Shot board** — the bible's shot table (section B4); **storyboard** — in the storyboard-first model (W10) the four-part planning artefact of production-pipeline ch. 2 (camera setup system + panels + take/cut table + layout map); elsewhere drawn/previs frames with motion arrows. **Storyboard panel** — one look-free planning frame (grey sketch or blockout frame) with its setup tag and motion arrows; panel pair `a/b` = start and end state of one shot; never a generation reference. **Camera setup (`K1…`)** — a named camera position fixed in the location's floor plan: position, axis side, height, focal length, move; every shot belongs to exactly one setup — always write "camera setup", never bare "setup" (which also names the Cinema Studio settings). **Take/cut table** — the W10 table of which shots share one take, their internal timecodes, cut type (model / manual), continuity and position locks and reference set per take (export schema in ch. 2). **State ladder** — the ordered list of an object's visible states across the act (intact → cracked → broken), each with its in-frame cause; every step spawns a state sheet or state pair. **Position lock** — a sentence (POSITIVE LOCKS in the block structure; a half-sentence inside the beat in a Caption Spine) fixing where each character and object starts, faces and ends relative to the anchor object, carried verbatim across all internal shots of a take (production-pipeline ch. 6).
- **Animatic** — the timed reel of look-free panels played to test order, rhythm, causality and per-shot `Len` before any consistency asset is built (W10 stage 4, optional); it revises the take/cut table only — rungs R1–R3 are defined there.
- **Artefacts by name:** **treatment** = prose + one shot table per scene (Workflow step 5) · **prompt shot list** (= shot-level script) = the same Shot IDs, one Render Slate + code block per take, followed by one risk register · **shot board** = the bible's status view of the same rows · **reference pool** = the bible's asset registry (section B3) · **delivery note** = the risk register block that closes a prompt shot list (Receipt KEYs are cited in its slates).
