Three documented exceptions: (a) **static short text locked via master plate** — content frozen in the reference image + prompt lock "exactly this one line, frozen and identical in every frame" (production-proven, platforms-models ch. 13b); (b) 🟡 MiniMax H3 has an official quoted-text channel (visible text in double quotes, verbatim, untranslated [MM-off]) and renders UI/text comparatively stably — syntax documented, quality practitioner-rated: test before relying. Dynamic/changing text stays red everywhere. 🟡 Exception (c) — DESIGNED typography as the product: Higgsfield Marketing Studio's motion-design presets (launch video, hypermotion product ad, 2D and editorial explainer, 3D real-estate flythrough with pricing overlays) render text overlays, numbers and animated charts as the generation's subject, and the vendor shows them "locked, not melting" including minutes of editorial text [H-off, P68 — vendor demo, not frame-checked here]; a different generation class from a video model rendering incidental text. Every word and number is still checked against the script before delivery, and the rule for generative FILM shots is unchanged. 🟡 Exception (a) confirmed on 2.5 by [P54]: a one-word character-intro title generated INTO the Seedream 5.0 Pro still and carried by Seedance 2.5 over 20 s with a spelling lock in the prompt ("the name is Dan — exactly D-A-N, not Dann, not Dane") — single short static word, plate-locked; still the exception. |
| Crowds | Clone extras, melting faces in distance | Multi-variant sheet (production-pipeline ch. 3) with extras as silhouette-distinct CLASSES ("heavy brute" / "light scout") — classes, not outfit variants, kill the clone read; crowds to mid/background; small faces stay unreliable even at high res; fog capped as a visible relation ("everything past the third rank dissolves into fog" — never a distance in metres, SKILL rule 7) hides background glitches at army scale (less needed at 4K, still works) [H-off, P25]; formations (66 dancers in rings around a singer) hold across cuts when positions and facing come from blockout boxes and only the movement is prompted [H-off, P66]; a cast of ten distinct extras saved as one element stops per-shot face regeneration [H-off, P69] |
| Hands + fine object manipulation | Finger errors, object morphing | Close-ups only as short single-action beats, cut away before the fine work; the handling invariant is written once as a lock sentence — inside the beat on the Caption Spine (ch. 12h), as a POSITIVE LOCKS line in the block structure ("ALWAYS by the handle") — there is no separate CRITICAL block |
| Vehicles/wheels/mechanics | Wrong rotation, illogical mechanics | See rescue paths below |
| Long continuous camera moves | Collapse after several moves (proven in 2.5 too) | One move per shot; cuts instead of tours |
| Instrument fingering, precise sports technique | Approximate only | Frame around it; cutaways |
| Physics as hero (glass shattering exactly, complex fluid pours) | Plausible-but-wrong | Describe end state; hide peak behind cut |
| Tiny hero object carrying the beat (a key, a pill, a seed in a hand) | Object morphs, vanishes or changes size between frames; detail vs. size contradiction (ch. 24b) | Cut to an insert as its own short shot at close scale; carry the beat by the character's reaction; object as a prop sheet (production-pipeline ch. 4) |
| Dark, figure-less macro (no scale anchor, no figure, low light) | No scale read, no material read — the model fills with generic texture or invents a subject | Add a scale anchor or a figure (SKILL rule 9 on stylized projects), lift a motivated practical, or replace by a still + ellipsis |
| Continuous approach over distance (a walk/drive/flight that must close the gap on camera) | Scale collapses on the way (same class as wide-shot scale, above); the approach stalls or teleports | Two shots: departure state, arrival state — the distance is an ellipsis (manual cut); never one continuous take |
| Cut back onto the same emissive object (lamp, screen, fire) whose state must match frame-exactly | Brightness, colour temperature and shape differ between takes; the object appears "re-lit" | One state per state sheet (production-pipeline ch. 4); the second view inside the same take, or the object kept in one setup (W10 anchor composition); otherwise accept a grade-side match (post-audio-legal ch. 17) |
| **Wide shots** (stylized 3D; photoreal crowd scale too) | Scale and distance break at wide range; a flat camera path at constant height/speed leaves characters as dots (vendor-confirmed on Higgsfield's own short and its Hell Grind rebuild) | Open the take on a close/medium of the character and transition into the wide inside the same generation; positions locked by the previs/clay render, not by the wide (pixar-look §10) |
| Faces that must stay blank (silent passengers, listeners with no beat) | Model animates them anyway — micro-expressions, drift | Hide by design with a motivated occlusion: reflective glass, backlight silhouette, hat brim, distance — copy-ready GLASS block in video-prompting 12e |
| **Mirror/reflection beats** where a reflected face or pose must match the subject frame-exactly | Reflected face/pose diverges from the subject; reflection doubled, missing, or lagging a beat behind | 🟡 (derivation, not yet [PP]-tested) Reflections as texture/light — glass, water, wet street, chrome — stay GREEN on Seedance 2.5 (§1). For a story mirror beat: Seedance 2.5 only, static camera, ONE readable face in frame — either the reflection alone (subject from behind / over the shoulder) or the subject alone with the mirror as shape (film-craft §2 frame-in-frame); never subject and reflection both readable; otherwise split subject and reflection across a cut. 🟢 Blockout rescue [H-off, P66]: a camera passing THROUGH a mirror held in one 15-s continuous take when the set was blocked as a mirrored twin with both characters moving in sync and the mirror as an opening (production-pipeline ch. 8 protocol b). |

records.title: 2. Red/yellow list (avoid or mitigate)
records.text: **Feasibility answer ("can this scene be generated?") — fixed shape:** one verdict line (green / yellow with rescues / red), then a feasibility table (the pre-decision form of the rule-11 risk register; once the director decides, kept rows move into the rule-11 register unchanged in meaning): Beat or element | Rating 🟢🟡🔴 | Failure (§2 row) | Rescue (§3) | Decision (keep / rescue / cut — the director's, left blank until they decide). Never answer in prose only and never rewrite the scene silently.

records.title: 3. Rescue paths for red/yellow action elements
records.text:
## 3. Rescue paths for red/yellow action elements
- **Fights/multi-person action:** never one long choreography. Decompose into **attack–reaction beats as separate short clips** (attack = clip, reaction = clip), characters locked via references; the EDIT is the fight choreography. Write contacts + settling per beat (video-prompting ch. 14).
- **Stunt that will not generate → shoot it yourself [H-off, P24]:** two bodies in constant contact over a prop (a struggle for a gun in a car: limbs fused, weapon vanishing) would not converge in text; the feature-film fix was stunt performers in a real car filmed on a phone, fed as MOTION reference — the model laid the cast, interior and light over it. One day of phone footage instead of a week of iterations; the only place a text-to-video-only production stepped outside its rule (production-pipeline ch. 8 phone-shot blocking).
- **Dance/choreography move by move [H-off, P48]:** "'dances' means nothing to Seedance" — write the moves: "two head nods, shoulders rolling one at a time, a knee dip, a finger snap, a quarter spin at the door"; per cut one register ("slow head bob left and right" · "sharp footwork, skips, stomps, quick weight shifts" · "locking style, arms snapping into frozen geometric poses" · "wide arms, shoulder isolations, stopping on the beat"); the track as timing input (video-prompting ch. 14b).
- **Vehicles/wheels:** hide wheel rotation — night/rain (motivated motion blur), framing above wheel height, parallel tracking (wheel detail unreadable), cockpit coverage; wheel close-ups only as short beats with water/mud eruption as distraction.
- **Subject vs. camera motion:** never combine opposing directions (subject runs right + dolly-in = mush) — one motion direction dominates per shot.
- **Animals:** short single beats, no long behavior chains; image reference instead of species name for fantasy/hybrid creatures.
- **Moving crowds:** multi-variant sheet + crowd in mid/background layer only; foreground extras directed individually.
- **Crowd scale — never a number, always three layers [H-off, P25]:** "the prompt never says show a thousand samurai": one sharp warrior up front, a dense crowd behind him, silhouettes fading into the mist — about 40 soldiers read clearly and the brain fills in the rest. Pair with the fog cap (§2) and silhouette classes. A synchronised army drop-into-stance is a legitimate held ENDING STATE (formation reads as drilled, not as animation — the async rule applies to individuals, video-prompting ch. 12).
- **Degradation looks as rescue style:** VHS/CCTV/16mm grain has built-in fault tolerance — a footage format (style-control §6b) is a legitimate rescue for risk shots.

records.title: 4. Format matrix (what each look forgives)
records.text:
## 4. Format matrix (what each look forgives)
| Format | Fit | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Pixar/stylized 3D** | **Excellent — safest "cinema look"** | Stylization absorbs physics/texture errors; audiences expect no real physics. Look definition and evidence: pixar-look.md |
| High-action anime | Excellent | Speed lines/held poses mask model weaknesses |
| UGC/found footage | Excellent | Degradation hides artifacts |
| Photoreal drama, static dialogue | Good with discipline | Reverse plates + framing recycling mandatory |
| Flat 2D/limited animation | Hard | Punishes every wobble; simple motion only (style-control §5b) |
| Photoreal action with hero physics | Hardest | Plan rescue cuts per risk shot |

records.title: 5. Camera & cut rules
records.text:
## 5. Camera & cut rules
One camera verb per shot · fixed camera grammar per sequence in the shot table's Framing column; in the prompt only the one camera line where continuity across cuts demands it (12h element 5 / OPTICS+CAMERA) · lock positions by previs/clay render or plate, not by the take's opener — the establishing wide is a SHOT, not the opening beat, for crowd scale and stylized 3D (§2 wide-shot row); a plain photoreal two-hander may still open wide · never cross the axis (state it) · match cuts across scene borders bind on identical motion · hectic cuts exactly at hard motion = model hiding failure → reject take.

records.title: 5b. Lighting consistency: directional light vs. whole-body brightness [PP]
records.text:
## 5b. Lighting consistency: directional light vs. whole-body brightness [PP]
🟢 **Directional light and whole-body brightness adjectives on the same object are mutually exclusive.** Once a prompt demands a light DIRECTION, phase, or partial shading on an object (moon phase, backlight, terminator, half-shadow, rim light), never pair it with global brightness words for that same object — "bright", "fully lit", "luminous", "brightly glowing", "strong contrast". Whole-body words grab the entire object and override the phase: documented failure — a moon prompted with a side-lit phase (lit side toward a low sun, shadow side away) PLUS "clear bright lunar disc" rendered as a fully lit disc with no shadow side, physically inconsistent with the stated sun position.
🟢 **Instead:** describe light exclusively per direction — which side/surface is lit, which lies in shadow. If contrast is wanted, name the contrast of the LIT EDGE against the background ("the lit edge stands out against the black sky"), never the brightness of the whole object.
Memory hook: a phase instruction only wins when no contradicting brightness word stands next to it.

records.title: 6. Model quick profiles (for shot assignment)
records.text:
## 6. Model quick profiles (for shot assignment)
**Prompt technique is a project decision (SKILL rule 4); the containers per model are in ch. 21 / 12g.** Seedance 2.0 know-how holds on 2.5 unless a documented difference says otherwise (video-prompting ch. 14b table: timestamps, multi-view references, action wording, constraint words).

records.title: 6. Model quick profiles (for shot assignment)
records.text:
Per-shot decision rule: Seedance 2.5 whenever references, edits, long takes or choreography matter; Seedance 2.0 for simple UGC-realism shots and drafts (production-pipeline ch. 11); H3 for 2D/anime line quality, quoted on-screen text or cheap hosted 2K; Veo 3.1 for photoreal environments; Kling 3.0 for directed movement in stylized-photoreal; Grok for stylized fast tests; Flux 3 Video for calm dialogue. Ties → the motion ladder; name the pick in the slate.
| Model | Strengths | Limits / slop accent |
|---|---|---|
| **Seedance 2.0** | resolution: native 4K last documented on Higgsfield under HF-CS4-HIST@2026-08 (platforms-models ch. 13 archive, unverified since — working assumption 1080p until the live output dropdown shows 4K), 15-s takes, cost/quality champion, UGC home turf | Peak at take end fails; plastic skin tendency; [P56] keeps 2.0 for SIMPLE shots where 4K crispness matters (Aug 2026), but its physics and reference placement lost to 2.5 in every staged test |
| **Seedance 2.5** | 30-s takes (extension chains ≈60 s; 180 s beta is Dreamina-only), 50 refs (30i/10v/10a incl. @Clay Render + voice refs), **edit suite** (region/timestamp-scoped, camera-perspective, green-screen, subject-swap, audio-category — video-prompting ch. 14b), complex continuous camera, choreography with weight, in-shot transformations, multi-stage emotions, reflections, skin texture; best adherence with eight references and best emotion progression in the [P56] four-model test | ~2× price; resolution platform-dependent (Higgsfield 1080p since Aug 2026, one practitioner aggregator run at 1080p/30 s with sound, Sep 2026 [P19], Dreamina 480/720p; 4K on Higgsfield only via Upscale / FLUX 3 Video Upscaler per HF-WEB@2026-09-04 — no native 2K/4K verified; other surfaces: read the live form); real-face references are rejected by most hosted surfaces (moderation plan + face-grid fallback: post-audio-legal ch. 20); baked-in artifacts → upscaler; logic decays with take length; in-frame text still broken |
| **Veo 3.1** | Polished cinematic realism, environments, ingredients/first-last/extension | Physics-correct motion fights stylized looks |
| **Kling 3.0** | Directed movement, multi-shot storytelling, strongest stylization of the photoreal class, MotionControl | Style drift per generation (ch. 21 sequence rule); 2–3× rerolls for anime |
| **MiniMax H3 (Hailuo 3)** | 2D/anime line quality, official quoted-text channel + stable UI/text 🟡, LoRA style lock, physics (passes glass test), cheap, native 2K hosted, Ref2VA omni mode (9i/3v/3a), V2V edits without masks, L2VA (events before the image) | Plastic under realism demands [P43, P56 — plastic tears, skin worse than 2.x], audio loops 🟡 [W], one beat per shot [MM-off], weak IP moderation 🟡 [W] (legally risky — practitioners market the local build for "copyrighted and unrestricted" content, post-audio-legal ch. 20); [P56] also logged an unprompted camera move in a static-camera test and a screen-direction flip between shots, while lyric text in a music-video test rendered cleanly |
| **Flux 3 Video** (BFL; on OpenArt and Higgsfield, Aug 2026) 🟡 [P56] | 20-s takes, 1080p, native audio; the most natural DIALOGUE voice of the four models in the test and a strong documentary / interview register; sharp faces and close-ups | Weakest prompt adherence in the test (camera-move chains and staged actions dropped), takes reference images literally (a white sheet background carried into the scene), comic drift, fast unintelligible delivery — route calm dialogue-heavy shots, not choreography; priced above 2.5 on OpenArt; no syntax profile here — write it in the project's technique (SKILL rule 4), camera mid-prompt as on Seedance (12g), with the platform's live docs as the receipt |
| **Grok Imagine 1.5** | Native stylization bias (anime/cartoon/art-directed), fast, cheap, native audio | Drifts cartoonish on photoreal intent; negatives unreliable; resolution: ch. 21 Grok line |
| **Wan 2.6/2.7/3.0** (open-weight family; version per surface — Higgsfield: Wan 3.0 / 3.0 Prime, OpenArt: WAN 2.7 and a WAN 3.0 page, 2026-09-04) | Open-weight, LoRA, multi-shot, reference-to-video, 1080p, budget | Less polished than top class |
| **PixVerse** | Fast social iteration, transition mode | Not for long-form/high-end. No syntax profile here — if a PixVerse prompt is requested, say so and write it in the project's technique (SKILL rule 4), camera mid-prompt as on Seedance (12g), with the platform's live docs as the receipt |

records.title: 6. Model quick profiles (for shot assignment)
records.text: ⚠️ **Resolution/duration cells above are capability notes, not receipts.** Before any resolution or duration goes into a Render Slate `Settings` row: apply the platform-ui-workflows.md output-configuration rule — use the LOWER verified value for the surface (Higgsfield: 1080p / 30 s under HF-CS4@2026-09-04), ask the user to read the live model/plan dropdown, and write `unverified` in the slate if neither is possible. Never write a reference key you did not check.

records.title: 6. Model quick profiles (for shot assignment)
records.text:
No universal winner: run the motion ladder (post-audio-legal ch. 19) per style/model before committing.
⚠️ **Retired/wound down — do not plan pipelines on:** Sora 2 (wind-down 2026) · Runway Gen-3 family (retired Jul 2026) · OpenArt Workflows (sunset Jan 2026). Current surfaces + retirement tracking: platform-ui-workflows.md.

records.title: Source registry — practitioner protocols [P] and evidence tags
records.text: Rules in the source-tagged reference files carry a source tag and a confidence label; this is the canonical legend (each reference file points here). Official tags ([H-off], [BD-off], [G-off], [K-off], [xAI-off], [MM-off], [F], [R-off], [OAI-off], [A]) point to vendor documentation; [W] to multi-source web research; [PP] to first-party production-session evidence. This file itemizes the practitioner protocols so a [P] number is checkable.

records.title: Source registry — practitioner protocols [P] and evidence tags
records.text:
**Tag legend (canonical):**
- 🟢 verified — multi-source, official, or production-proven · 🟡 plausible — single-source or untested · 🔴 marketing claim — verify yourself · ⚠️ source conflict — the sentence next to the marker settles it (SKILL.md Precedence).
- [PP] first-party production-session evidence · [W] multi-source web research · [A] platform academy docs.
- **Source tiers — claims are not weighted one to one.** Tier 1: the model vendor's own documentation and first-party measurement [PP]. Tier 2: platform tutorials and established practitioners (YouTubers, bloggers, filmmakers). Tier 3: single finds in social posts, videos and sites — often the home of a specific trick, but in a frontal contradiction with a vendor statement they do not win without striking proof; this keeps engagement-farming know-how out of the skill. A contradiction is settled by tracing BOTH sides: a canon line worded too generally is narrowed; evidence on both sides makes both variants admissible, one per prompt; a canon line whose evidence cannot be found is outdated. Know-how for an older model version holds on the newer one until version-specific information says otherwise.
- [H-off] Higgsfield official · [BD-off] ByteDance official (read in the original since 2026-09-18: 2.5 prompt guide, 2.5 tutorial, 2.0 series guide, `sd25-pe` skill, Seed launch blog; earlier entries via verified reproductions) · [G-off] Google official (Veo docs, Cloud blog) · [K-off] Kling official user guides · [xAI-off] xAI official docs · [MM-off] MiniMax official H3 prompt-writing guides · [F] fal.ai official · [R-off] Runway official · [OAI-off] OpenAI cookbook/docs · [X-ext] community skill, partially officially confirmed.
- [G2] / [NB] GPT Image (2 / 2.5) / Nano Banana guide clusters · [G2-gallery] GPT Image official prompt-gallery patterns.
- [P1–P69] practitioner and vendor-thread protocols — itemized in the table below; P1–P16 are not itemized and count as single-source 🟡.
- Unlabeled text (SKILL.md, workflows, production-bible, film-craft, director-recipes, genre-baselines, worked-example) is house doctrine and ranks as 🟢.

The announcement page was read first-party on 2026-09-09 (live read, SKILL rule 17). Two evidence classes to keep apart: the **API model IDs + parameters** and the **surface facts** (rollout to all ChatGPT/Work/Codex tiers; Sketch/Templates/on-image comments/shareable prompts; C2PA metadata + invisible watermark on outputs → post-audio-legal ch. 20) are 🟢 [OAI-off] (recheck the live app for exact controls); the **capability-improvement claims** (edit locality, identity/style hold, ~50% speed, world knowledge, transparency, less style drift) are first-party but vendor 🔴 — production-A/B-verify before promoting to 🟢, and they do NOT retroactively update the [PP]/[P17]/[P20]/[P41] findings established on the `gpt-image-2` generation. records.title: Source registry — practitioner protocols [P] and evidence tags
records.text: **First-party production session 2026-09-11 [PP] — figure-less dark exterior location anchor, `gpt-image-2` generation.** Eight consecutive runs on ONE stylized, figure-less, dark exterior set anchor; every finding below is measured or read off a direct run-to-run comparison, not inferred. What it contributed: **word budget as a hard, model+version-scoped rule** (1259-word prompt → flat-ground and uneven-tower instructions present in full and both ignored; same content at ~300 words landed both on the next run) and the **refinement ratchet** as the named agent-side failure mode with its replace-don't-append counter-rule → style-control §2, image-model-logic 24b item 8 · the **counterweight sentence** (exceptions described without the class default → a field of nothing but exceptions; one leading sentence about the normal state delivered both) → 24a · the **Avoid-list budget** (lists grown to ~35 entries displacing the scene description) and the **protected world-rule subset** (a trim dropped "sky gradient" and the banned twilight gradient returned immediately — sky median 12 at the top vs 35 above the horizon) → 24f, pixar-look §9 item 5 · **quantifiers replaced by a mass noun that carries the disorder** → 24e · the **§9 faceting scoping bug** (an unscoped silhouette refinement read as a global material instruction → facetted low-poly floor) → pixar-look §9 refinements · **one-sentence reference roles** beating paragraph-length "Do NOT copy" blocks (150–200 words out of a 300-word budget, no better binding) and the **literal `@token` rule** (an attached image addressed as "the reference image" did not bind) → style-control §7 Rules 0b/1b · **prompt-stated aspect ratio does not set the canvas** ("ultra-wide 16:9" in the prompt, square output) → style-control §2 layout rule. ⚠️ Provenance: measured on the `gpt-image-2` generation, which GPT Image 2.5 supersedes; the mechanisms are model-general but the NUMBERS are not — re-measure the budget and the behaviour on 2.5 before treating them as current (the 2.5 improvement claims remain 🔴, see the refresh note above). Seven of these findings became checks 1–7 of the still-prompt lint, image-model-logic 24i (check 8 came from the 2026-09-14 session).

records.title: Source registry — practitioner protocols [P] and evidence tags
records.text: **First-party production session 2026-09-14 [PP] — division of labour and the Caption Spine; Seedance 2.5 in Higgsfield Cinema Studio, 720p, 10 s, `t2v`, 0–2 references.** Context: a stylized-3D short, ~30 takes over four weeks, prompted in the ch. 12 block structure as the skill prescribed it at the time (v3.3) (1,100–1,300 words, all ● blocks, POSITIVE LOCKS, FOV/Kelvin/distances, a `Do not copy` line per reference) at roughly 80 % rejects, with structural rejects — wrong scale, camera morph, event missing or wrong, reference fighting — in every iteration round, typically P01–P04 plus an edit per take. Control test on one take: a ~250-word prompt in the Caption Spine shape (title sentence · STYLE line · character line · timecode beats · "End with …" · one prohibition sentence), four runs, one new variable each — (1) no references, (2) + figure sheet, (3) + location plate as style reference, (4) + one camera line. Findings, all read off the four runs: the same beat structure (medium → insert → return/wide) in four of four, cuts at 5.4–5.7 s and 7.8–8.1 s — reproducible at structure level, polish-only variance (roll class, no iteration) → **the Caption Spine as technique A of the prompting-technique menu** (video-prompting ch. 12h, SKILL rule 4 — chosen per project with the director, never one-size-fits-all) and **the economy doctrine with the division of labour** (SKILL.md, after Role) · every reference did exactly its one job with no `Do not copy` line in the prompt → the one-job reference sentence (12h; SKILL rule 5; style-control §7 Rule 1) · one camera line ("locked off, low, at the height of …, looking across … toward …; the camera does not move") made the insert cut return to the same axis — continuity those block prompts had prescribed five blocks for and regularly missed → the optional single camera line (12h) · a lead's scale that had failed for weeks under metre, degree and body-length statements landed in the first run on one relational half-sentence ("his back level with the top step") → **scale and distance as relations, SKILL rule 7**; 12c/12d reframed as look controls, never defaults; image-model-logic 24b item 5 / 24d / 24i check 8; production-pipeline ch. 3 sheet sizes; the shot-table `Framing` column without degrees · contrast diagnosis of the failed block prompts (scale stated up to six times, camera four, one prop's damage five, everything a third time in POSITIVE LOCKS; 10–30 negations per prompt; numbers in prose — 63°, 2800K, 9000K, "four body-lengths", "a hand's width", half-second stamps; reader-addressed meta sentences; rate instructions; references attached and then told what not to transfer) → the lint measures (12h; SKILL checklist step 5, slate `Lint` row) and the remove → change → add repair order (SKILL rule 15; W5; W8). Remaining faults were roll-class polish, not structure. Provenance: one model (Seedance 2.5), one surface (Cinema Studio, 720p), one look (stylized 3D), four control runs on one take — the doctrine generalizes to the class by mechanism (a specialist model over-instructed averages the instructions, SKILL rule 15) and is house doctrine (🟢) for every video model; first-party runs exist so far only on Seedance 2.5 — log the first run on another model against this entry. Nothing project-specific is carried: character, location and shot names in the skill's examples are the fictional LIGHTCAT set.

records.title: Story Structures: Dramaturgical Containers (Ch. 23)
records.text: # Story Structures: Dramaturgical Containers (Ch. 23)

records.title: Story Structures: Dramaturgical Containers (Ch. 23)
records.text: **Contents — read only the part the spine, checklist or routing row names:** 23a story intake gate (run first) · 23b classic containers · 23c alternative containers · 23d format-specific containers · 23e masters' rules (applied as lints) · 23f choosing and mixing · 23g the causal chain and the mandatory change lint.

records.title: Story Structures: Dramaturgical Containers (Ch. 23)
records.text: Tags and confidence labels: legend in sources.md. The story comes from the USER — this file never replaces it (candidate-synopsis ideation only when asked, production-pipeline ch. 2). It exists for the moment after intake: the user has a story seed, and it needs a dramaturgical container before treatment work starts (production-pipeline ch. 2). Same seed, different container, different film: a Simpsons episode, a Python film, Star Wars, and a Tarantino picture could all start from "someone loses everything over a small lie" and land in four different worlds. Offer containers like recipes: max 2 candidates, one line each, the user picks.

records.title: 23a. Story intake gate (run BEFORE offering structures)
records.text: ## 23a. Story intake gate (run BEFORE offering structures)

records.title: 23a. Story intake gate (run BEFORE offering structures)
records.text:
Check the user's story for filmable completeness — a lint, not a writing seminar:
protagonist + concrete want? · engine (conflict, question, or tension that pulls forward)? · a turn (something changes irreversibly)? · an ending (even a direction)? · whose POV? · fits the target length? · premise — one sentence "X leads to Y" that the ending proves (23e Egri; bible section B2)?
Gaps → targeted questions, grouped into the single intake message (SKILL Workflow 1). A gap the director leaves open, or a "just do it" / batch run: deliver 1–2 options labeled `PROPOSAL A/B — not canon` inside the deliverable (SKILL rule 14) — never fill a gap silently, never more than two options. A complete-enough story proceeds to container choice; structure gaps found later are paid in rendered takes, not in rewritten pages — catch them here.

records.title: 23b. Classic containers
records.text: ## 23b. Classic containers

records.title: 23b. Classic containers
records.text: **Hollywood three-act (Syd Field's paradigm)** — Shape: setup (world + want, inciting incident ~10–15%) → **Plot Point I** (the event that flings into act 2) → confrontation (rising obstacles, midpoint reversal, all-is-lost) → **Plot Point II** (triggers the ending — Wilder's second-act curtain) → resolution (climax, new equilibrium). Beat-sheet refinements (Save-the-Cat-style percentages) are optional scaffolding on top. Fits: the default for narrative 5 min+; audiences parse it without effort. Signals: clear goal, clear opposition. AI note: act structure maps 1:1 onto sequence planning; the midpoint reversal is the natural place for a look/palette shift (film-craft color arc).

records.title: 23b. Classic containers
records.text: **Hero's journey (monomyth)** — Shape: departure (ordinary world, call, refusal, mentor, threshold) → initiation (trials, ordeal, reward) → return (transformed, elixir). Star Wars is the canonical execution. Fits: myth, adventure, fantasy, transformation arcs, family animation (want-vs-need maps onto it). Signals: a world to cross into; a protagonist who must change. AI note: the threshold crossings are your biggest set-piece/look changes — budget new location assets per world, not per scene.

records.title: 23b. Classic containers
records.text: **Five-act (Freytag/Shakespeare)** — Shape: exposition → rising action → climax at the CENTER → falling action → catastrophe/denouement. Fits: tragedies, rise-AND-fall arcs (Scorsese pairing), prestige-drama episodes. Signals: the fall is the point; the peak belongs in the middle. AI note: the long back half needs its own visual escalation plan — decay dramaturgy (grade, light) carries what plot repetition would bore.

records.title: 23c. Alternative containers
records.text: ## 23c. Alternative containers

records.title: 23c. Alternative containers
records.text: **Kishōtenketsu (ki–shō–ten–ketsu)** — Shape: introduction → development (deepening, no escalating conflict) → TWIST (a recontextualizing element, not an antagonist) → reconciliation. The East Asian four-act; Ghibli's slice-of-life films live here (Kiki: vignettes of settling in, then the crisis-twist, then quiet resolution). Fits: quiet wonder, slice-of-life, family, essay-adjacent fiction. Signals: no villain, no race — the story wants to breathe. AI note: a gift for generation — calm held shots, "ma" beats, no action chains; pair with Miyazaki/Ozu recipes.

records.title: 23c. Alternative containers
records.text: **Nonlinear / chapter structure** — Shape: story order ≠ plot order; chapters or interleaved timelines whose MEANING assembles at the end (Tarantino: shuffled chapters; Nolan: parallel lines converging). Fits: crime, puzzles, ensemble webs. Signals: the reveal of HOW pieces connect is the payoff. AI note: generation order is free anyway — the risk is continuity per timeline (ledger mandatory, post-audio-legal ch. 19); label every shot with its timeline; the audience needs one identifying cue per timeline (palette, ratio or grain — style-control era looks).

records.title: 23c. Alternative containers
records.text: **Mosaic / fragment (associative)** — Shape: moments, not scenes, linked by emotional association and voice-over; time dissolves (Malick). Fits: memory, grief, love-and-loss, poetic essay. Signals: the user's material is feelings and images more than events. AI note: the most generation-friendly container of all — short independent clips, no continuity chains, VO carries coherence (no lip-sync).

records.title: 23c. Alternative containers
records.text: **Circular / bookend** — Shape: ending returns to the opening image/scene with transformed meaning. Cheap to build, strong closure; combines with any container above. AI note: generate opening and closing from the SAME anchor still with changed light/grade — a controlled, prompt-friendly rhyme.

records.title: 23c. Alternative containers
records.text: **Vignette / anthology** — Shape: self-contained segments under one theme, world, or object; optional frame story; runners/callbacks stitch. Fits: omnibus shorts, sketch features, anthology horror. AI note: resets continuity per segment — ideal when asset drift risk is high; each segment can even own a different recipe (declare it, don't drift into it).

records.title: 23c. Alternative containers
records.text: **A24 / elevated-genre dramaturgy** 🟡 — critic-distilled, not an official studio doc; the studio's actual "concept" is business-side (director-driven, low budget, creative control, strangeness preserved — never sand it down). The narrative pattern across its catalog: a GENRE CONTAINER carries a psychological core as metaphor (possession film = inheritance of family trauma; folk horror = grief seeking a container); slow-burn pacing with anticipatory dread instead of jump-beats; tone/vibe as the organizing principle over plot mechanics; exposition near zero — interiority externalized in images and behavior (show-don't-tell as doctrine); tonal blends licensed (comedy inside horror, dread inside romance); endings resolve the EMOTION, not necessarily the plot — ambiguity is allowed to stand. Fits: psychological horror/drama, festival-style shorts, auteur pieces. Signals: the user names a feeling or wound first and a genre second. AI note: slow-burn = long held shots (extension chains, reroll budget); the metaphor layer lives in production design and recurring motifs — put the motif objects into the asset order from day one; pair with Kubrick/Lynch/Villeneuve structures + Young/Fraser light.

records.title: 23d. Format-specific containers
records.text: ## 23d. Format-specific containers

records.title: 23d. Format-specific containers
records.text: **Sitcom episode (Simpsons shape)** — Shape: cold-open gag (often unrelated) → act 1 establishes a premise that PIVOTS into the real story (the famous misdirect: the episode is never about how it starts) → A-plot braided with B-plot (C optional) → escalation → resolution that RESETS the status quo. ~22 min native, scales down. Fits: episodic comedy, animated series. AI note: the reset is an asset strategy — recurring sets/cast amortize across episodes (production bible ch. 22a rule 6); the act-1 pivot licenses a mid-episode location/look change.

records.title: 23d. Format-specific containers
records.text:
**Series formats (TV & YouTube): episodic universe vs. serialized film** — decide the pole FIRST; it is the most consequential format decision a series makes:
- **Episodic (stable universe):** every episode self-contained; the status quo resets; the universe changes at most at SEASON boundaries. Each episode carries its own complete container (sitcom shape, case-of-the-week three-act); viewers can enter anywhere. AI note: the economically ideal series form — cast sheets, sets, and trained identities amortize across episodes while the continuity risk RESETS per episode; universe changes are season-boundary decisions, recorded in the project bible (ch. 22a rule 6).
- **Serialized (the overlong film):** one continuous arc chopped into episodes — plan it AS a film first (any 23b/23c container), then cut episode boundaries at reveal/reversal points; each episode still needs its own micro-shape: entry hook (or recap device), internal rise, an OUT (cliffhanger or resonance beat). Viewers must enter at episode 1. AI note: the hardest continuity class — wardrobe, props, injuries, time-of-day carry ACROSS episodes; shot board and continuity ledger span the whole season (one bible, no per-episode reset). Generation order stays free — placement is fixed in the paper plan, exactly like scattered soundbites.
- **The hybrid (standard TV pattern):** episodic A-plot + a serialized B-arc that surfaces in a few beats per episode and takes over in finales; the B-arc is a season-level container (usually a reveal ladder) — track its beats in the bible or they drift.
- **Anthology series (the third pole):** every episode its own story, cast, even look — the universe is a THEME, tone, or frame device (the brand is the continuity). Each episode picks its own container and may pick its own recipe; only the frame device, title grammar, and one tonal contract persist. AI note: zero cross-episode continuity burden AND full per-episode asset freedom — the format where AI series production is cheapest per minute; the bible shrinks to the tonal contract + frame device. A **limited series** is simply the serialized pole with a fixed ending — plan it strictly as one film, never leave the arc open.
- **YouTube series:** the episode is a retention object — hook inside the first 15–30 seconds (no slow cold open unless the channel brand carries it), typical 8–15-min bodies, an out that hands off to the next episode (end-screen logic). Branding — intro, framing, palette, the channel's style anchor — IS the universe marker. Episodic entries win discovery (the platform serves single episodes to new viewers); serialized needs a recap device for enter-anywhere viewers. Title/thumbnail promise is decided at SCRIPT stage, and the episode must pay it — an unpaid thumbnail is a broken contract, not marketing.

records.title: 23d. Format-specific containers
records.text: **Sketch logic (Python shape)** — Shape: one absurd premise escalated relentlessly; NO resolution owed — exit at the peak, interrupt, or break the form itself (abrupt endings, intertitles, animation inserts). A sketch FILM is anthology + runners/callbacks wearing a loose quest frame. Fits: absurdist comedy, sketch features. Signals: the joke is the engine; a plot would slow it down. AI note: form-breaks legitimize model discontinuity (the ZAZ/Brooks recipe's Python variant is the visual grammar); every sketch is a fresh generation context — cheap.

records.title: 23d. Format-specific containers
records.text: **Short-film dramaturgy** — Shape: ONE situation, ONE turn; enter at the latest possible moment, leave at the earliest; ending lands as sting, reversal, or image-answer. Under ~3 min: a single reversal is the whole story — a compressed three-act is a feature synopsis, not a short. Fits: social clips, festival shorts, spec pieces. AI note: the turn shot deserves the reroll budget; everything else is economy.

records.title: 23d. Format-specific containers
records.text: **Documentary spines** (argument structure — interview production mechanics in production-pipeline ch. 7b, look defaults in genre-baselines) — Pick ONE: essay/thesis (claim unfolded in chapters — Wenders/Malick tone), chronological/biographical (era grammar as chapters), investigative reveal ladder (staged revelations, true-crime pacing — withhold like a thriller), observational arc (vérité: a situation ripens on its own clock), portrait mosaic (facets, not timeline). AI note: the spine decides the edit BEFORE generation — B-roll is generated to prove the narration, so lock narration first (audio-first, ch. 18 logic); disclosure rules ch. 20 apply throughout.

records.title: 23d. Format-specific containers
records.text: **Interview dramaturgy** (the layer between spine and staging — production mechanics in production-pipeline ch. 7b) — Five working rules: **(1) Paper edit first:** in AI production the transcript IS the script — every soundbite is written before anything is generated (audio-first), so the film's argument is built at transcript level, not discovered in the edit bay; write answers AS soundbites (one thought each, cuttable at both ends). **Cut order ≠ interview order:** a good interview is never obliged to run chronologically as conducted — soundbites are placement-free building blocks, scattered across acts wherever the argument needs them (the "last" answer may open the film), and the emotional arc (composed → cracking → silence) is AUTHORED from bites, not inherited from a conversation. Two crafts make that work: phrase every bite self-contained (the question folded into the answer, no "as I said before", no dangling referents), and assign each bite its film position in the paper edit BEFORE generation. **(2) Voice functions:** cast interviewees like characters — witness (was there), expert (explains), adversary (holds the counter-position), heart (the emotional center); every voice earns its screen time through its function, and no voice serves two functions in the same act. **(3) The conflict engine:** contradiction editing — opposing answers cut against each other CREATE the debate (opposing look sides, production-pipeline ch. 7b, make it spatial); conflicting accounts of one event are the doc's Rashomon container. **(4) Hook and reveal placement:** cold-open on the strongest soundbite as the film's promise; withhold the key witness or the decisive answer the way a thriller withholds the monster (reveal ladder); Mamet's three questions apply to interview segments too — a segment no one needs RIGHT NOW is B-roll fodder, not an act beat. **(5) The held silence:** the emotional peak of an interview is the pause, the swallow, the look away — hold the face and do NOT cut to B-roll there; it is the one moment the B-roll escape is forbidden (and the shot that earns the reroll budget, production-pipeline ch. 7b).

records.title: 23d. Format-specific containers
records.text:
**Online-native short formats** (where AI generation is used heaviest) — four working shapes, all governed by retention dramaturgy: hook inside 0–3 s (visual question or mid-action entry — never an establishing shot), re-hook every 20–30 s (new open loop before the last one closes), payoff that answers the opening promise, loop-friendly ending where the platform rewards rewatches.
- **Vertical micro-drama serial** (ReelShort-class: 60–90-s episodes, 50–100 per season, 9:16): melodrama escalation with a cliffhanger EVERY episode end and a reversal every 3–5 episodes; paywall/subscribe gates sit right after the biggest cliffhangers — dramaturgy and monetization are one system. Staging for 9:16: tight singles, faces huge, one action per frame, verticals in production design; wides barely read. AI note: the highest-volume AI series format — plan like the serialized pole (paper plan for the season, boundaries at cliffs), produce in batches per location; the tight-single grammar plays directly into identity-lock strengths.
- **Faceless VO formats** (explainer, listicle, story-time, doc-style channels): the biggest AI channel class — VO spine + generated B-roll, no on-camera human, no lip-sync anywhere. Structure: hook → promise → segmented payoffs (each segment its own mini-loop) → final payoff + handoff. Production is the doc path (production-pipeline ch. 7b B-roll logic + 23d paper edit) minus interviews.
- **Skit / POV character series:** a recurring character or POV premise in 20–60-s episodic bites — the episodic pole in micro form: character sheet + voice profile amortize, every skit self-contained, the character IS the brand. Formats: recurring-situation escalation, POV-of-X, character-reacts.
- **Part-series (Part 1/2/3):** one short story chopped at its strongest withhold — a serialized micro-arc riding discovery: part 1 must work as pure hook alone, each part re-establishes in one shot (no recap text), the final part pays everything. AI note: generate all parts as ONE production (one continuity context), release chopped.

records.title: 23d. Format-specific containers
records.text: **Music video / commercial** — concept-repetition-escalation, beat-locked; full defaults live in the Music film and Commercial/Ad baselines (genre-baselines.md) — this file only reminds: these formats may skip narrative entirely; ONE committed visual concept outperforms a compressed plot.

records.title: 23e. Masters' rules (sourced pearls — apply as lints, don't recite)
records.text: ## 23e. Masters' rules (sourced pearls — apply as lints, don't recite)

records.title: 23e. Masters' rules (sourced pearls — apply as lints, don't recite)
records.text: 🟢 **The causation test (Parker/Stone, NYU writing seminar 2014):** take the outline beats — if "and then" fits between two beats, "you're fucked; you've got something pretty boring." Between every pair of beats must fit **"therefore"** or **"but"** (consequence or reversal). Run it mechanically over every outline and treatment at the script stage (production-pipeline ch. 2); an "and then" seam is a cut candidate or a missing turn. Full causal doctrine + the MANDATORY change lint: ch. 23g.

records.title: 23e. Masters' rules (sourced pearls — apply as lints, don't recite)
records.text: 🟢 **The three scene questions (Mamet, memo to The Unit writers):** every scene must answer — **who wants what? · what happens if they don't get it? · why now?** A scene that answers none is information, not drama — and "the audience tunes in for drama, not information": move exposition into conflict or cut it. Use as the scene-level lint after the causation test passes at beat level.

records.title: 23e. Masters' rules (sourced pearls — apply as lints, don't recite)
records.text: 🟢 **Wilder's rules (via Cameron Crowe, Conversations with Wilder) — the five with teeth here:** a clean line of action for the protagonist (one traceable want through the whole film) · **a third-act problem is really a first-act problem** (fix setup, not climax) · the Lubitsch 2+2: let the audience add it up — never show the four (elegance = hidden plot mechanics; ellipsis is also the AI rescue tool, so this pearl pays twice) · the second-act curtain triggers the ending (plant the trigger consciously) · act three builds, then STOPS — don't hang around after the last event. **Plus the VO law:** voice-over must ADD to the image, never describe what the audience already sees — the binding rule for every VO-driven container (mosaic, Scorsese momentum, doc spines).

records.title: 23e. Masters' rules (sourced pearls — apply as lints, don't recite)
records.text: 🟢 **Non-submersible units (Kubrick):** design the film as ~6–8 indestructible sequence blocks — each one so strong it survives on its own — and keep the connective tissue between them minimal. For AI production this is doctrine, not metaphor: it IS sequence-first planning (film-craft §8 sequence approach; production-pipeline ch. 2 stages) — invest story and reroll budget in the units, bridge between them with ellipsis.

records.title: 23e. Masters' rules (sourced pearls — apply as lints, don't recite)
records.text: 🟢 **The value turn (McKee, Story):** a scene earns its place only if a value charge FLIPS across it (safe→threatened, hope→despair, together→alone); no flip, no scene. The cutting corollary to Mamet's three questions — run both, they catch different failures.

records.title: 23e. Masters' rules (sourced pearls — apply as lints, don't recite)
records.text: 🟢 **The premise (Egri, The Art of Dramatic Writing):** one sentence — "X leads to Y" — that the ENDING proves. Settle it at intake; every container above is only the delivery mechanism for a proven premise, and an unprovable premise is the earliest, cheapest rewrite you will ever get.

records.title: 23e. Masters' rules (sourced pearls — apply as lints, don't recite)
records.text: (The cutting-room counterpart — Murch's Rule of Six, emotion above all — lives in film-craft §4.)

records.title: 23f. Choosing (and mixing)
records.text: ## 23f. Choosing (and mixing)

records.title: 23f. Choosing (and mixing)
records.text:
1. Intake gate first (23a) — an incomplete story fits no container.
2. Format + genre narrow the field (a 30-s spot never gets a hero's journey; a series gets the sitcom/series shape).
3. Offer max 2 containers with one-line rationale; the user picks — exactly like recipe choice, and usually BEFORE it (structure shapes the shot list more than the look does).
4. Containers mix like recipes: one dominant + one device (three-act + bookend; kishōtenketsu twist inside a sitcom B-plot). More than two = mush.
5. Record the choice in the production bible (style contract section) — structure is canon once approved.

records.title: 23g. The causal chain — doctrine and the mandatory change lint
records.text: ## 23g. The causal chain — doctrine and the mandatory change lint

records.title: 23g. The causal chain — doctrine and the mandatory change lint
records.text: Why this section is binding: episodic, causally disconnected plotting is the DOCUMENTED native failure mode of LLM writing (documented in the LLM-story-generation literature — sources.md; scaffolding systems exist precisely because raw LLM output adds events instead of causing them). Addition is cheaper than consequence for the model — so the lint below is not optional craft polish, it is the guard against the writer itself. An event without cause is story slop exactly as a guessed beat is prompt slop (SKILL rule 14).

records.title: The doctrine (sourced)
records.text:
### The doctrine (sourced)
🟢 **Plot IS causality** (Forster, Aspects of the Novel): "The king died and then the queen died" is a story; "the king died, and then the queen died of grief" is a plot — the difference is the whole craft.
🟢 **Propter hoc, not post hoc** (Aristotle, *Poetics*, §§9–10 of the treatise — an external citation, not a skill chapter): events must be "the consequence, necessary or probable, of the antecedents"; plots "in which the episodes succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence" are "the worst."
🟢 **The chain reaction** (McKee, Story): "motivated actions cause effects that in turn become the causes of yet other effects" — the inciting incident is "the primary cause for all that follows," rippling causally to the climax.
🟢 **Coincidence has a direction** (Coats/Pixar #19; McKee): "Coincidences to get characters into trouble are great; coincidences to get them out of it are cheating." McKee: bring coincidence in early so meaning can build from it, and "never use it to turn an ending. This is deus ex machina, the writer's greatest sin."
🟢 **Deus ex machina** (Aristotle ch. 15): the unraveling "must arise out of the plot itself." A rescue from outside the causal chain erases meaning and emotion. Narrow exception: deliberate, signaled comedy/parody (Life of Brian's spaceship) — the audience must be meant to SEE the device.
🟢 **Plant and payoff, both directions** (Chekhov, letter 1889): "One must never place a loaded rifle on the stage if it isn't going to go off. It's wrong to make promises you don't mean to keep." Every payoff was planted; every prominent plant pays off (payoff economics: film-craft §7).
🟢 **Consequence carries** (Swain, scene/sequel): a scene's outcome becomes a later scene's motivation (goal→conflict→disaster → reaction→dilemma→decision). An outcome nothing reacts to is a dead end.

records.title: The change lint — run on EVERY proposed script/treatment/beat change, before the proposal is offered
records.text:
### The change lint — run on EVERY proposed script/treatment/beat change, before the proposal is offered
A session that proposes a story change answers these eight in its own head first; a change that fails any of them is not offered, it is fixed or dropped. When offering the change, NAME its upstream cause and downstream consequence explicitly — a proposal that cannot state both is not ready.
1. **Therefore/but:** does the new/changed beat connect to its neighbors with "therefore" or "but" — or only "and then"?
2. **Propter hoc:** which prior ON-SCREEN event causes this one? None in the script = episodic addition.
3. **Coincidence direction:** does any coincidence create trouble (allowed, first half) or resolve it (forbidden)?
4. **Ending turn:** is the climax produced by the protagonist's prior choices and ESTABLISHED capabilities — no new character, object, ability, or luck after the midpoint?
5. **Plant/payoff ledger:** everything the change uses was planted; everything it plants will pay off. Flag orphans both ways.
6. **Deletion ripple:** if this beat were deleted, would a later beat stop making sense? No = causally disconnected — justify or cut.
7. **Scene turn + Mamet:** does the scene flip a value AND both advance the plot and stand alone (who wants what · what if they don't · why now)?
8. **Removal rewiring:** when the change REMOVES or alters a beat, every beat that was caused by it is re-wired or flagged — never left orphaned.
